title: Unauthorized minting via open setEducationHub when EducationHub is disabled
description: setEducationHub has a bootstrap pattern: if l.educationHub == address(0) it lets ANY caller set it with no authorization check; only overwriting a non-zero value requires the executor. OrgDeployer only calls setEducationHub when params.educationHubConfig.enabled is true (OrgDeployer.sol:495-497). When an org is deployed with EducationHub disabled, l.educationHub stays address(0) forever, so the unauthenticated branch remains reachable indefinitely. mint()'s authorization modifier _checkTaskOrEdu (lines 157-162) treats l.educationHub as a fully-privileged minter. An attacker can therefore point educationHub at an address they control and mint arbitrary ParticipationToken supply.
impact: Unlimited unauthorized token minting. Because HybridVoting's ERC20_BAL class reads live balanceOf (src/libs/HybridVotingCore.sol:147) as voting weight, minting arbitrary tokens grants arbitrary voting power, i.e. governance takeover of any org that deployed without EducationHub. This is reachable by a completely unprivileged external actor.
scenario: 1. Org is deployed via OrgDeployer with educationHubConfig.enabled = false; setEducationHub is never called, so l.educationHub == address(0). 2. Attacker deploys a contract MintBot. 3. Attacker calls token.setEducationHub(address(MintBot)) — passes because the l.educationHub == address(0) branch has no auth check. 4. MintBot calls token.mint(attacker, 2**200) — _checkTaskOrEdu passes since _msgSender() == l.educationHub. 5. Attacker now holds dominant balanceOf and controls all HybridVoting ERC20_BAL votes, passing malicious proposals through the Executor.
recommendation: Do not allow unauthenticated first-set. Either (a) require _msgSender() == l.executor for all setEducationHub/setTaskManager calls (have OrgDeployer call them as/through the executor, or during deploy while deployer is still authorized), or (b) gate the first-set on a one-shot deployer/initializer authorization that is consumed atomically at deploy. Given the deploy is atomic today, the cleanest fix is onlyExecutor plus wiring these setters inside initialize or an executor-authorized bootstrap. The identical bootstrap pattern in setTaskManager (lines 185-196) is only safe because OrgDeployer always calls it unconditionally at OrgDeployer.sol:494; harden both for defense in depth.
exploitReasoning: The bootstrap branch in setEducationHub is real and open: src/ParticipationToken.sol:202-204 — `if (l.educationHub == address(0)) { l.educationHub = eh; emit ...; }` with NO caller authorization; only the else-branch overwrite (line 206) requires `_msgSender() == l.executor`. initialize() (lines 97-134) never sets l.educationHub, so it defaults to address(0). OrgDeployer only calls setEducationHub at src/OrgDeployer.sol:495-497 guarded by `if (params.educationHubConfig.enabled)`; grep confirms this is the sole production caller. Therefore a disabled-EduHub org leaves l.educationHub == address(0) permanently, keeping the unauthenticated branch reachable forever. mint()'s guard _checkTaskOrEdu (lines 157-162) treats l.educationHub as a fully-privileged minter (`_msgSender() != l.educationHub` reverts, else allowed). The test testSetEducationHubOnceAndByExecutor (test/ParticipationToken.t.sol:60-66) proves intended behavior: the first call is made with NO vm.prank (arbitrary sender) and succeeds, only the overwrite is executor-gated. The developers' own fix script explicitly documents this: script/fixes/AddEducationHubDecentralPark.s.sol:42 "ParticipationToken.educationHub == 0x0 -> first-call setEducationHub is open." The governance-takeover leg is real too: ParticipationToken is wired as the ERC20_BAL voting asset (OrgDeployer.sol:716 votingParams.participationToken, hybridClasses), and HybridVotingCore.sol:147 reads live balanceOf(voter) as weight; _update auto-delegates to self on first mint (ParticipationToken.sol:360-362) so minted tokens count immediately. Note this differs from the identical setTaskManager pattern (lines 185-196) only because taskManager is ALWAYS set unconditionally at OrgDeployer.sol:494, closing that window atomically in the deploy tx — whereas the EduHub window never closes when disabled.
safetyReasoning: The exploit path is real and unmitigated. (1) ParticipationToken.setEducationHub (src/ParticipationToken.sol:198-210) has an open bootstrap branch: when l.educationHub == address(0) it sets the address with NO authorization check (only the overwrite branch at line 206 requires the executor). (2) initialize (lines 97-134) never sets l.educationHub, so it starts as address(0). (3) OrgDeployer.sol:494 ALWAYS calls setTaskManager (closing taskManager's identical bootstrap branch), but line 495-496 only calls setEducationHub when params.educationHubConfig.enabled is true. ModulesFactory.sol:113 likewise only deploys EducationHub when enabled. So an org deployed with EducationHub disabled leaves l.educationHub == address(0) permanently, keeping the unauthenticated branch reachable forever. (4) mint (line 295) is gated by onlyTaskOrEdu → _checkTaskOrEdu (lines 157-162), which authorizes any caller equal to l.educationHub with no hat requirement. An attacker calls setEducationHub(attackerContract), then attackerContract calls mint(to, huge) and it passes. (5) HybridVotingCore.sol:147 reads live balanceOf for ERC20_BAL voting weight, so minted supply becomes voting power (subject to the voter also holding the class hat per line 142 and clearing minBalance at line 148 — a secondary condition that constrains the attacker's own vote but not the unlimited-mint primitive, which can target any address including a colluding member-hatted holder).

title: Correct answer is trivially recoverable on-chain — any member auto-passes every module and farms tokens
description: Module answers are stored as answerHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(id, correctAnswer)) where correctAnswer is a uint8 (createModule line 206). completeModule (line 237) accepts the answer if keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(id), answer)) == m.answerHash. The module id is public (emitted in ModuleCreated, returned by nextModuleId/getModule) and correctAnswer has only 256 possible values (0..255). The hash preimage is therefore a 1-of-256 brute force. Any address holding a member hat can, for any module, iterate answer = 0..255, compute keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(id), a)), compare to the on-chain answerHash (readable via storage slot or by simply calling completeModule with each guess), and find the correct answer without ever reading the learning content. There is no commit-reveal, no per-user salt, and no secret entropy — the 'quiz' provides zero gating.
impact: The entire purpose of EducationHub (reward participation tokens for genuinely completing learning modules) is defeated. A member can auto-complete every module and mint the full payout (ParticipationToken.mint is authorized for EducationHub via onlyTaskOrEdu). Combined with permissionless-to-any-creator module creation, this is an unbounded token-farming vector for anyone with a member hat, diluting the org's participation token and its governance/reward weight.
scenario: 1. Creator creates module id=0 with createModule(title, hash, payout=5, correctAnswer=3); answerHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(0), uint8(3))). 2. Learner (any member) loops guesses off-chain: for a in 0..255 compute keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(0), uint8(a))); at a=3 it matches the on-chain answerHash. 3. Learner calls completeModule(0, 3) — mint(learner, 5) fires and the progress bit is set — without engaging with content. 4. Repeat across every module for full payout each.
recommendation: Do not derive the gate from a low-entropy on-chain hash. Use commit-reveal with a secret the contract never learns, an executor/creator-signed EIP-712 completion attestation per (learner, id), or move answer validation off-chain to a trusted attestor before mint. Any on-chain-checkable predicate over a 256-value answer space is inherently brute-forceable.
exploitReasoning: src/EducationHub.sol line 206 stores answerHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(id, correctAnswer)) where id is uint48 (public — emitted in ModuleCreated at line 208, readable via nextModuleId() at line 291) and correctAnswer is uint8 (256 possible values). completeModule at line 237 accepts the answer iff keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(id), answer)) == m.answerHash, with answer typed uint8. The full preimage space is therefore exactly 256 candidates over a public id, so the correct answer is recoverable by brute force off-chain (or by reading m.answerHash from storage) without ever reading the learning content. There is no per-user salt, no commit-reveal, and no secret entropy. On a match, line 239 calls l.token.mint(_msgSender(), m.payout); ParticipationToken.sol line 137/159 (onlyTaskOrEdu) confirms EducationHub is an authorized minter, so the payout is really minted. completeModule is gated only by onlyMember (line 233 → line 143), which any member-hat wearer satisfies. _setCompleted (line 269) marks the module complete per-user, so each module yields its payout once per member regardless of genuine learning.
safetyReasoning: The on-chain answer commitment is trivially reversible. src/EducationHub.sol:206 stores answerHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(id, correctAnswer)) where id is uint48 (public: emitted in ModuleCreated line 208, returned by nextModuleId line 291) and correctAnswer is uint8 (0..255). completeModule (line 237) accepts answer when keccak256(abi.encodePacked(uint48(id), answer)) == m.answerHash and then mints m.payout (line 239). Both preimage inputs are public/low-entropy: with a known id, the answer is a 1-of-256 brute force computable off-chain instantly — no salt, no per-user entropy, no commit-reveal. The test suite confirms this hash is intended as the sole gate (test/EducationHub.t.sol:254 expects InvalidAnswer.selector on a wrong answer), so a member bypassing it by brute force violates intended behavior. EducationHub is an authorized minter of ParticipationToken (src/ParticipationToken.sol:157-159 _checkTaskOrEdu allows executor/taskManager/educationHub), so a forged completion mints real governance/reward tokens.

title: Permissionless executeData lets anyone redirect freshly-bridged USDC to an attacker-owned ZKP2P deposit
description: executeData has no access control on msg.sender and no cryptographic binding between the delivered USDC and the CashOutParams.depositor supplied in callData. The only gate is a balance check: available = balanceOf(this) - totalFailedAmount, and if available >= amounts[0] it creates a ZKP2P deposit whose owner is params.depositor (fully attacker-controlled). The Bungee delivery model transfers USDC to the relay in one step and calls executeData in a subsequent (or separate solver-triggered) step, so during the window where victim USDC sits in the relay unassigned, anyone can call executeData with their own depositor and requestHash and capture the deposit. requestHash is attacker-chosen and is used only for the failed-deposit dedup mapping, so it provides no protection. The CCTP and createDepositFromBalance paths are owner-gated precisely because of this concern (see their comments at 218-221 and 259), but executeData is left open, contradicting the contract's own threat model.
impact: Theft of another user's bridged cash-out amount. The victim's USDC becomes a ZKP2P sell order owned by the attacker; the attacker completes the P2P fill and receives the fiat. Loss scales with the value in transit.
scenario: 1. Victim initiates a $500 cash-out on Arbitrum; Bungee bridges 500 USDC to the relay on Base. 2. Attacker monitors the relay's USDC balance (or mempool). 3. As soon as the 500 USDC lands but before Bungee's own executeData call is mined, attacker calls executeData(requestHash=keccak(anything), amounts=[500e6], tokens=[usdc], callData=abi.encode(CashOutParams{depositor: attacker, paymentMethod: attackerVenmo,...})). 4. available = 500e6 - 0 >= 500e6, so createZkp2pDeposit runs with depositTo(attacker,...). 5. Attacker owns the ZKP2P deposit; victim's funds are gone.
recommendation: Restrict executeData to the trusted Bungee executor/gateway address (store it in storage, validate msg.sender), or bind the delivered funds to the depositor via a signed/attested requestHash that the relay verifies matches params. At minimum gate executeData the same way completeCashOut and createDepositFromBalance are gated, or verify msg.sender is the Bungee inbox.
exploitReasoning: executeData (src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:121-158) has no msg.sender gate and no cryptographic binding between the delivered USDC and params.depositor, which is fully attacker-controlled via callData (decoded at line 132). The only guard is `available = IERC20(usdc).balanceOf(address(this)) - totalFailedAmount; if (available < expectedAmount) revert` (lines 139-140). This guard only protects previously-reserved failed-deposit funds — it does nothing to prove that the *fresh* USDC in the relay belongs to the depositor named in callData. On success it calls createZkp2pDeposit -> IEscrowV2Minimal(escrow).depositTo(params.depositor, ...) (line 213), creating a ZKP2P sell order owned by params.depositor. requestHash (line 122) is attacker-chosen and only used for the failed-deposit dedup mapping (lines 150-156), so it adds no protection. The contract's own siblings are gated for exactly this reason: completeCashOut requires msg.sender==owner with the comment "Owner-only to prevent front-running attacks where an attacker substitutes CashOutParams for a valid CCTP message" (lines 218-221, 229), and createDepositFromBalance requires msg.sender==owner "to prevent unauthorized deposit creation" (lines 259-261). The comment on createDepositFromBalance (lines 256-258) — "Used when bridge delivers USDC without calling executeData (e.g., Bungee depositRoute, direct transfer, or CCTP mint)" — proves the developers know USDC can land in the relay unassigned, i.e. a window exists where executeData's balance check passes for whoever calls first. executeData is left permissionless, contradicting the threat model applied to its two siblings.
safetyReasoning:
CashOutRelay.executeData (src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:121-158) has no msg.sender check. Its only gate is `available = IERC20(usdc).balanceOf(address(this)) - totalFailedAmount; if (available < expectedAmount) revert` (lines 139-140). params.depositor is decoded straight from attacker-supplied callData (line 132) and passed to `depositTo(params.depositor, depositParams)` in createZkp2pDeposit (line 213), which mints a ZKP2P deposit OWNED by params.depositor while pulling USDC from the relay (msg.sender). requestHash is only used for the failed-deposit dedup mapping (lines 150-155), so it is not a binding. There is no cryptographic link between the delivered USDC and the claimed depositor.

The safety of this hinges entirely on whether USDC ever rests in the relay "unassigned." The production integration script script/cashout/cashout-e2e.mjs proves it does: it uses Bungee's `depositRoute` (line 121, a plain transfer to a Bungee deposit address with NO executor callback), then Step 4 (lines 151-169) POLLS the relay's on-chain balance until USDC arrives, then Step 5 (lines 186-191) creates the deposit in a SEPARATE transaction via createDepositFromBalance. So in the real deployment there is a multi-minute window where victim USDC sits in the relay with available > 0 before the owner's trigger tx is mined.

The team gated createDepositFromBalance (line 261: `if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();`) and completeCashOut (line 229) with owner-only checks precisely to stop an attacker from substituting their own CashOutParams for unassigned funds — see the explanatory comments at lines 218-221 and 256-259. executeData is the functionally-equivalent third entrypoint to that same balance-check-then-depositTo logic, but it was left permissionless, directly contradicting the contract's own threat model. The test testSecurity_AttackerCannotStealFailedDeposits (lines 474-502) only proves an attacker can't steal ALREADY-FAILED (reserved) funds — it does not cover freshly-arrived, not-yet-triggered funds, which are exactly what `available` exposes.

title: ParticipationToken.setEducationHub / setTaskManager first-call is permissionless — unprivileged actor can bind a malicious minter and mint unlimited voting power
description: setTaskManager and setEducationHub use a 'first write is open' pattern: when the stored address is address(0), ANY caller may set it (no executor/owner check), and only subsequent overwrites require msg.sender==executor. setEducationHub does not even validate the input is non-zero. The participation token's mint() is gated by _checkTaskOrEdu(), which authorizes l.executor, l.taskManager, and l.educationHub. Thus whoever controls l.educationHub (or l.taskManager) can mint arbitrary PT, and PT is the governance/voting weight for HybridVoting and member/approver gating elsewhere. In the atomic OrgDeployer.deployFullOrg path these are set in the same transaction (OrgDeployer.sol:494-496) so front-running is not possible there. But when an org is deployed with educationHubConfig.enabled == false, l.educationHub stays address(0) permanently and the first setEducationHub call remains open forever — exactly the 'add an EducationHub later via governance' flow documented in script/fixes/AddEducationHubDecentralPark.s.sol, whose own comments state 'setEducationHub's first-call is open'.
impact: An unprivileged attacker can seize unlimited governance token issuance for any org that did not deploy an EducationHub, enabling a governance takeover (mint enough PT to pass HybridVoting proposals) and defeating member/approver gating that keys off PT/hats. Loss of governance control.
scenario: 1) Org X is deployed with educationHubConfig.enabled=false, so ParticipationToken.educationHub == address(0). 2) Attacker deploys MaliciousMinter with a function that calls token.mint(attacker, 1e24). 3) Attacker calls ParticipationToken.setEducationHub(MaliciousMinter) — the l.educationHub==address(0) branch executes with no caller check and succeeds. 4) Attacker calls MaliciousMinter, which calls token.mint(...); _checkTaskOrEdu passes because _msgSender()==l.educationHub. 5) Attacker now holds dominant voting weight and can pass arbitrary HybridVoting proposals (executor actions). The same attack applies to setTaskManager for any org where taskManager is unset when governance intends to add one later.
recommendation: Require executor (or an explicitly authorized deployer during a bootstrap window) for BOTH the first and subsequent calls, e.g. gate the whole function with onlyExecutor and have OrgDeployer perform the initial wiring while it (transiently) holds executor/authority, or add a dedicated bootstrap-deployer address like TaskManager.deployer that is cleared after setup. At minimum reject address(0) and never allow an unauthenticated caller to bind a minter.
exploitReasoning: src/ParticipationToken.sol:198-210 setEducationHub uses a "first write is open" pattern: when l.educationHub==address(0) (line 202) it assigns eh with NO caller check and does not even require eh!=0; only the else branch (line 206) enforces _msgSender()==l.executor. mint() at line 295 is gated by onlyTaskOrEdu -> _checkTaskOrEdu (line 157-162), which authorizes any _msgSender() equal to l.executor, l.taskManager, OR l.educationHub. So whoever controls l.educationHub can mint arbitrary PT. OrgDeployer.sol:494-496 sets taskManager unconditionally but only calls setEducationHub when params.educationHubConfig.enabled is true; when disabled, l.educationHub remains address(0) permanently. test/DeployerTest.t.sol:4858-4874 proves this exact flow: after a deploy with educationHubConfig.enabled=false, token.setEducationHub(0x456) succeeds with the default (unprivileged) msg.sender and no prank, and the test comment says "first setter can set it." script/fixes/AddEducationHubDecentralPark.s.sol:42 confirms in production comments "ParticipationToken.educationHub == 0x0 -> first-call setEducationHub is open." PT is the governance weight: HybridVotingCore.sol:147 computes token-class voting power via IERC20(cls.asset).balanceOf(voter), and PT auto-delegates to self on mint (_update, line 360-362), so minted PT is immediately live voting weight. The taskManager leg of the finding is NOT practically reachable (OrgDeployer line 494 always sets taskManager since ModulesFactory always deploys one), but the educationHub leg is fully real.
safetyReasoning: The code confirms the finding. ParticipationToken.setEducationHub (src/ParticipationToken.sol:198-210) has no access check on the first write: when l.educationHub==address(0) (line 202) it stores the caller-supplied address with NO msg.sender==executor check and NO non-zero validation, only gating subsequent overwrites (line 206). setTaskManager (185-196) is the same pattern but validates non-zero. mint() at line 295 is gated by onlyTaskOrEdu -> _checkTaskOrEdu (157-162), which authorizes l.executor, l.taskManager, AND l.educationHub. So whoever sets l.educationHub gains unlimited mint authority over the governance token. Reachability of the empty-educationHub state is real: OrgDeployer.deployFullOrg only calls setEducationHub when params.educationHubConfig.enabled is true (src/OrgDeployer.sol:495-496), and ModulesFactory only deploys the EducationHub when enabled (src/factories/ModulesFactory.sol:112-113), leaving result.educationHub==address(0) otherwise. Thus any org deployed with educationHubConfig.enabled==false has l.educationHub==address(0) permanently, and the first-call setEducationHub stays open forever. This is not theoretical: script/fixes/AddEducationHubDecentralPark.s.sol:42 documents a live Gnosis org (DecentralPark) in exactly this state ("ParticipationToken.educationHub == 0x0 -> first-call setEducationHub is open"). PT is the voting weight for HybridVoting's ERC20_BAL class (src/libs/HybridVotingCore.sol:147 balanceOf(voter)). The taskManager arm of the finding is NOT reachable via OrgDeployer because setTaskManager is called unconditionally at OrgDeployer.sol:494, so l.taskManager is always bound atomically at deploy — only the educationHub arm is the live vector, as the finding itself notes.

title: claimHatsWithUser / registerAndClaimHats mint fully caller-controlled hat IDs — privilege escalation if any org hat has a permissive eligibility module
description: claimHatsWithUser and the two registerAndClaimHats* functions forward an arbitrary caller-supplied claimHatIds array straight to Executor.mintHatsForUser, which calls Hats.mintHat for each id. QuickJoin performs NO check that the requested hats are the org's member hats or that the caller/user is entitled to them — it delegates ALL authorization to the Hats EligibilityModule (see docstring at lines 333-336). Hats.mintHat (Hats.sol:246-250) only enforces (a) the caller/Executor wears an admin hat of the target hat and (b) isEligible(wearer, hatId). The Executor wears the org top hat, so it is admin of every hat in the tree. Therefore the ONLY thing standing between an arbitrary user (who merely holds any username) and minting themselves an Executive/Admin/Voting hat is the eligibility module returning false for that hat. If any privileged hat in an org is (mis)configured with a permissive/open eligibility module — a very common pattern for 'self-serve' member hats — claimHatsWithUser([privilegedHatId]) grants it with no vouch.
impact: If any high-privilege hat's eligibility module returns eligible-by-default (as open member hats typically do), any address with a registered username can self-mint that hat via claimHatsWithUser, escalating to whatever governance/permission that hat confers (e.g. voting power, task-manager admin, executive role). The safety of the entire vouch-claim design is fully outsourced to per-hat eligibility configuration with no defense-in-depth in QuickJoin.
scenario: 1. An org configures member hat M with an open eligibility module (eligible=true for everyone) so people can self-join, and also — by mistake or reuse of the same module — hat X (a privileged role) shares/permits that open eligibility. 2. Attacker registers any username (registerAccount('x')). 3. Attacker calls qj.claimHatsWithUser([X]). 4. QuickJoin passes [X] to Executor.mintHatsForUser -> Hats.mintHat(X, attacker): Executor is admin, isEligible returns true -> attacker now wears privileged hat X with zero vouch.
recommendation: Add defense-in-depth in QuickJoin: constrain claimHatIds to a governance-approved 'claimable hats' allowlist (analogous to memberHatIds) rather than accepting arbitrary ids, or require the target hat to be marked vouch-gated. At minimum, document loudly that every hat reachable through the Executor's admin authority MUST have a strict eligibility module, and add a test asserting a non-eligible caller cannot self-mint a privileged hat.
exploitReasoning:
The call path is real and unguarded. QuickJoin.claimHatsWithUser (src/QuickJoin.sol:337-347) is a public function whose only precondition is that msg.sender holds a username (line 339-340); it then forwards a fully caller-controlled claimHatIds array to IExecutorHatMinter(l.executor).mintHatsForUser (line 343). QuickJoin is authorized as a hat minter on the Executor at deploy (OrgDeployer.sol:524 setHatMinterAuthorization(quickJoin,true)), so Executor.mintHatsForUser (Executor.sol:141-152) passes the authorizedHatMinters check and calls l.hats.mintHat(hatIds[i], user) for each id. QuickJoin performs NO membership/allowlist check on claimHatIds — the docstring (QuickJoin.sol:333-336) explicitly outsources all authorization to the eligibility module. registerAndClaimHats (356-377) and registerAndClaimHatsWithPasskey (387-421) do the same. A username is trivially self-obtained: UniversalAccountRegistry.registerAccount(string) (UniversalAccountRegistry.sol:97-99) is permissionless (msg.sender self-registers), and registerAndClaimHats bundles sig-registration + claim.

The only gate is Hats.mintHat's isEligible(wearer,hatId) -> EligibilityModule.getWearerStatus. Critically, the finding UNDERSTATES the precondition: it is not an exotic misconfig, it is the SHIPPED DEFAULT. The standard role-config builder _buildSimpleRoleConfigs (test/DeployerTest.t.sol:212, 224-243) sets defaults: RoleEligibilityDefaults({eligible:true, standing:true}) and vouching.enabled:false for EVERY role, and HatsTreeSetup.sol:250-251 batchSetDefaultEligibility applies role.defaults.eligible verbatim per hat. In EligibilityModule.getWearerStatus (EligibilityModule.sol:949-960), when vouching is disabled it returns eligible = hierarchyEligible = defaultRules[hatId].eligible, which is true for ALL addresses with no per-wearer rule. The default org has role 0 = members and role 1 = executive (both default-eligible, no vouch), and role 1 is privileged (taskCreator/hybridProposalCreator/ddCreator/tokenApprover bitmaps, DeployerTest.t.sol:255-265). So any username holder can call claimHatsWithUser([executiveHatId]) and self-mint the executive hat with zero vouch. Vouch-gating only kicks in when an org explicitly opts into vouching config (configureVouching) with default-eligible flipped false — the very defense-in-depth the finding says is missing.
safetyReasoning:
The mechanical chain in the finding is accurate: QuickJoin.claimHatsWithUser (src/QuickJoin.sol:337-347) forwards an arbitrary caller-supplied claimHatIds array to Executor.mintHatsForUser (src/Executor.sol:141-152), which only checks authorizedHatMinters[msg.sender] and then calls hats.mintHat per id. The Executor wears the org top hat so it is admin of every hat, meaning the sole gate is EligibilityModule.getWearerStatus. For a hat with vouching disabled and defaultEligible=true, getWearerStatus (src/EligibilityModule.sol:949-960 falling back to defaultRules at 933-937) returns eligible=true for any address. So the arithmetic of the escalation holds ONLY IF a privileged hat is configured with open eligibility.

However this is not a QuickJoin security bug, for two decisive reasons:

1. Correct-by-design delegation. The vouch-claim path explicitly delegates all authorization to the EligibilityModule — this is documented (src/QuickJoin.sol:333-336) and directly tested. testClaimHatsWithVouching (test/DeployerTest.t.sol:7190-7347) deploys the EXECUTIVE hat with defaults.eligible=false + vouching enabled (lines 7220-7223), and Test 2 (lines 7306-7316) asserts a non-vouched attacker's claimHatsWithUser reverts precisely because eligibility returns false. The intended safety invariant is: privileged hats MUST be configured defaultEligible=false with vouching. QuickJoin faithfully implements this contract.

2. QuickJoin adds ZERO attack surface. The claimed escalation requires a privileged actor to misconfigure a privileged hat with defaultEligible=true and no vouching. But EligibilityModule.claimVouchedHat (src/EligibilityModule.sol:868-886) has NO _isVouchingEnabled guard — it mints ANY hat for which getWearerStatus(msg.sender,hatId) returns eligible && standing, permissionlessly, with no username requirement. So under the exact misconfiguration the finding posits, any address can already self-mint that hat directly via claimVouchedHat(hatId), independent of QuickJoin. QuickJoin's path is in fact strictly narrower (it additionally requires a registered username, src/QuickJoin.sol:339-340). The 'caller-controlled hat IDs' framing therefore does not introduce any escalation that isn't already inherent to the open-eligibility configuration at the module layer.

The residual issue — that configuring a privileged hat with defaultEligible=true (the DeployOrg backwards-compat default at script/org/DeployOrg.s.sol:267-269) makes it self-mintable — is a design/documentation hazard in the eligibility model, reachable only through a privileged configuration mistake, and is NOT specific to or caused by QuickJoin. In a correctly-configured org there is no unprivileged escalation path.

title: Global POA guardian can seize any passkey account; completeRecovery is fully permissionless
description: The guardian stored in each account (l.guardian) is copied at initialize() from the factory's single global config.poaGuardian (PasskeyAccountFactory.createAccount lines 244-255 pass config.poaGuardian into initialize). initiateRecovery is onlyGuardian and initiateRecovery+completeRecovery together let the guardian install an attacker-controlled P256 key. completeRecovery (line 350) has NO access control ('Anyone can call after delay passes') and, once the delay elapses, deletes ALL existing credentials (lines 368-379) and installs only the recovery credential (lines 384-391). Because one global POA address is the guardian for every account created by the factory, a malicious or compromised guardian can drain every passkey account protocol-wide. The account owner's only defense is cancelRecovery, which requires either the guardian itself or a self-call via a validated UserOp (onlyGuardianOrSelf, line 416) within the recovery delay window — a user who is offline, or whose signCount ordering is stuck (see separate finding), cannot defend.
impact: A single compromised/rogue global guardian key can take over and drain every PasskeyAccount deployed by the factory. This is a protocol-wide single point of failure over all user funds held in passkey wallets.
scenario: 1) PoaManager sets config.poaGuardian = G at factory init. 2) Every account created inherits guardian G. 3) G is compromised (or malicious). 4) Attacker calls initiateRecovery(newCredId, attackerX, attackerY) as G on victim account. 5) Owner is offline / does not cancel within recoveryDelay (min 1 day). 6) After the delay ANY address calls completeRecovery(recoveryId): victim's credentials are wiped and attacker's key becomes the sole active credential. 7) Attacker signs UserOps with attackerX/Y and drains the account.
recommendation: Reconsider the single-global-guardian model: make the guardian per-account and owner-chosen at enrollment, or require a multi-guardian/threshold scheme, or gate completeRecovery so it cannot be triggered by an unrelated party and add an owner veto that survives the owner being offline (e.g., require the recovery credential to be pre-authorized, or add a longer, owner-configurable cooldown plus on-chain notification). At minimum document the trust assumption prominently and use a timelock/multisig for the guardian key.
exploitReasoning: The code mechanics in the finding are all accurate. initialize() at src/PasskeyAccount.sol:146 sets l.guardian = guardian_, and PasskeyAccountFactory.createAccount always passes the single global config.poaGuardian (lines 253/291) for EVERY account. initiateRecovery (line 322, onlyGuardian) queues an arbitrary attacker-controlled P256 key with only a non-zero X/Y check (line 323). completeRecovery (line 350) has NO access control and, once request.executeAfter has elapsed (line 362), wipes ALL existing credentials (lines 368-379) and installs only the recovery credential as sole active key (lines 384-391). One global guardian therefore governs recovery for all accounts. However, this is a TRUSTED-ROLE compromise, not an unprivileged takeover: (1) guardian-assisted recovery is an intended feature and the guardian being able to install a key IS its purpose; the "attacker" in the primary path is the guardian key itself being compromised/malicious. (2) completeRecovery being permissionless is by-design (interface NatSpec line 223: "Anyone can call after delay passes") and only executes an already-guardian-authorized, delay-elapsed, cancellable request — permissionless completion of an authorized action is not itself a vuln. (3) Owners can fully opt out: setGuardian (line 301, onlySelf) has no zero-address guard, so setGuardian(address(0)) makes onlyGuardian (line 101) revert for any real caller, disabling recovery entirely. (4) The MIN_RECOVERY_DELAY of 1 day (line 55) plus cancelRecovery (line 416, onlyGuardianOrSelf) and the RecoveryInitiated event give owners a monitor-and-cancel window. So the substance is a real centralization / single-point-of-failure design risk, not the claimed unprivileged protocol-wide drain.
safetyReasoning: Mechanics are exactly as described. PasskeyAccountFactory.createAccount (lines 244-255) copies the single global config.poaGuardian into each account's initialize(...guardian_...). poaGuardian is one factory-wide address, set at init and changeable only by PoaManager via setPoaGuardian (onlyPoaManager, factory:167-169) — so every account created inherits the SAME guardian. In PasskeyAccount, initiateRecovery (line 322) is onlyGuardian and lets the guardian stage an arbitrary attacker P256 key (credentialId/pubKeyX/pubKeyY). completeRecovery (line 350) has NO access control and, once request.executeAfter has passed (delay min MIN_RECOVERY_DELAY = 1 day, line 55/362), deletes ALL existing credentials (loop lines 368-379) and installs the recovery credential as the sole active credential (lines 384-391). The only owner defense is cancelRecovery (line 416, onlyGuardianOrSelf) within the delay window. Therefore a compromised or malicious global POA guardian key can take over every PasskeyAccount that still uses the default guardian and whose owner is offline during the delay. The permissionless completeRecovery is not itself the flaw (the key install is gated at onlyGuardian initiateRecovery); the flaw is the shared global guardian single point of failure, which the finding also correctly identifies.

title: announceWinner permanently consumes the proposal even when execution reverts, and burns the winning batch on any executor failure
description: announceWinner sets prop.executed = true at line 425 (before winner calc and before execution) and the executor call is wrapped in try/catch (lines 438-441). If l.executor.execute reverts for a transient/fixable reason (e.g. target temporarily paused, hat toggle not yet ready, or a batch call that fails on the first attempt), the failure is swallowed via ProposalExecutionFailed and the proposal is left permanently marked executed. There is no re-announce or retry path (the AlreadyExecuted guard at line 424 blocks any second call). The winning option's on-chain action is therefore lost forever with no recovery, even though the vote was valid.
impact: A validly-passed governance decision (e.g. minting a coordinator hat, releasing a treasury payment) can silently fail to take effect and can never be re-triggered. The DAO must create and re-vote an entirely new proposal. For time-sensitive executions this is a governance-availability problem.
scenario: 1. Creator makes an election proposal whose winning batch calls Executor->Hats.mintHat. 2. Voting passes for option 1. 3. Before anyone calls announceWinner, an admin momentarily pauses the Hats target or the target reverts due to a transient condition. 4. Someone calls announceWinner(id): prop.executed=true is set, execute() reverts, the catch emits ProposalExecutionFailed, Winner(id,1,true) is emitted. 5. The condition clears seconds later, but any further announceWinner(id) reverts AlreadyExecuted. The hat is never minted.
recommendation: Either (a) do not set executed=true until after a successful execute (move the flag set into the success branch, keeping a separate reentrancy guard which already exists), or (b) if execution fails, leave executed=false so announceWinner can be retried, while still recording the winner. At minimum document that a failed execution is final and unrecoverable so operators design batches accordingly.
exploitReasoning: The cited code in src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol matches the finding exactly. Line 424 `if (prop.executed) revert VotingErrors.AlreadyExecuted();` is the single-shot replay guard; line 425 `prop.executed = true;` sets executed BEFORE any execution. The winning batch execution at lines 438-441 is wrapped in try/catch: `try l.executor.execute(id, batch) {} catch (bytes memory reason) { emit ProposalExecutionFailed(id, winner, reason); }` — a revert from the executor is swallowed, not propagated, so the transaction succeeds and `executed` stays true. Because line 424 blocks any second call, a batch whose execution reverted can never be re-attempted. announceWinner is permissionless: its only modifiers are `nonReentrant, exists(id), isExpired(id), whenNotPaused` (line 414-419) with no hat/role gate (confirmed against modifiers at lines 85/238/248 and the hat-gated create/vote paths at 232/374 which announceWinner deliberately does not use). The intended single-shot design is codified by the test at test/DirectDemocracyVoting.t.sol:759-764 (`testReplay`), which expects the second announceWinner to revert AlreadyExecuted. The identical pattern in src/libs/HybridVotingCore.sol:159-160,223-228 confirms this is the deliberate protocol design, not an accident — but the design has the described flaw: a transient executor revert permanently consumes the proposal.
safetyReasoning: The cited code matches the finding exactly. In DirectDemocracyVoting.announceWinner: line 424 `if (prop.executed) revert VotingErrors.AlreadyExecuted();` then line 425 `prop.executed = true;` runs BEFORE winner calc (427) and before execution (438). The executor call is wrapped in try/catch (438-441) that merely emits ProposalExecutionFailed and swallows the revert. Executor.execute (src/Executor.sol:155) is atomic and reverts on ANY failing sub-call (`if (!ok) revert CallFailed(i, ret);` at 165) and reverts when paused (`whenNotPaused` at 155) — so a transient target pause, hat-toggle-not-ready, or first-attempt failure propagates into the catch. There is exactly one setter of `executed` (grep confirms only line 425) and no re-announce/retry function, so the `AlreadyExecuted` guard permanently blocks any second attempt. The winning batch's on-chain action (e.g. mintHat, treasury release) is lost with no recovery. The identical pattern exists in HybridVotingCore.sol (159-160, 223-227), showing it is a deliberate design choice — but the effect described is real and reachable.

title: Module payout can be set up to type(uint128).max, far above the protocol MAX_PAYOUT of 1e24
description: createModule (line 197) and updateModule (line 219) validate payout only as `payout == 0 || payout > type(uint128).max`, accepting any value up to ~3.4e38. Elsewhere the protocol caps participation-token payouts at ValidationLib.MAX_PAYOUT = 1e24 via requireValidPayout. EducationHub bypasses this and mints m.payout directly through ParticipationToken.mint, which enforces no upper bound (src/ParticipationToken.sol:295-299 only rejects zero).
impact: A creator-hat wearer or the executor can create a module whose per-completion payout is up to 3.4e38 tokens, wildly inflating supply and skewing supply-weighted governance/reward math. Combined with the answer brute-force finding, it becomes catastrophic minting.
scenario: 1. Creator calls createModule(title, hash, payout=type(uint128).max, correctAnswer=1). 2. Any member (via finding #1) calls completeModule and receives ~3.4e38 ParticipationTokens in a single mint. 3. Supply and governance weight are irrecoverably distorted.
recommendation: Use ValidationLib.requireValidPayout(payout) (cap 1e24) in both createModule and updateModule to stay consistent with TaskManager/ParticipationToken payout ceilings.
exploitReasoning: The code matches the finding's factual claims. src/EducationHub.sol:197 (createModule) and :219 (updateModule) validate payout only as `if (payout == 0 || payout > type(uint128).max) revert InvalidPayout();`, accepting any value up to ~3.4e38. This bypasses the protocol-wide cap ValidationLib.MAX_PAYOUT = 1e24 (src/libs/ValidationLib.sol:19, enforced via requireValidPayout/requireValidPayout96). TaskManager consistently uses requireValidPayout96 (TaskManager.sol:644, 735, 1089) to cap payouts at 1e24, so EducationHub is genuinely inconsistent with the rest of the protocol's participation-token minting policy. completeModule (EducationHub.sol:239) mints m.payout directly via l.token.mint(), and ParticipationToken.mint (src/ParticipationToken.sol:295-299) only rejects zero amount / zero address — it enforces NO upper bound. So a module with payout=type(uint128).max would mint ~3.4e38 ParticipationTokens per completion, distorting total supply and supply-weighted governance/reward math. HOWEVER, the finding's severity/actor framing is wrong: createModule/updateModule are gated by onlyCreator (EducationHub.sol:147-151), which requires the caller to wear a creator hat OR be the executor — both privileged, org-appointed roles. An unprivileged member cannot set the payout. The "combined with answer brute-force finding #1 → catastrophic" narrative overstates it: the excessive mint is reachable by any member calling completeModule with the correct answer once the module exists, but the ROOT cause (setting an oversized payout) requires a privileged creator, so this is a privileged-misconfiguration / missing-invariant bug, not an unprivileged exploit.
safetyReasoning: Code confirms the missing cap. EducationHub.sol:197 (createModule) and :219 (updateModule) validate payout only as `payout == 0 || payout > type(uint128).max`, so any value up to ~3.4e38 (≈3.4e20 whole tokens at 18 dec) is accepted and stored in Module.payout (uint128, line 42/206/221). completeModule (line 239) mints m.payout directly via l.token.mint. ParticipationToken.mint (lines 295-299) enforces only `to != 0` and `amount != 0` — no upper bound. This is inconsistent with the rest of the protocol: ValidationLib.MAX_PAYOUT = 1e24 (1M tokens) and TaskManager.sol:644/735/1089 all call requireValidPayout96 to enforce that cap; EducationHub calls requireValidTitle (line 196/218) but never requireValidPayout, so it bypasses the intended cap. So the mismatch between the protocol's documented/enforced 1e24 cap and EducationHub's uint128 ceiling is real.

title: A single marginal voucher can unilaterally burn a legitimately-worn vouched hat
description: revokeVouch lets any address that previously vouched remove its vouch. When the config has combineWithHierarchy == false and the decremented count falls below quorum, and the wearer has no specific rules and currently wears the hat, revokeVouch calls hats.setHatWearerStatus(hatId, wearer, false, false), which burns the wearer's hat. Because a member becomes a wearer as soon as quorum is exactly met (via claimVouchedHat), the voucher who supplied the marginal (quorum-th) vouch can single-handedly revoke a validly-seated member at any later time. There is no cooldown, no admin confirmation, and no distinction between 'still gathering vouches' and 'already seated'.
impact: Any one of the minimum-quorum vouchers can grief/eject a seated member of a vouch-only role (e.g. a Delegate/committee seat) at will, removing their hat and thus their governance power. For a quorum of 1 this means a single member can seat and then eject any address; for quorum N it means any of the N vouchers is a unilateral kill switch on that member.
scenario: Org configures hat H with configureVouching(H, quorum=1, membershipHatId=M, combineWithHierarchy=false), defaultEligible=false. Alice (wears M) calls vouchFor(Bob, H); Bob now has count=1>=quorum, is eligible, and calls claimVouchedHat(H) to mint H. Later Alice calls revokeVouch(Bob, H): newCount = 0 < quorum=1, isWearerOfHat(Bob,H)=true, hasSpecificWearerRules[Bob][H]=false, combineWithHierarchy=false -> the module calls setHatWearerStatus(H, Bob, false, false), burning Bob's hat and stripping his role/vote. Bob had done nothing wrong.
recommendation: Decouple revocation-of-a-pending-application from revocation-of-a-seated-wearer. Either (a) do not auto-burn a hat on revokeVouch (leave burning to an explicit superAdmin action / clearWearerVouches), or (b) only auto-burn while the wearer is NOT yet wearing the hat, or (c) require the count to have dropped due to a superAdmin call. At minimum, gate the auto-burn branch behind a config flag so orgs opt into unilateral revocation.
exploitReasoning: The cited path is real and reachable. revokeVouch (src/EligibilityModule.sol:795) lets any address that holds a current-epoch vouch record for (hatId, wearer) remove it: the only gate is lines 804-807 (wearerVouchEpoch matches current epoch AND l.vouchers[hatId][wearer][msg.sender] is true for the current epoch). It decrements the count (line 811-812) and, at lines 820-825, if !_shouldCombineWithHierarchy(config.flags) && newCount < config.quorum && l.hats.isWearerOfHat(wearer, hatId) && !l.hasSpecificWearerRules[wearer][hatId], it calls l.hats.setHatWearerStatus(hatId, wearer, false, false), which burns the wearer's hat. There is no state that distinguishes "still gathering vouches" from "already seated": a vouch-seated member has hasSpecificWearerRules == false (they were seated purely via the vouch path, getWearerStatus lines 941-955), so all four conditions hold. quorum can be 1 (configureVouching enables on quorum>0, batchConfigureVouching line 710), so a single marginal voucher who supplied the quorum-th vouch can, after the wearer claims via claimVouchedHat (line 868, which mints once effectiveVouchCount>=quorum), later revoke and burn the hat. This burn-on-revoke is confirmed intended by testVouchingRevocation (test/DeployerTest.t.sol:2241-2255) which asserts eligibility drops to false/false after one revoke drops below quorum — the code behaves as designed; the finding correctly identifies the governance/griefing consequence, not a code-logic mismatch.
safetyReasoning: The exploit path is fully present in code with no mitigating guard. configureVouching (src/EligibilityModule.sol:669-683) accepts quorum=1 and combineWithHierarchy=false. claimVouchedHat (868-886) mints the hat once effectiveVouchCount>=quorum (getWearerStatus, 941-946) and does NOT write hasSpecificWearerRules — only setWearerEligibility/_setWearerEligibilityInternal (277,289) set that flag, so a pure vouch-claimed member has hasSpecificWearerRules[wearer][hatId]==false. revokeVouch (795-826) is gated only by whenNotPaused and the "you personally vouched in the current epoch" check (804-807); there is no cooldown, no admin confirmation, and no distinction between 'still gathering vouches' and 'already seated'. When !_shouldCombineWithHierarchy && newCount<quorum && isWearerOfHat(wearer,hatId) && !hasSpecificWearerRules (820-822), it calls hats.setHatWearerStatus(hatId, wearer, false, false) at 824, burning the seated member's hat. I searched for any guard (cooldown, already-claimed flag, re-vouch lock, admin gate) and found none. The tests (testVouchingRevocation, DeployerTest.t.sol:2212-2265) explicitly assert that revoking below quorum flips eligibility to false, confirming the burn is the intended consequence — so the marginal-voucher unilateral revoke is genuinely reachable, not blocked anywhere.

title: getWearerStatus grants eligibility with zero vouches when a vouch+combine hat has defaultEligible=true (no on-chain guard)
description: In getWearerStatus, when vouching is enabled AND combineWithHierarchy is true, the result is `eligible = hierarchyEligible || vouchEligible`. If setDefaultEligibility(hatId, true, true) is set on such a hat, hierarchyEligible is true for EVERY address (defaultRules applies to all wearers without specific rules), so the vouch quorum is entirely bypassed: any address is eligible and can claimVouchedHat immediately. The codebase explicitly acknowledges this as a footgun but pushes prevention entirely to the frontend (see DeployerTest.testVouchGatingBoundaryAndComboMisconfig, step 3 'DOCUMENTED MISCONFIG the frontend must prevent').
impact: A single superAdmin (governance) misconfiguration — a legitimate-looking setDefaultEligibility call — silently converts a vouch-gated role into open-join, letting anyone self-mint a gated hat (delegate/committee seat) and acquire governance power. Because the two calls (configureVouching combine=true, setDefaultEligibility(true)) are independently valid, no on-chain check catches the dangerous combination.
scenario: Hat H configured with quorum>=1, combineWithHierarchy=true, defaultEligible=false (properly gated). Governance later executes setDefaultEligibility(H, true, true) (e.g. copy-paste from an open-join role, or a malicious proposal disguised as routine). Now for any stranger S with no vouches: hasSpecificWearerRules[S][H]=false -> defaultRules -> hierarchyEligible=true -> eligible = true||false = true. S calls claimVouchedHat(H) and mints the gated role with zero vouches.
recommendation: Enforce the invariant on-chain rather than only in the UI: in setDefaultEligibility/batchSetDefaultEligibility (and configureVouching), revert if enabling defaultEligible=true on a hat that has vouching enabled with combineWithHierarchy, or make getWearerStatus ignore the hierarchy default (not per-wearer overrides) for vouch+combine hats. Relying on an off-chain frontend to prevent a governance-reachable loss-of-gate is fragile.
exploitReasoning: The code at EligibilityModule.sol matches the finding exactly. In getWearerStatus: lines 933-937 fall back to defaultRules[hatId] whenever hasSpecificWearerRules[wearer][hatId] is false (i.e. for any stranger), so hierarchyEligible = defaultRules eligible bit. Line 943 gates vouchEligible on effectiveVouchCount >= config.quorum. Lines 949-952: when vouching is enabled AND combineWithHierarchy is set, `eligible = hierarchyEligible || vouchEligible`. If setDefaultEligibility(hatId, true, true) has been called, defaultRules gives hierarchyEligible=true and hierarchyStanding=true for every address, so eligible=true||false=true even with zero vouches; the standing guard at 963-965 does not fire because defaultStanding is also true. claimVouchedHat (868-886) then calls this.getWearerStatus, sees eligible && standing == true, and mints the gated hat to msg.sender. No on-chain check couples configureVouching(combine=true) with setDefaultEligibility(true); both are independently valid onlySuperAdmin writes. The project's own test testVouchGatingBoundaryAndComboMisconfig (DeployerTest.t.sol lines 2017-2024) asserts exactly this: after setDefaultEligibility(hat,true,true) on a vouching+combine hat, stranger2 with zero vouches becomes eligible/eligible, and the test comment (1981-1987) states this is deliberately left un-guarded on-chain and pushed to the frontend.
safetyReasoning: The described behavior is real and directly confirmed by both code and test. In getWearerStatus, when vouching is enabled and combineWithHierarchy is set, the result is `eligible = hierarchyEligible || vouchEligible` (line 951). hierarchyEligible is derived from defaultRules[hatId] for any wearer lacking specific rules (lines 933-938): if hasSpecificWearerRules[wearer][hatId] is false it falls through to l.defaultRules[hatId]. So after setDefaultEligibility(hatId, true, true) (lines 244-252, which writes defaultRules), EVERY address with no specific rules gets hierarchyEligible=true, making `eligible = true || vouchEligible = true` regardless of vouch count — the quorum is fully bypassed. claimVouchedHat (lines 868-886) calls this.getWearerStatus and only requires `eligible && standing`, so any stranger can self-mint the vouch-gated hat with zero vouches. This is not hypothetical: DeployerTest.testVouchGatingBoundaryAndComboMisconfig steps (2)->(3) at lines 2010-2024 assert exactly this — a stranger2 with zero vouches becomes eligible(true,true) immediately after the setDefaultEligibility flip. The test NatSpec (lines 1981-1987) explicitly states "There is intentionally NO on-chain contract change for H1" and that the dangerous combo is prevented only in the frontend. I searched the write paths and confirmed no on-chain guard couples configureVouching(combine=true) with setDefaultEligibility(true): they are independent onlySuperAdmin setters. HOWEVER, the trust boundary caps severity: setDefaultEligibility and all batch variants are gated by onlySuperAdmin (lines 194-197, 244-247), and HatsTreeSetup.sol:298 transfers superAdmin to the org's Executor — the DAO execution layer only callable by the authorized voting contract. So the dangerous flip requires a passed governance proposal, not an unprivileged actor.

title: All deposited ETH is permanently locked — no withdraw path from EntryPoint exists
description: Every ETH inflow — depositForOrg, donateToSolidarity, registerAndConfigureOrg (msg.value), and depositToEntryPoint — is forwarded to IEntryPoint.depositTo(address(this)). The contract exposes NO function that ever calls IEntryPoint.withdrawTo (the interface declares it, but PaymasterHub never invokes it), and there is no addStake/unlockStake/rescue. Consequently the paymaster's entire EntryPoint balance (org deposits, the solidarity fund, and any accidental over-deposit) can only ever leave the contract as gas reimbursement to the EntryPoint. There is no admin, PoaManager, or org path to reclaim funds — e.g. after an org winds down, its unspent deposit is unrecoverable, and mis-sent funds are lost forever.
impact: Permanent loss of access to all funds beyond what gas sponsorship consumes. An org that over-funds, or the protocol wishing to migrate the solidarity fund to a new hub during an upgrade, cannot recover any ETH. Because the hub is UUPS-upgradeable a withdraw could be added later, but the currently deployed implementation strands funds and offers no emergency exit.
scenario: 1. Org Alpha's treasurer calls depositForOrg{value: 1 ether}(alpha). 2. Alpha shuts down / migrates before spending it. 3. No caller (org admin, operator, PoaManager) can move that 1 ETH out of the EntryPoint; validate/postOp only spend it on gas for Alpha's own UserOps, which never happen again. The ETH is locked indefinitely. Same applies to a fat-fingered donateToSolidarity or a depositToEntryPoint call.
recommendation: Add a guarded withdrawal path, e.g. withdrawOrgDeposit(orgId, to, amount) callable by org admin that decrements org.deposited (bounded by deposited-spent) and calls EntryPoint.withdrawTo, plus a PoaManager-gated solidarity/emergency withdraw. Gate carefully so one org cannot pull another org's or the solidarity fund's balance.
exploitReasoning: Traced every ETH-movement path in src/PaymasterHub.sol. Inflows: depositForOrg->_depositForOrg (line 566), donateToSolidarity (line 583), registerAndConfigureOrg (payable, routes through _depositForOrg), and depositToEntryPoint (line 1179) all call IEntryPoint(...).depositTo{value:...}(address(this)) — deposit-only. Grep of the whole file confirms depositTo is the ONLY EntryPoint funds call; withdrawTo/withdrawStake/addStake/unlockStake/rescue/emergency appear nowhere in src/. IEntryPoint.withdrawTo IS declared (src/interfaces/IEntryPoint.sol:6) but is invoked zero times in src/. The full function list (lines 188-1979) has no receive/fallback/delegatecall/arbitrary .call{}. Inheritance is IPaymaster, Initializable, UUPSUpgradeable, ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable, IERC165 — NOT eth-infinitism/OZ BasePaymaster, so no inherited owner withdraw. The only outflow of the EntryPoint deposit is gas reimbursement consumed by the EntryPoint itself in postOp. Tests confirm this: the only withdrawTo in test/ is on the mock EntryPoint (PaymasterHubSolidarity.t.sol:26), never called via the hub; all 'refund' references are counter-accounting in postOp, not ETH withdrawal. So org deposits, solidarity fund, and any over/mis-sent ETH can only leave as gas for that same org's UserOps; once an org stops operating its residual balance is stranded.
safetyReasoning: Read PaymasterHub.sol in full (2003 lines). Confirmed every ETH inflow forwards to EntryPoint.depositTo(address(this)): depositForOrg (L566), donateToSolidarity (L583), registerAndConfigureOrg msg.value (L356 -> _depositForOrg -> L566), and depositToEntryPoint (L1179). Grepped the entire contract and its libs (PaymasterPostOpLib, PaymasterGraceLib): there is NO withdrawTo, withdrawFromEntryPoint, withdrawStake, addStake, unlockStake, rescue, sweep, .call{value}, .transfer, .send, or selfdestruct anywhere. IEntryPoint.sol:6 does declare withdrawTo(address payable,uint256) but PaymasterHub never invokes it (zero references). So the only ETH-out path is gas reimbursement consumed by EntryPoint during UserOp execution. An org's unspent deposit, the solidarity fund, and any over-deposit therefore cannot be moved out by any caller (org admin, operator, or PoaManager) in the currently deployed implementation. Corroborating evidence of intent-vs-code mismatch: test/PaymasterHub.t.sol.skip:620-636 (testDepositAndWithdraw) calls hub.withdrawFromEntryPoint(recipient, 2 ether) and an older depositToEntryPoint{value}() signature with no orgId arg — i.e. an earlier version HAD a withdraw function that the current contract dropped, so the omission is a regression, not a deliberate lockbox. The one real mitigant the finding itself flags: the hub is UUPS-upgradeable (_authorizeUpgrade L1554, PoaManager-gated), so a withdrawFromEntryPoint can be re-added by upgrade and all stranded ETH recovered — funds are not irrecoverably lost, only inaccessible until an upgrade. docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md:615 lists "Withdraw org deposits" under PoaManager's Cannot list, but that is an anti-rug guarantee (governance can't seize org deposits), not a statement that no reclaim path should exist; it does not justify the total absence of any recovery route.

title: Grace-period spend limit and solidarity match are bypassable within a single bundle (no validation-time reservation of solidarity)
description: _checkSolidarityAccess enforces org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod + maxCost <= grace.maxSpendDuringGrace (grace) and requiredSolidarity <= solidarityRemaining (tier), but these are read-only checks. solidarityUsedThisPeriod and solidarity.balance are only mutated later in postOp (_updateOrgFinancials, lines 993-996). Unlike per-subject budgets (_checkBudget reserves maxCost into usedInEpoch, line 1924) and org deposits (_checkOrgBalance reserves into org.spent, line 705/721), the solidarity accounting has NO validation-time reservation. A bundler can therefore include multiple UserOps for the same org in one bundle; every validate sees the same pre-postOp solidarityUsedThisPeriod (e.g. 0) and passes, then every postOp charges solidarity, summing beyond the grace cap / tier match allowance.
impact: An org can consume more solidarity than its grace maxSpendDuringGrace or tier matchAllowance permits in a single bundle, over-drawing the shared fund at other orgs' expense. Magnitude is bounded per bundle by solidarity.balance and per-UserOp maxCost/gas caps, so it is limited abuse rather than a full drain, but it defeats the documented per-period solidarity limits.
scenario: 1. Unfunded org in grace, maxSpendDuringGrace=0.01 ETH, solidarity funded. 2. Attacker (org member) submits a bundle with 2 UserOps each maxCost=0.006 ETH. 3. validate #1: solidarityUsedThisPeriod(0)+0.006<=0.01 -> pass. validate #2 (same bundle, no postOp yet): still 0+0.006<=0.01 -> pass. 4. Both postOps run: _updateOrgFinancials charges fromSolidarity=actual each, solidarityUsedThisPeriod ends at ~0.012 > 0.01. Grace cap exceeded. Same pattern over-draws tier match allowance post-grace.
recommendation: Reserve solidarity at validation time analogous to budgets/deposits: increment org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod (and optionally a pending-solidarity counter) by the projected solidarity portion of maxCost during validate, then reconcile to the actual amount in postOp (mirroring adjustBudget). Alternatively track a per-org in-flight reservation so concurrent bundle ops see each other's draws.
exploitReasoning: The gap is real and unambiguous in the code. `_checkSolidarityAccess` (src/PaymasterHub.sol:442) is declared `internal view` and performs only read-only comparisons: line 467 checks `org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod + maxCost > grace.maxSpendDuringGrace` (grace path) and line 486 checks `requiredSolidarity > solidarityRemaining` (tier path). Neither branch writes any state. The org-level solidarity counters are mutated ONLY in postOp: `_updateOrgFinancials` bumps `org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod += fromSolidarity` (line 993) and `solidarity.balance -= fromSolidarity` (line 996). This contrasts directly with the two sibling checks that DO reserve at validation time for exactly this bundle-safety reason: `_checkBudget` reserves `budget.usedInEpoch += maxCost` (line 1924, with a comment at 1922-1923 explaining bundle safety) and `_checkOrgBalance` reserves `org.spent += maxCost` (lines 705/721, with a docstring at 685-687 explicitly stating "This ensures bundle safety: multiple UserOps for the same org in one bundle cannot bypass the balance check because each validation sees the reserved amounts"). In the grace-unfunded path `_checkOrgBalance` returns 0 with no reservation at all (line 714). `validatePaymasterUserOp` (line 599) has no `nonReentrant` guard and no cross-op dedup; per ERC-4337 the EntryPoint runs every op's validation phase before any postOp, so all validations in a bundle observe the same pre-postOp `solidarityUsedThisPeriod`. `subjectKey` is per-(subjectType,subjectId) (lines 1594/1606), so distinct member accounts/hats in the same org get independent per-subject budgets but share the single org-level `solidarityUsedThisPeriod` and the global `solidarity.balance`, meaning the per-subject budget reservation does not bound aggregate solidarity draw. The postOp grace path (line 939) reverts InsufficientFunds if solidarity is short, but that routes to `_postOpFallback`, which uses `clampedDeduction` (line 839) and never reverts — so the fund is over-drawn, not protected. The existing test `testSameBundle_TwoOpsReservations` (test/PaymasterGracePeriod.t.sol:791) exercises bundle-safety for the deposit path only; there is no analogous coverage for the solidarity path, confirming the reservation was simply not implemented for solidarity.
safetyReasoning:
The finding accurately describes the code. `_checkSolidarityAccess` (src/PaymasterHub.sol:442) is declared `view` and only READS `org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod` and `solidarity.balance`. The grace-cap check (line 467: `org.solidarityUsedThisPeriod + maxCost > grace.maxSpendDuringGrace`) and the tier match-allowance check (lines 481-488) are pure read-only comparisons. The actual mutation of `solidarityUsedThisPeriod` (line 993) and `solidarity.balance` (line 996) happens only in `_updateOrgFinancials`, called from `postOp` (line 779).

By contrast, the two sibling checks explicitly reserve at validation time for bundle safety: `_checkBudget` increments `budget.usedInEpoch += maxCost` (line 1924, with comment "Reserve maxCost for bundle safety"), and `_checkOrgBalance` increments `org.spent += maxCost` (lines 705/721, with comment lines 686-687 "This ensures bundle safety: multiple UserOps for the same org in one bundle cannot bypass the balance check"). The solidarity accounting has no analogous reservation.

Under ERC-4337 handleOps, EntryPoint runs ALL `validatePaymasterUserOp` calls before any `postOp`. So for a bundle of N UserOps against the same grace-period org (zero deposits), each validation reads the same pre-postOp `solidarityUsedThisPeriod` (e.g. 0). In the grace branch, `_checkOrgBalance` returns 0 (line 714) so there is no org-deposit reservation either, and the ONLY validation-time reservation is the per-subject budget in `_checkBudget`. Because `subjectKey` for SUBJECT_TYPE_ACCOUNT is `keccak256(subjectType, subjectId=sender)` (line 1594), distinct attacker-controlled member accounts get distinct budgets — so the per-subject budget does NOT bound the aggregate solidarity draw across subjects. Each op's postOp then charges `fromSolidarity` (line 993), summing past `maxSpendDuringGrace`. The identical gap applies post-grace to the tier `matchAllowance` (lines 481-488). docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md lines 202-208, 267 confirm these are intended per-period caps, so the code diverges from documented intent.

title: Counterfactual account address depends on mutable guardian/recoveryDelay config, so governance changes brick pre-registered/pre-funded accounts
description: getAddress() builds the CREATE2 init code from initData that embeds config.poaGuardian and config.recoveryDelay (lines 285-293), and createAccount() does the same (lines 247-255). Because BeaconProxy's constructor args (beacon + initData) are part of the CREATE2 creation code, the predicted address changes whenever PoaManager calls setPoaGuardian or setRecoveryDelay. UniversalAccountRegistry stores username→getAddress(...) results (lines 163, 285) and QuickJoin/onboarding compute the address ahead of deployment. If the global guardian or recovery delay is updated after a user's address is computed/registered/funded but before the account is deployed, the later createAccount deploys at a DIFFERENT address than the one registered or funded, orphaning the mapping and any ETH sent to the counterfactual address, and breaking the ERC-4337 initCode-derived sender check (deployment reverts / mismatched sender).
impact: A routine governance action (rotating the POA guardian or tuning the recovery delay) silently invalidates every not-yet-deployed counterfactual account: pre-funded ETH becomes stranded, username→address registrations point at the wrong address, and initCode-based first deployments fail.
scenario: 1) User computes address AA = getAddress(cred,x,y,salt) and sends 0.1 ETH to AA, or registers a username → AA in UniversalAccountRegistry. 2) PoaManager calls factory.setPoaGuardian(newG). 3) User (or QuickJoin) later calls createAccount(cred,x,y,salt): initData now embeds newG, so the deployed address is BB != AA. 4) The 0.1 ETH is stranded at AA and the username maps to the wrong contract.
recommendation: Do not embed mutable global config in the account's init code/salt. Either (a) initialize the account with no guardian/delay and have the account pull them lazily from the factory (it already reads maxCredentials via _getMaxCredentials), or (b) pass guardian/delay in a way excluded from the CREATE2 preimage, or (c) make guardian/recoveryDelay immutable once the factory is live. Ensure getAddress is a pure function of (credentialId,pubKeyX,pubKeyY,salt) only.
exploitReasoning: The mechanism is real and directly visible in code. In getAddress (src/PasskeyAccountFactory.sol:285-293) the initData embeds config.poaGuardian and config.recoveryDelay, and line 296-297 packs that initData into the BeaconProxy creation code: abi.encodePacked(type(BeaconProxy).creationCode, abi.encode(l.accountBeacon, initData)). The predicted address is Create2.computeAddress(create2Salt, keccak256(proxyBytecode)) (line 301), so it is a function of keccak256(proxyBytecode) which includes the config. createAccount uses the identical construction (lines 247-260). Critically, _computeSalt (lines 365-371) hashes only credentialId/pubKeyX/pubKeyY/salt and does NOT include the config — so nothing pins the config to the salt. Therefore setPoaGuardian (line 167) or setRecoveryDelay (line 177) mutates l.globalConfig, and every subsequent getAddress/createAccount for a not-yet-deployed account resolves to a different address. Test Passkey.t.sol:226-244 confirms the deployed address embeds the guardian set beforehand. Consumers depend on this: UniversalAccountRegistry.registerAccountByPasskeySig (line 163) and setProfileMetadataByPasskeySig (line 285) derive user = getAddress(...) and store username->user / advance nonces at that counterfactual address, potentially in a separate tx from deployment. If governance changes config between registration/funding (T1) and createAccount (T2), the account deploys at BB != AA, orphaning the username mapping and stranding any ETH pre-sent to AA.
safetyReasoning: The mechanism is exactly as described in the real code. In getAddress (PasskeyAccountFactory.sol:285-293) and createAccount (247-255), the same initData is built by abi.encodeWithSelector(PasskeyAccount.initialize.selector, address(this), credentialId, pubKeyX, pubKeyY, config.poaGuardian, config.recoveryDelay) reading the CURRENT global config. That initData is embedded into the BeaconProxy creation code: getAddress at line 297 does abi.encodePacked(type(BeaconProxy).creationCode, abi.encode(l.accountBeacon, initData)) and hashes it for Create2.computeAddress (301); createAccount deploys `new BeaconProxy{salt}(l.accountBeacon, initData)` (260). Since constructor args are part of CREATE2 creation code, the predicted/deployed address is a function of config.poaGuardian and config.recoveryDelay. Both are mutable: setPoaGuardian (167-171) and setRecoveryDelay (177-181) are onlyPoaManager governance ops that rewrite l.globalConfig with no per-account snapshotting. PasskeyAccount.initialize actually consumes both values (PasskeyAccount.sol:132-147), so they're structurally required in initData — not removable without a redesign. Downstream, UniversalAccountRegistry stores username→getAddress(...) at registration (registerAccountByPasskeySig line 163) and QuickJoin computes/deploys via createAccount (QuickJoin.sol:245,320,413,449). If the global guardian or recovery delay changes between address computation/funding/registration and the eventual createAccount, the deployed address differs, orphaning ETH sent to the counterfactual address and pointing the username mapping at the wrong contract. _register (UniversalAccountRegistry.sol:362-373) reverts UsernameTaken if the username hash already maps to the stale address, so self-heal by re-registering the same name is blocked. No guard, invariant, or snapshot mitigates this — the finding stands.

title: DirectDemocracyVoting is wired with execution machinery it can never use (only HybridVoting is authorized on Executor)
description: Step 10 sets the Executor's sole `allowedCaller` to `result.hybridVoting` (`Executor.setCaller` allows exactly one caller and `Executor.execute` reverts `UnauthorizedCaller` for anyone else). Yet DirectDemocracyVoting is deployed with a full execution surface: it accepts `ddInitialTargets` as allowed execution targets, stores per-option `IExecutor.Call[][]` batches, validates targets in `announceWinner`, and calls `l.executor.execute(id, batch)` (`src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:438`). Because DD is never authorized on the Executor, every DD proposal that carries an execution batch hits the `try/catch` at line 438-441, fails with `UnauthorizedCaller`, and only emits `ProposalExecutionFailed`. There is no code path in this deployer (or in Executor, which supports a single caller) to ever grant DD execution rights.
impact: An org configured expecting DirectDemocracy-governed on-chain actions (the deployer explicitly passes `ddInitialTargets` execution targets and DD validates them) will have those actions silently no-op forever. Proposals are marked `executed=true` with `ProposalExecutionFailed` emitted, so a poll can appear 'passed' while its on-chain effect never applies. This is a latent governance trap rather than a takeover: the failure is caught, so no funds move incorrectly, but the org's expressed intent (execute via DD) is unachievable through this deployment path.
scenario: 1. Deployer calls `deployFullOrg` with `ddInitialTargets = [treasury]` intending DD-governed transfers. 2. Deploy wires `setCaller(hybridVoting)` only. 3. Members create a DD proposal with a batch calling `treasury`. 4. It passes; `announceWinner` validates the target, calls `executor.execute`, which reverts `UnauthorizedCaller`; the catch emits `ProposalExecutionFailed`; `executed` is set true. 5. The treasury action never happens, yet the proposal is closed and cannot be retried.
recommendation: Decide the intended model and make the code self-consistent: either (a) document + enforce that DirectDemocracyVoting is polling-only and remove/deploy it without the execution-batch surface and `ddInitialTargets`, or (b) if DD is meant to govern, extend Executor to authorize multiple callers (or a governance router) and register DD as an authorized caller during deploy. At minimum, revert at deploy time if `ddInitialTargets` is non-empty while DD cannot be an authorized executor, so operators are not misled.
exploitReasoning: All cited facts hold against the real code. In OrgDeployer.sol the shared Executor is created once (result.executor) and passed to BOTH voting modules: DD is deployed via _deployVotingMechanisms -> GovernanceFactory.deployVoting -> ModuleDeploymentLib.deployDirectDemocracyVoting with executorAddr = result.executor and initialTargets = params.ddInitialTargets (OrgDeployer.sol:487-488, 724; ModuleDeploymentLib.sol:273-291). DD.initialize stores that executor and marks each ddInitialTarget in allowedTarget (DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:152-180). DD carries a full execution surface: it stores per-option IExecutor.Call[][] batches (line 62/316), validates targets on creation (_validateTargets, 260-269) and again in announceWinner (433), then calls l.executor.execute(id, batch) at line 438 inside a try/catch that only emits ProposalExecutionFailed on revert (438-441), after unconditionally setting prop.executed = true at 425. Executor.execute reverts UnauthorizedCaller unless msg.sender == allowedCaller (Executor.sol:156). At OrgDeployer.sol:527 setCaller(result.hybridVoting) makes HybridVoting the sole allowedCaller, and Executor.setCaller only permits a one-time first set (allowedCaller must be address(0)) restricted to owner() (Executor.sol:91-98); ownership is then renounced at 561 (owner() becomes address(0)). Executor supports exactly ONE caller (single allowedCaller field, 44). Therefore a DD proposal with a non-empty winning batch: any DD creator creates it, it passes, anyone calls announceWinner (isExpired), target validation passes, execute reverts UnauthorizedCaller, catch emits ProposalExecutionFailed, prop.executed=true, Winner emitted valid=true — the on-chain action never occurs and cannot be retried (AlreadyExecuted guard at 424). This directly contradicts documented behavior: DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md:34 lists 'On-Chain Execution | Winning proposals can automatically execute smart contract calls', and the deployer explicitly wires ddInitialTargets as execution targets. So the intent/code mismatch is real.
safetyReasoning: The deployer wires the Executor's sole allowedCaller to HybridVoting only (OrgDeployer.sol:527), and Executor.execute reverts UnauthorizedCaller for any other sender (Executor.sol:156). Executor supports exactly ONE caller: setCaller is first-time-only (Executor.sol:91-98), and proposeCaller/acceptCaller merely REPLACE the caller (Executor.sol:101-120), so HV and DD can never both be authorized. Meanwhile GovernanceFactory initializes DirectDemocracyVoting with the SAME executor address and the deployer's ddInitialTargets as allowedTargets (GovernanceFactory.sol:284,297-298). DD.announceWinner validates the target and calls l.executor.execute(id, batch) inside a try/catch (DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:428-441); because DD is never the Executor's allowedCaller, that call always reverts UnauthorizedCaller, is caught, and only ProposalExecutionFailed is emitted. Critically, prop.executed=true is set unconditionally at line 425 BEFORE the try, and line 424 reverts AlreadyExecuted on any retry — so a DD proposal that "passed" is permanently closed with its on-chain effect never applied. Docs confirm this defeats intended behavior: DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md:582 states DD on-chain execution makes governance "binding rather than merely advisory," and ORG_DEPLOYER.md documents DD's full execution surface. The DD test only uses a permissive MockExecutor (DirectDemocracyVoting.t.sol:13-24) with no allowedCaller gate, so it never exercises the real single-caller restriction — masking the bug. No guard, comment, or design note anywhere indicates DD is intentionally advisory-only in the deployed org. The finding's code claims and line numbers are accurate.

title: PaymasterHub.reinitializeProtocolAdmin has no access control — first caller after upgrade seizes protocolAdmin (rule-add + cross-chain admin) via front-running
description: `reinitializeProtocolAdmin(address _admin)` is `external reinitializer(2)` with NO caller check; it sets `MainStorage.protocolAdmin = _admin`. `protocolAdmin` is a privileged principal: it bypasses the poaManager check in `adminBatchAddRules` (line 1041: `if (msg.sender != m.poaManager && msg.sender != m.protocolAdmin) revert`) and in the cross-chain admin path (line 1242). The intended flow (script/upgrades/UpgradeAndFixVouchRules.s.sol line 214) is for the upgrade script to call this atomically right after upgrading the impl, but nothing enforces that the legitimate deployer wins the race.
impact: On any PaymasterHub proxy where the impl that first introduced reinitializer(2) has been deployed but `reinitializeProtocolAdmin` has not yet been consumed, an attacker who front-runs the admin's setup transaction becomes `protocolAdmin` permanently (reinitializer is one-shot). As protocolAdmin they can whitelist arbitrary (target, selector) paymaster rules across orgs, redirecting solidarity-fund gas sponsorship to attacker-controlled calls.
scenario: 1. Governance upgrades the PaymasterHub beacon/impl to the version containing reinitializer(2) but does not bundle the reinitializeProtocolAdmin call in the same block. 2. Attacker monitors the mempool, sees the impl is live and version is still 1. 3. Attacker calls `hub.reinitializeProtocolAdmin(attacker)` — passes (no auth, version advances 1→2). 4.
