Legit admin's later call reverts (already reinitialized). 5. Attacker calls `adminBatchAddRules` to allow sponsored calls to arbitrary targets, draining sponsored gas.
recommendation: Gate reinitializeProtocolAdmin to poaManager/owner (e.g. `if (msg.sender != _getMainStorage().poaManager) revert NotPoaManager();`). Even though it is one-shot, an unauthenticated privileged setter is unsafe; always bundle privileged reinitializers with an access check rather than relying on atomic scripting.
exploitReasoning: The cited code is exactly as described. src/PaymasterHub.sol:241 `function reinitializeProtocolAdmin(address _admin) external reinitializer(2)` has no caller check and sets `_getMainStorage().protocolAdmin = _admin` (line 242). `protocolAdmin` is a privileged principal that bypasses the poaManager gate in `adminBatchAddRules` (line 1041: `if (msg.sender != m.poaManager && msg.sender != m.protocolAdmin) revert`) and in `setSolidarityFee` (line 1242, same condition). The upgrade path cannot close the race atomically: PoaManager.upgradeBeacon (src/PoaManager.sol:93-106) performs a bare `beacon.upgradeTo(newImpl)` with NO upgradeAndCall/post-upgrade delegatecall, so `reinitializeProtocolAdmin` is necessarily a separate transaction after the beacon points at the new impl. The intended flow in script/upgrades/UpgradeAndFixVouchRules.s.sol confirms this: step 2 upgrades the beacon (line 204-208), then step 3 calls `pm.reinitializeProtocolAdmin(deployer)` as a distinct tx (line 211-214) with the developer's own comment "callable by anyone, runs once". OZ Initializable reinitializer(2) is one-shot, so whoever wins the race becomes permanent protocolAdmin. A concrete front-run sequence therefore exists and produces a bad, irreversible outcome.
safetyReasoning: The finding accurately describes the code. `reinitializeProtocolAdmin(address _admin)` at src/PaymasterHub.sol:241-243 is `external reinitializer(2)` with NO caller check and directly sets `_getMainStorage().protocolAdmin = _admin`. `reinitializer(2)` is one-shot: once consumed the value cannot be changed by this path again (the script itself verifies this at UpgradeAndFixVouchRules.s.sol:258-264). `protocolAdmin` is a privileged principal that bypasses the poaManager gate in `adminBatchAddRules` (line 1041: `if (msg.sender != m.poaManager && msg.sender != m.protocolAdmin) revert`) and in `setSolidarityFee` (line 1242, same disjunction). `adminBatchAddRules` (lines 1037-1050 → _setRulesBatch storage) whitelists arbitrary (target, selector) rules with `allowed: true` for every already-registered org (adminHatId != 0), i.e. it can redirect the paymaster's sponsored-gas coverage to attacker-chosen call paths across all registered orgs. The exploit window is real, not hypothetical: the deploy script's own comment at line 211 states the function is "callable by anyone, runs once," and the version note at line 19 ("v16 burned without protocolAdmin, v17 without setSolidarityFee protocolAdmin") shows this reinitializer path is actively used across upgrades. Crucially, the production broadcast path (Step2_UpgradeAndFix, lines 89-174) upgrades the beacon cross-chain via Hyperlane (`upgradeBeaconCrossChain`, ~5-min relay per the code comment at line 172) and does NOT bundle a `reinitializeProtocolAdmin` call in the same transaction — the reinit only appears in the fork-only DryRun contract (line 214). So on a chain where the new impl becomes live but reinit has not yet been consumed, any EOA can front-run and permanently seize protocolAdmin. I searched for any modifier, onlyOwner/onlyPoaManager guard, or msg.sender check on the function and found none. I could not find any mitigation in the code.

title: PaymasterHubLens.wouldValidate can never validate onboarding or org-deploy sponsorship (dead branches)
description: wouldValidate() reads OrgConfig for the passed `orgId` and rejects with (false,"OrgNotRegistered") at line 218 when cfg.adminHatId==0, and rejects with (false,"OrgIdMismatch") at line 226 when the decoded orgId != the passed orgId. Only AFTER that do the SUBJECT_TYPE_POA_ONBOARDING (line 229) and SUBJECT_TYPE_ORG_DEPLOY (line 237) branches run. But those two paths require the decoded orgId to be bytes32(0) (the branches themselves enforce `decodedOrgId != bytes32(0)` => reject, mirroring PaymasterHub lines 622/636). To reach the onboarding branch a caller must pass orgId==0 so that line 226 passes — but then line 218 (cfg.adminHatId==0 for the zero org, which is never registered) already returned "OrgNotRegistered". PaymasterHub itself validates onboarding/org-deploy BEFORE any org-registration check (PaymasterHub.sol lines 619/633, before the org lookup at 646), so the lens diverges from the contract: for every onboarding/org-deploy UserOp that the hub WOULD sponsor, wouldValidate returns false.
impact: Off-chain callers/bundlers using wouldValidate() as a pre-flight simulation for gasless onboarding or free org-deploy UserOps always get a false negative, so they will skip or reject operations the hub would actually sponsor. No on-chain fund loss (view only), but the predictor is wrong for two entire sponsorship classes, defeating its purpose.
scenario: A bundler wants to check whether a POA onboarding UserOp (paymasterAndData encodes subjectType=0x03, decodedOrgId=0) will be sponsored. It calls lens.wouldValidate(orgId, userOp, maxCost). If it passes orgId=someRegisteredOrg, line 226 returns "OrgIdMismatch" (decoded 0 != org). If it passes orgId=0 to satisfy line 226, line 218 returns "OrgNotRegistered" (org 0 has adminHatId 0). Either way false — but PaymasterHub.validatePaymasterUserOp would accept it.
recommendation: Reorder wouldValidate to decode paymasterAndData first and branch on subjectType==POA_ONBOARDING / ORG_DEPLOY BEFORE the OrgConfig registration and orgId-equality checks, matching PaymasterHub.validatePaymasterUserOp ordering (version check, then onboarding/org-deploy, then org path). For those two subject types skip the org lookup and the decodedOrgId!=orgId comparison entirely.
exploitReasoning:
The bug is real and provable from the code. In PaymasterHubLens.wouldValidate (src/PaymasterHubLens.sol):
- Line 217-218: reads getOrgConfig(orgId) for the PASSED orgId and returns (false,"OrgNotRegistered") when cfg.adminHatId==0.
- Line 226: returns (false,"OrgIdMismatch") unless decodedOrgId == passed orgId.
- Lines 229-234 (onboarding) and 237-242 (org-deploy) only return (true,...) when decodedOrgId==bytes32(0) (else lines 230/238 reject as Invalid*Request).

To reach a true return in either branch you need decodedOrgId==0 (lines 230/238) AND decodedOrgId==passed orgId (line 226) => passed orgId==0. But org 0 is never registrable: PaymasterHub._registerOrg line 368 reverts InvalidOrgId when orgId==bytes32(0), so getOrgConfig(0).adminHatId is always 0, so line 218 returns (false,"OrgNotRegistered") first. The two true-branches are therefore unreachable dead code.

This diverges from the hub itself: PaymasterHub.validatePaymasterUserOp handles SUBJECT_TYPE_POA_ONBOARDING (line 619) and SUBJECT_TYPE_ORG_DEPLOY (line 633) in the if/else-if BEFORE the org-registration check, and the org.adminHatId==0 check only runs in the else branch (line 647) for normal per-org ops. For onboarding/org-deploy the hub requires decoded orgId==bytes32(0) (lines 622/636) and never touches org registration. So for every onboarding/org-deploy UserOp the hub would sponsor, the lens returns false — exactly as the finding describes.
safetyReasoning: The lens's onboarding (lines 229-234) and org-deploy (lines 237-242) branches are structurally unreachable in a way that returns true. Both branches require decodedOrgId == bytes32(0) (lines 230, 238 reject any non-zero decodedOrgId, mirroring PaymasterHub lines 622/636). But two earlier guards make orgId==0 impossible to satisfy: line 226 (`if (decodedOrgId != orgId) return (false, "OrgIdMismatch")`) forces the passed orgId to equal decodedOrgId==bytes32(0); and line 218 (`if (cfg.adminHatId == 0) return (false, "OrgNotRegistered")`) — where cfg = hub.getOrgConfig(orgId) — always rejects orgId==bytes32(0), because the zero org is never registered so getOrgConfig(0) returns a zero-initialized OrgConfig with adminHatId==0 (struct at Lens lines 13-19). So: pass a real orgId => line 226 fails "OrgIdMismatch"; pass orgId==0 => line 218 fails "OrgNotRegistered". Either way wouldValidate returns false for every onboarding/org-deploy UserOp. This diverges from PaymasterHub.validatePaymasterUserOp, which handles SUBJECT_TYPE_POA_ONBOARDING (line 619) and SUBJECT_TYPE_ORG_DEPLOY (line 633) BEFORE the org-registration lookup (which lives only in the else branch at lines 645-647), so the hub WOULD sponsor these ops. Constants confirmed (lines 95-101): SUBJECT_TYPE_POA_ONBOARDING=0x03, SUBJECT_TYPE_ORG_DEPLOY=0x04, RULE_ID_GENERIC=0. No test exercises wouldValidate with these subject types, so the dead branches were never caught. I found no guard or intended-design reason that rescues these branches — the ordering is a genuine logic bug.

title: Unbounded pollHatIds array makes every vote() O(n) over an attacker/creator-chosen list, enabling gas-griefing of a restricted poll
description: createProposal accepts hatIds with no length cap (unlike numOptions capped by MAX_OPTIONS and batches capped by MAX_CALLS). All hatIds are pushed into p.pollHatIds (lines 330-339). On every vote to a restricted poll, vote() linearly scans p.pollHatIds calling l.hats.isWearerOfHat per entry (lines 381-390) until a match is found or the array is exhausted. A creator can set an arbitrarily large pollHatIds (e.g. thousands of unmatched hat IDs) so that legitimate voters who wear the real allowed hat placed last, or voters who must scan the full array, pay large gas per vote or exceed the block gas limit.
impact: A malicious or careless proposal creator can make a restricted poll effectively unvotable (each vote runs out of gas), or make voting prohibitively expensive, undermining the department-decision use case. Because this contract is typically gas-sponsored via PaymasterHub, it can also drain sponsored gas.
scenario: 1. A creator-hat holder calls createProposal with hatIds containing 5,000 fabricated hat IDs plus the real engineering hat last. 2. An engineer calls vote(): the loop at 381-390 performs up to 5,000 isWearerOfHat cross-contract calls before matching the real hat, blowing past the block gas limit and reverting. 3. No eligible member can vote; the poll is bricked.
recommendation: Introduce a MAX_POLL_HATS cap (mirroring MAX_OPTIONS/MAX_CALLS) and enforce it in _initProposal before pushing. The pollHatAllowed O(1) mapping already exists (line 49) — vote() should consult that mapping directly rather than looping over pollHatIds, eliminating the per-vote linear scan entirely.
exploitReasoning: The described code path is real and accurate. In src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol, _initProposal pushes every element of the caller-supplied `hatIds` into `p.pollHatIds` (lines 330-339) with NO length cap — contrast the explicit caps `numOptions > MAX_OPTIONS` (line 281) and `batchLen > MAX_CALLS` (line 262). In vote(), when `p.restricted` is true, the loop at lines 381-390 linearly scans `p.pollHatIds` calling `l.hats.isWearerOfHat(_msgSender(), p.pollHatIds[i])` per entry, breaking only on a match. Notably an O(1) `pollHatAllowed[hatId]` mapping is already populated at line 334 but is only read by the view function at lines 520-522, never in the vote() hot path — so the linear scan is a genuine, avoidable inefficiency. A creator who places the real allowed hat last among thousands of fabricated IDs forces legitimate voters to pay for the full scan of cross-contract calls, potentially exceeding the block/paymaster gas limit and reverting every vote. HybridVoting shares the identical pattern (HybridVotingProposals.sol:115-116, HybridVotingCore.sol:42-53), confirming this is a design-wide choice, not a one-off.\n\nHowever the claimed 'medium' severity overstates real impact. createProposal is gated by `onlyCreator` (line 352 → modifier lines 229-236), which requires the caller to hold a trusted org creator hat (or be the executor). There is NO unprivileged path. A malicious creator who wants to brick a poll has trivial equivalent alternatives: simply not create the poll, or create a restricted poll listing a single hat that nobody wears — both leave the poll unvotable with zero effort. The 5,000-fabricated-hat construction is a strictly worse way to accomplish sabotage that a trusted creator can already do. The realistic residual risk is a careless (not malicious) creator passing an oversized list, degrading gas for their own department's voters.
safetyReasoning: The mechanics are exactly as described. In _initProposal (src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:330-339) hatIds is copied into p.pollHatIds with NO length cap — unlike numOptions (capped at MAX_OPTIONS=50, line 281) and batch length (capped at MAX_CALLS=20, line 262). In vote() (lines 378-392) the restricted path performs a linear scan `for (i < pollHatLen)` calling `l.hats.isWearerOfHat(_msgSender(), p.pollHatIds[i])` per entry, breaking only on first match (line 385). isWearerOfHat wraps balanceOf (Hats.sol) which does SLOADs plus potential external eligibility/toggle staticcalls, so each iteration costs thousands of gas. Critically, an O(1) `pollHatAllowed` mapping IS populated at line 334 and is even documented as the "O(1) hat lookup" (docs/DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md:294), yet vote() ignores it and uses the O(n) array instead — a clear intent-vs-code mismatch. There is no guard, cap, or mitigation in the code that prevents a large pollHatIds array. HybridVotingCore.sol:45 has the identical unused-mapping pattern, confirming this is a systemic oversight, not intentional. No mitigation exists.

title: announceWinner is blocked while paused, letting the Executor permanently lock every proposal outcome (and their queued Executor calls)
description: announceWinner carries the whenNotPaused modifier. Pause/unpause are executor-gated (pause()/unpause() -> onlyExecutor). Because the winning batch of a proposal can only ever be executed inside announceWinner (there is no separate execute path and no way to finalize a proposal while paused), pausing the contract after a proposal's voting window closes but before finalization prevents the outcome from ever being announced or executed. Unlike vote() (where pausing merely halts new voting), blocking finalization is a terminal state for that proposal: votes are already cast and immutable, the endTimestamp has passed, and there is no un-pause-independent path to read out the winner on-chain or trigger the queued Executor calls.
impact: A compromised or malicious Executor-controlling majority can indefinitely censor any already-decided proposal it dislikes (e.g. one that would remove its own power), including proposals whose winning batch calls back into governance. Even absent malice, an emergency pause freezes not just new voting but the finalization/execution of all in-flight votes, which is a governance-liveness hazard.
scenario: 1. Org runs a proposal whose winning batch would replace the current voting module or slash a role. 2. The faction controlling the Executor waits until block.timestamp > endTimestamp. 3. Executor calls hv.pause(). 4. Anyone calling announceWinner(id) reverts with Paused(). 5. The proposal can never be finalized or executed while pause persists; the controlling faction simply never unpauses, permanently nullifying the vote.
recommendation: Remove whenNotPaused from announceWinner (finalizing an already-closed vote should not be pausable), or add an explicit non-pausable finalize path. Pausing should stop new votes/proposals, not the read-out and execution of completed ones.
exploitReasoning: The mechanical claims are accurate: announceWinner has whenNotPaused (src/HybridVoting.sol:292) and is the only finalization/execution path — it sets p.executed=true (src/libs/HybridVotingCore.sol:160) and executes the winning batch only inline (lines 220-229); no separate execute function exists. pause()/unpause() are onlyExecutor (src/HybridVoting.sol:178-184). However, the finding's severity/impact framing is wrong on two decisive points. (1) Pausing is NOT reachable by an unprivileged actor. pause() requires _msgSender()==executor (line 175), and Executor.execute only accepts the allowedCaller = the voting contract itself (src/Executor.sol:155-156). So triggering a pause requires a *winning governance proposal* whose batch calls hv.pause(). The "malicious faction controlling the Executor" is therefore a governance-majority actor, who already can swap the voting module, change the executor via setConfig(EXECUTOR) (lines 226-230), etc. — the pause DoS grants no capability beyond what that majority already holds. (2) The "permanent lock" claim is false. _paused is a single bool (line 71); proposal state (votes, endTimestamp, executed=false) persists across pause/unpause with no wipe. After unpause, announceWinner succeeds normally because endTimestamp has passed and executed is still false — so the block lasts only for the pause duration, not permanently, unless governance chooses never to unpause (a capture premise, not a code bug). The same whenNotPaused-on-announceWinner pattern exists in DirectDemocracyVoting (src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:419) and testPauseUnpause (test/HybridVoting.t.sol:326) confirms pause is an intentional executor-gated design.
safetyReasoning: The code property the finding describes is real. `announceWinner` (src/HybridVoting.sol:288-296) is the ONLY function that computes the winner and dispatches the queued Executor batch — there is no separate execute/finalize path and no unpause-independent winner readout (grep confirms only pause/unpause/setters and vote/announceWinner are mutating externals; `winner`/`executed` appear only inside announceWinner). It carries `whenNotPaused` (line 292), and the underlying HybridVotingCore.announceWinner (lines 156-231) is where the Executor.execute call happens (line 223). So while `_paused` is true, an already-expired, already-voted proposal genuinely cannot be finalized or executed: votes are immutable, endTimestamp has passed, and `_checkExpired` + the pause check both hold. DirectDemocracyVoting shares the identical pattern (lines 414-419). HOWEVER, `pause()`/`unpause()` are `onlyExecutor` (lines 178-184, _checkExecutor line 174-176). The Executor only runs batches that governance itself passed, so reaching a pause requires already controlling the governance majority / Executor — an entity that can also swap the executor via ConfigKey.EXECUTOR (line 226-230), rewrite classes/threshold, etc. It is NOT reachable by an unprivileged actor, so the "malicious majority censors a vote" scenario is not a privilege escalation — that actor already dominates governance. The one non-redundant risk is a legitimate emergency pause (intended to halt vote()) also freezing settlement of in-flight decided proposals until unpause — a recoverable, privileged-only liveness gap, not fund loss or unprivileged takeover.

title: deleteProject strands in-flight tasks and their budget accounting without checking for active tasks
description: deleteProject wipes l._projects[pid] (exists=false, spent=0, bountyBudgets cleared, all managers cleared) and clears per-project hat permission overrides, but does not verify the project has no non-terminal tasks. Tasks still store projectId=pid. completeTask (line 890) reads t.projectId and only checks REVIEW permission via _checkPerm — it never checks p.exists. After deletion the project's managers and project-specific perms are gone, so only the executor or a holder of a GLOBAL REVIEW hat can complete such a task, and completing it still mints PT (line 904) with no budget backing (spent was zeroed). Conversely, CLAIMED/SUBMITTED tasks with no global-REVIEW holder become permanently uncompletable and uncancellable (cancelTask is UNCLAIMED-only and also has no project to roll back into).
impact: Deleting a project with active tasks either (a) permanently locks claimers' completed work / bounty payouts (no reviewer can reach them, no cancel path), or (b) lets a global-REVIEW holder mint PT for tasks whose budget no longer exists, defeating per-project cap accounting. Reachable by any creator-hat wearer or executor via a single deleteProject call.
scenario: Creator creates project P with cap; a task under P is CLAIMED and SUBMITTED by a worker. A creator-hat holder calls deleteProject(P). P.managers and P's project REVIEW override are erased. If no one holds a global REVIEW hat, completeTask(id) reverts Unauthorized forever and cancelTask reverts BadStatus (not UNCLAIMED) — the worker's submitted work and any escrowed bounty are stranded.
recommendation: Block deleteProject when the project has any non-terminal task (track an activeTaskCount per project, incremented on create and decremented on complete/cancel), or require the project be drained first. At minimum document and gate the behavior so an admin cannot orphan claimed work.
exploitReasoning:
The finding rests on a false premise about Solidity `delete` semantics. `deleteProject` (line 468) does `delete l._projects[pid]`, but the `Project` struct (lines 113-120) contains two mappings — `managers` (line 114) and `bountyBudgets` (line 119). Solidity's `delete` cannot clear mapping members; only value fields (`cap`, `spent`, `exists`) are zeroed. So contrary to the finding, project managers and bounty budgets are NOT cleared.

Prong (a) permanent lock is refuted: `completeTask` (line 891) uses `_checkPerm` → `_isPM` bypass, and `_isPM` (line 1377) returns true for `who == l.executor` OR `p.managers[who]`. Since the executor (the DAO) is a universal PM and manager mapping entries survive `delete`, `completeTask`/`rejectTask` remain reachable by the executor and any pre-existing project manager. No task becomes permanently uncompletable.

Prong (b) cap-defeat over-mint is refuted: `completeTask` (lines 903-909) only mints `t.payout` and transfers bounty — it never adjusts `p.spent`. PT cap is enforced at creation (line 653) / assignment (line 1097). After deletion `exists=false`, and pid is never resurrected (set true only in `_createProjectCore` line 391 from `nextProjectId++` line 388), so `createTask` (line 648) and `assignTask` (line 1093) both revert `NotFound` — no new tasks can be minted against the defunct project. The zeroed `spent`/`cap` is therefore inert; there is no way to over-mint past a cap.
safetyReasoning: deleteProject (src/TaskManager.sol:440-470) executes `delete l._projects[pid]` (line 468) and wipes every project-specific permission override (lines 456-466) with NO check for non-terminal tasks. The test at test/TaskManager.t.sol:3842-3846 even creates a task under a project then deletes it, confirming the missing guard is intentional-but-unguarded behavior. Tasks retain projectId=pid. After deletion: (1) completeTask (line 888-891) calls `_checkPerm(pid, REVIEW)`; since `delete l._projects[pid]` cleared `p.managers`, `_isPM` (line 1375-1378) is false for everyone except `l.executor`, and `_permMask` (line 1367-1368) now falls back to `rolePermGlobal` only because `rolePermProj[pid][hat]` was deleted — so a SUBMITTED task can be completed ONLY by the executor or a wearer of a GLOBAL REVIEW hat. (2) cancelTask (line 940-944) is UNCLAIMED-only, so it reverts BadStatus for CLAIMED/SUBMITTED tasks. (3) For an UNCLAIMED task, cancelTask line 947 `if (p.spent < t.payout) revert SpentUnderflow()` also reverts because `delete` zeroed p.spent — so even the UNCLAIMED cancel path is broken (strengthens the finding beyond its own description). Bounty tokens are held by the contract and only released via completeTask's safeTransfer (line 908), so escrowed bounties on stranded tasks are unreachable without a completer. The finding's core claim (missing active-task guard → stranded work/bounties) is verified against real code.

title: Owner can finalize and reclaim a distribution before eligible users can claim, because the claim-period timer is anchored to checkpointBlock (in the past) instead of the creation block
description: finalizeDistribution gates on `block.number < dist.checkpointBlock + minClaimPeriodBlocks`. `checkpointBlock` is required to be strictly in the past at creation (line 139: `checkpointBlock >= block.number` reverts). The merkle snapshot is computed off-chain from the token's getPastVotes at `checkpointBlock`, which can legitimately be far in the past (e.g. a period boundary). The claim window that actually matters is measured from when the distribution is CREATED (that is when claimants first can call claimDistribution), not from the historical checkpoint. Because the timer is anchored to checkpointBlock, the real window available to claimants is `minClaimPeriodBlocks - (creationBlock - checkpointBlock)` blocks, which can be zero or negative.
impact: Unclaimed funds are returned to owner() (the Executor) prematurely; legitimate recipients who have not yet claimed lose their allocation for that distribution. This is an owner-controlled path, so it requires a malicious or careless Executor / governance action, but the on-chain guard that is supposed to protect claimants is ineffective.
scenario: 1) revenueShareToken checkpoint is at block 1000 (a real past period boundary). 2) At block 5000 the owner calls createDistribution(..., checkpointBlock=1000). Claimants can only begin claiming at block 5000. 3) The owner immediately calls finalizeDistribution(id, minClaimPeriodBlocks=4001). The guard checks `block.number (5000) < 1000 + 4001 = 5001` -> false at block 5001, so finalize succeeds one block after creation. 4) All unclaimed ETH/tokens are swept back to the owner before any recipient realistically claims. With minClaimPeriodBlocks <= (creationBlock - checkpointBlock) the window is entirely closed at creation time.
recommendation: Store the creation block (block.number at createDistribution) in the Distribution struct and anchor the finalize gate to `creationBlock + minClaimPeriodBlocks`, not `checkpointBlock + minClaimPeriodBlocks`. Alternatively enforce a minimum absolute deadline recorded at creation time.
exploitReasoning:
The mechanism the finding describes is real. In createDistribution, line 139 (`if (checkpointBlock >= block.number) revert InvalidCheckpoint();`) only requires checkpointBlock to be strictly in the past — it can legitimately be far in the past (e.g. a revenue-period boundary), and the merkle root is computed off-chain from getPastVotes at that block. Claimants cannot call claimDistribution until the distribution exists, i.e. the creation block. But finalizeDistribution line 275 gates on `block.number < dist.checkpointBlock + minClaimPeriodBlocks`, anchoring the timer to checkpointBlock rather than the creation block. So the window actually available to claimants is `minClaimPeriodBlocks - (creationBlock - checkpointBlock)`, which can be zero or negative. When unclaimed, funds are swept to owner() at lines 284-291, permanently barring those recipients from that distribution (claimDistribution reverts DistributionAlreadyFinalized once finalized, line 179). The arithmetic in the finding checks out.

However two facts limit the real severity. (1) minClaimPeriodBlocks is not a fixed protocol constant — it is an argument supplied by the owner at finalize time (line 269, `@param minClaimPeriodBlocks` in IPaymentManager.sol line 226). A malicious owner therefore does not need this bug at all: they can simply pass minClaimPeriodBlocks=0/1 and finalize immediately regardless of the anchor. This guard provides zero protection against a malicious owner, so the finding is not an unprivileged or privilege-escalation path. (2) The documented semantics in IPaymentManager.sol line 226 explicitly say "Minimum blocks that must pass since checkpoint" — so the code matches its stated intent; there is no code-vs-doc mismatch. The residual real issue is a footgun for an honest owner who passes a large minClaimPeriodBlocks expecting a real claim window measured from creation, while having chosen an old checkpoint — the window silently shrinks. All existing tests checkpoint at creationBlock-1 (e.g. PaymentManagerMerkle.t.sol lines 565-576), so they never exercise the old-checkpoint case.
safetyReasoning: The code matches the finding exactly. In createDistribution (src/PaymentManager.sol:139), `if (checkpointBlock >= block.number) revert InvalidCheckpoint();` forces checkpointBlock to be strictly before the creation block. In finalizeDistribution (lines 275-277), the guard is `if (block.number < dist.checkpointBlock + minClaimPeriodBlocks) revert ClaimPeriodNotExpired();` — anchored to checkpointBlock, not the creation block. Claimants cannot call claimDistribution until the distribution exists (creation block), yet the finalize timer already began counting at checkpointBlock. The effective claim window is `minClaimPeriodBlocks - (creationBlock - checkpointBlock)` blocks; if that gap >= minClaimPeriodBlocks the window is closed at/near creation. No mitigation exists in the code: there is no separate creationBlock field stored (the Distribution struct at lines 31-39 stores only checkpointBlock), and getDistribution/other paths never re-anchor the timer. The test suite masks this because every test sets `checkpointBlock = block.number` then `vm.roll(block.number + 1)` (e.g. lines 93/96), giving a fixed 1-block gap; test_RevertFinalizeDistribution_ClaimPeriodNotExpired only proves the guard fires with a fresh checkpoint, never with an old one. finalizeDistribution is onlyOwner (line 269), and owner is the Executor/governance, so triggering it requires a privileged action — this bounds severity to medium.

title: resolveRoleBitmap silently maps unconfigured roles to hat ID 0, producing a dead authorization entry instead of reverting
description: resolveRoleBitmap resolves each set bit to a hat ID via orgRegistry.getRoleHat(orgId, roleIdx). OrgRegistry.getRoleHat (src/OrgRegistry.sol:472-474) reads from a plain mapping and returns 0 for any roleIndex that was never registered for the org (no bounds check, no VersionUnknown-style revert). resolveRoleBitmap does not filter out zero results, so a bitmap bit pointing at an unconfigured/out-of-range role index yields hat ID 0 in the returned hatIds array. That 0 is then handed to HatManager.setHatInArray(...) during module initialization (e.g. GovernanceFactory.sol:245/275/279, ModulesFactory.sol, AccessFactory.sol) and stored as an authorized voting/creator/member hat. Because Hats Protocol never mints hat ID 0 (balanceOf(user,0)==0 for everyone — Hats.sol:1297 / isValidHatId requires id>0), the entry is permanently dead: it grants nobody the role and can never be satisfied. The mistake is silent — the org deploys 'successfully' but the intended role has no working authorization hat, and getHatCount/hat views report a bogus non-zero count that includes the dead 0 entry.
impact: An org configured with a roles bitmap whose bit index does not correspond to a registered role (off-by-one in the roles array, a role that failed to register, or a bit above the number of configured roles) deploys with a permission set that looks populated but contains an unusable hat 0. Whoever was supposed to hold that voting/creator/member permission cannot exercise it, and there is no error at deploy time to catch the misconfiguration. Fail-closed (not a takeover) but a real correctness footgun that can brick a role's governance rights until an executor manually fixes the hat array post-deploy.
scenario: 1. An org is deployed with 3 configured roles registered at indices 0,1,2 in OrgRegistry (roleHatOf[orgId][0..2] set). 2. The deploy config's ddCreatorRolesBitmap accidentally sets bit 3 (e.g. a 1-based vs 0-based mix-up, so bitmap=0b1000). 3. GovernanceFactory calls RoleResolver.resolveRoleBitmap(orgRegistry, orgId, 8); _countSetBits returns 1, the loop finds bit 3 set and calls getRoleHat(orgId, 3) which returns 0 (unregistered index). 4. hatIds = [0] is returned and passed into DirectDemocracyVoting init, which calls setHatInArray(l.creatorHatIds, 0, true) — creatorHatIds now = [0]. 5. Deployment succeeds with no revert. 6. The intended proposal-creator role holders call createProposal; HatManager.hasAnyHat checks balanceOf(user,0)==0 for all of them and reverts Unauthorized. The role's creation rights are silently disabled.
recommendation: In resolveRoleBitmap (and resolveRoleHats), skip or revert on hat ID 0: either revert with a custom error like UnregisteredRole(roleIdx) when getRoleHat returns 0, or drop zero entries and shrink the returned array (recompute count). Reverting is safer for a deploy-time path so misconfigurations surface immediately. Additionally, OrgRegistry.getRoleHat could reject roleIndex >= number of registered roles for the org.
exploitReasoning: The described mechanism is real end-to-end. OrgRegistry.getRoleHat (src/OrgRegistry.sol:472-474) reads a plain nested mapping roleHatOf[orgId][roleIndex] with no bounds check and no revert, so any unregistered/out-of-range roleIndex returns 0. RoleResolver.resolveRoleBitmap (src/libs/RoleResolver.sol:55-63) iterates set bits and does `hatIds[index] = orgRegistry.getRoleHat(orgId, roleIdx)` with no zero-filtering, so a bit at an unconfigured index produces a 0 entry in the returned array. That array is passed into module init (e.g. GovernanceFactory.sol:245/275/279 -> ModuleDeploymentLib -> DirectDemocracyVoting.initialize). DirectDemocracyVoting.initialize (src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:160-172) loops `HatManager.setHatInArray(l.creatorHatIds, initialCreatorHats[i], true)` unconditionally, and HatManager.setHatInArray (src/libs/HatManager.sol:24-42) pushes the hatId (including 0) without filtering. Hats Protocol never mints hat 0, so hasAnyHat (HatManager.sol:51-58) via isWearerOfHat returns false for that entry for every user. Net: the intended role has a permanently dead authorization hat, deploy succeeds silently, and creatorHats()/getHatCount report a bogus non-zero count including the 0 entry. No guard anywhere rejects hat 0.

title: depositToEntryPoint credits no org accounting — operator funds are silently donated to the shared pool
description: depositToEntryPoint forwards msg.value to EntryPoint.depositTo(address(this)) but never touches _getFinancialsStorage()[orgId].deposited, org.periodStart, or solidarity.numActiveOrgs. The docs (docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md line 591, 'Operator Hat ... Deposit to EntryPoint (fund paymaster)') present this as the way an operator funds their org. In reality the deposited ETH is added to the raw EntryPoint balance the hub uses to pay the network, but the org's on-chain budget (deposited/spent) is unchanged, so _checkOrgBalance and _updateOrgFinancials still see the org as unfunded. The funds effectively subsidize the global pool / whichever orgs happen to spend, not the depositing org.
impact: An operator following the documented funding flow loses the org's money to the shared pool: the org gets zero credit toward its deposit balance / tier / solidarity match, while the ETH is consumed paying gas for arbitrary orgs. This is a fund-misattribution footgun that directly contradicts the documentation.
scenario: 1. Org Beta's operator calls depositToEntryPoint{value: 0.5 ether}(beta) intending to fund Beta. 2. getOrgFinancials(beta).deposited is still 0; Beta remains 'unfunded' and, post-grace, cannot pass _checkSolidarityAccess (InsufficientDepositForSolidarity). 3. The 0.5 ETH sits in the EntryPoint and is spent paying gas for any org's UserOps until exhausted. Beta received no benefit.
recommendation: Either remove depositToEntryPoint, or make it call _depositForOrg(orgId, msg.value) so org.deposited is credited exactly like depositForOrg. If a shared-pool concept is truly intended, document it explicitly and separate it from per-org accounting.
exploitReasoning: The finding's core premise — that `depositToEntryPoint` is documented as "the way an operator funds their org" and therefore misattributes org funds — is false. The contract itself documents this function as the SHARED POOL top-up, not org funding: src/PaymasterHub.sol lines 1173-1175 read "Deposit funds to EntryPoint for gas reimbursement (shared pool)" and "Any org operator can deposit to shared pool." It intentionally does NOT touch per-org accounting. The dedicated org-funding function is `depositForOrg` / `_depositForOrg` (lines 503-569), which credits `org.deposited` (line 548), initializes/resets `org.periodStart` (lines 553-556), and increments `solidarity.numActiveOrgs` (lines 560-562). The docs consistently use `depositForOrg` for org funding in every worked example: docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md lines 232, 694, 722, 763, and lines 238-241 explicitly list what `depositForOrg` increments. The doc bullet the finding cites (line 591, "Deposit to EntryPoint (fund paymaster)") is an operator-permission list item that correctly describes topping up the paymaster's shared EntryPoint balance — a necessary ERC-4337 liquidity operation (the hub must hold EntryPoint balance to sponsor any UserOp). The test at test/PasskeyPaymasterIntegration.t.sol:167-173 confirms the two are distinct, complementary ledgers: line 168 comment "Fund PaymasterHub via EntryPoint deposit" then line 171 comment "Deposit for org in PaymasterHub" — both are called in setup. No ETH is "lost": it does exactly what the name and NatSpec say (raises the shared EntryPoint balance the hub draws from to pay the network).
safetyReasoning:
The mechanics in the finding are fully verified. `depositToEntryPoint` (src/PaymasterHub.sol:1177-1183) only calls `IEntryPoint.depositTo{value: msg.value}(address(this))` and emits `DepositIncrease`. It never writes `org.deposited`, `org.periodStart`, or `solidarity.numActiveOrgs`. The spending gates read exclusively from those tracked fields: `_checkSolidarityAccess` (line 455) computes `depositAvailable = org.deposited - org.spent` and reverts `InsufficientDepositForSolidarity` (line 476) when `depositAvailable < grace.minDepositRequired`; `_checkOrgBalance` (line 696) and `_updateOrgFinancials` (line 935) use the same field. So an operator's ETH raises only the physical shared EntryPoint balance (`IEntryPoint.balanceOf(address(this))`, line 1181) that reimburses bundlers for ALL orgs, while the depositing org's tracked budget stays 0 and, post-grace, still fails `InsufficientDepositForSolidarity`. The correct org-funding function is the permissionless `depositForOrg` (line 503 → `_depositForOrg`, lines 548/553/562), which does credit `deposited`/`periodStart`/`numActiveOrgs`; `donateToSolidarity` (line 575) credits `solidarity.balance`. Neither is what `depositToEntryPoint` does.

Where I diverge from the finding: the code's own NatSpec (lines 1174-1175) explicitly labels this function "Deposit funds to EntryPoint for gas reimbursement (shared pool)" and "Any org operator can deposit to shared pool" — i.e., the contract-level intent IS a pool contribution, and the function behaves as its own doc-comment says. The docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md canonical funding example (line 232) also correctly uses `depositForOrg`. The real defect is the misleading operator-permission bullet docs/PAYMASTER_HUB.md:591 "Deposit to EntryPoint (fund paymaster)" combined with the function name, which invites an operator to misuse `depositToEntryPoint` as org funding. This is a genuine correctness/UX footgun (CONFIRMED) but not high severity: no unprivileged actor loss, no attacker theft, no lock — an operator voluntarily donates their own org's ETH to the common physical pool by following a misleading bullet. That is medium.

title: PoaManager owner can push arbitrary (malicious/incompatible) implementation to every Mirror-mode org with no allowlist, timelock, or storage-layout check
description: upgradeBeacon() only checks newImpl != address(0) and newImpl.code.length > 0, then calls beacon.upgradeTo(newImpl). Every org SwitchableBeacon running in Mirror mode reads this global beacon's implementation() live, so the new impl becomes the delegatecall target for all mirror-mode orgs in the same transaction. There is no allowlist of vetted implementations, no timelock/delay, and no storage-layout compatibility check. In production the PoaManager owner is a single EOA (0xA6F4...b2c9) via Hub/Satellite; ownership is a plain Ownable/Ownable2Step chain with no multisig enforced in-contract.
impact: A compromised or malicious PoaManager owner (single EOA) instantly gains full control of the logic executed by every Mirror-mode org: it can drain org funds, mint governance tokens, rewrite Hats, or brick storage across the entire protocol in one tx. This is the single largest authority concentration in the subsystem.
scenario: 1. Attacker compromises the owner EOA of PoaManagerHub (or the EOA that owns PoaManager directly on a satellite). 2. Attacker deploys a malicious ParticipationToken impl with a backdoor mint(). 3. Attacker calls Hub.upgradeBeaconLocal("ParticipationToken", malicious, "v99") → poaManager.upgradeBeacon → beacon.upgradeTo(malicious). 4. Every org whose ParticipationToken SwitchableBeacon is in Mirror mode now delegatecalls the malicious impl on the next call; attacker mints tokens / drains value across all such orgs. No org action or delay intervenes.
recommendation: This is partly by-design centralization, but harden it: (a) require the PoaManager owner to be a multisig/timelock in deployment docs and ideally enforce a timelock on upgradeBeacon so Mirror-mode orgs get a warning window to pin; (b) consider validating newImpl against an on-chain allowlist / the registry before pushing; (c) document prominently that Mirror mode is a live trust delegation to the protocol owner. At minimum add a mandatory delay + event so orgs can pinToCurrent() defensively.
exploitReasoning: The technical call path in the finding is real and fully verified. PoaManager.upgradeBeacon (src/PoaManager.sol:93-106) guards only `newImpl == address(0)` (line 94) and `newImpl.code.length == 0` (line 95), then unconditionally calls `beacon.upgradeTo(newImpl)` (line 103) — no allowlist, no timelock/delay, no storage-layout compatibility check. The beacon here is the org-shared `UpgradeableBeacon` created in `addContractType` (line 79). BeaconDeploymentLib.createBeacon (src/libs/BeaconDeploymentLib.sol:31,45) wires each org's SwitchableBeacon `mirrorBeacon` to exactly this PoaManager `UpgradeableBeacon` (`poa.getBeaconById(typeId)`). SwitchableBeacon.implementation() in Mirror mode reads `IBeacon(mirrorBeacon).implementation()` live (src/SwitchableBeacon.sol:82-84), so a new impl becomes the delegatecall target for every Mirror-mode org in the same tx. Access is a plain single-owner chain: PoaManager is `Ownable(msg.sender)` (PoaManager.sol:9), reachable via PoaManagerHub.upgradeBeaconLocal/upgradeBeaconCrossChain (src/crosschain/PoaManagerHub.sol:64,77 — `onlyOwner`, Ownable2Step) and PoaManagerSatellite.upgradeBeaconDirect (src/crosschain/PoaManagerSatellite.sol:115-119). Per project docs the production owner is a single EOA (0xA6F4...b2c9). So the mechanism (all-org logic swap with no delay/allowlist/layout check, controlled by one EOA) is exactly as described. What downgrades this from the claimed 'high' unprivileged-risk: the ONLY actor who can trigger it is the most-trusted protocol key (owner). This is the intended, documented BeaconProxy upgrade model — SwitchableBeacon explicitly offers Mirror as sovereignty tier 1 ('org auto-follows the POA global beacon'), with Static/custom-beacon tiers (pin/pinToCurrent/setMirror, SwitchableBeacon.sol:96-126) as the opt-out for orgs that don't want to trust the protocol owner. There is no privilege-escalation or unprivileged path — it is a centralization/trust-concentration and missing-timelock observation, not an exploitable bug.
safetyReasoning: The technical mechanics are accurate but describe the intended, inescapable behavior of a BeaconProxy upgrade system, not a code defect. PoaManager.upgradeBeacon (src/PoaManager.sol:93-106) is gated by `onlyOwner` and only calls `beacon.upgradeTo(newImpl)` after zero-address/code-length/same-impl checks — this is exactly what OpenZeppelin's UpgradeableBeacon is designed to do. SwitchableBeacon.implementation() (src/SwitchableBeacon.sol:81-90) reads `IBeacon(mirrorBeacon).implementation()` live in Mirror mode, so a global upgrade does propagate to all Mirror-mode orgs — but Mirror mode is a *voluntary, org-owned* choice (`autoUpgrade=true`, SwitchableBeacon owner is the org's Executor). The design explicitly documents three sovereignty tiers (SWITCHABLE_BEACON.md:9-17, 30-31): an org that does not want to delegate upgrade authority to POA runs in Static mode (pin/pinToCurrent, lines 111-126) or setMirror() to its own custom beacon. Choosing Mirror mode is definitionally choosing to follow POA's beacon. No unprivileged actor can trigger upgradeBeacon — every path (PoaManagerHub.upgradeBeaconLocal/CrossChain lines 64-79, adminCall) is `onlyOwner`. There is no missing guard whose absence is a bug; the proposed allowlist/timelock/storage-layout check are design-hardening ideas, and none of them can remove the beacon owner's fundamental authority without removing the upgrade feature itself.

title: createDepositFromBalance requestHash derived from block.timestamp can collide and permanently strand recovery funds
description: createDepositFromBalance builds requestHash = keccak256(abi.encode(params.depositor, block.timestamp)). If the ZKP2P deposit creation fails (escrow reverts), it records failedDepositor[requestHash]/failedAmount[requestHash]. Two owner calls with the same depositor in the same block (or an earlier failed record with the identical (depositor, timestamp)) collide: the second call hits `if (failedDepositor[requestHash] != address(0)) revert RequestHashAlreadyFailed()`, which reverts the whole call and drops the second batch of funds into an unrecoverable state for that call, or (if the first was a success and second fails) can associate a recovery record whose amount does not match the actually-held balance. Because available is the FULL current balance each time, a failed createDepositFromBalance records failedAmount = entire balance including any other users' fresh funds, and totalFailedAmount is bumped by the whole balance — cross-contaminating unrelated deliveries into one depositor's recovery record.
impact: Owner-triggered footgun that can mis-assign recovery funds or block a legitimate second deposit; in the cross-contamination case a failed createDepositFromBalance assigns ALL relay USDC (including another user's freshly delivered funds) to a single depositor's recoverFailed claim.
scenario: 1. User A's 50 USDC is delivered but not yet deposited. 2. Owner calls createDepositFromBalance(depositor=B) intending to process B's separate 30 USDC delivery, but available = balanceOf - totalFailedAmount = 80 (A's 50 + B's 30). 3. Escrow reverts. 4. failedDepositor[hash]=B, failedAmount[hash]=80, totalFailedAmount=80. 5. B calls recoverFailed and drains 80 USDC — including A's 50.
recommendation: Derive requestHash from a monotonic nonce or an explicit per-delivery identifier rather than block.timestamp, and pass an explicit amount to createDepositFromBalance (bounded by available) rather than sweeping the entire balance, so unrelated deliveries are not co-mingled into one recovery record.
exploitReasoning: Confirmed the code matches the citation. In createDepositFromBalance (src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:260-277): line 264 `available = IERC20(usdc).balanceOf(address(this)) - totalFailedAmount` captures the ENTIRE non-reserved relay balance; line 268 attempts the deposit with that full `available`; on escrow failure lines 272-274 set `failedDepositor[requestHash]=params.depositor`, `failedAmount[requestHash]=available`, `totalFailedAmount += available`. Because the amount is the whole balance rather than a per-delivery amount, any other user's still-un-deposited USDC co-resident in the relay is swept into a single depositor's deposit (on success) or recovery record (on failure). recoverFailed (line 282-295) then lets that depositor drain the full `failedAmount`, i.e. another user's funds. This is a genuine logic property, and it is unique to createDepositFromBalance — executeData (line 135-155) uses `expectedAmount = amounts[0]` (a specific delivered amount), NOT the whole balance, so it does not cross-contaminate. The finding correctly isolates the bug to this function. However two parts of the finding are overstated: (1) the requestHash=keccak256(abi.encode(depositor, block.timestamp)) collision on line 267 causes at most a same-block revert (RequestHashAlreadyFailed on line 271), and a revert leaves funds in the contract to be re-processed in a later block — it does NOT "permanently strand" funds; (2) the whole path is owner-only (line 261 `if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner()`), so it is an operational footgun requiring an owner to trigger it while another user's funds are un-processed in the shared multi-tenant relay, not an unprivileged exploit. No unit test exercises createDepositFromBalance; the e2e script (script/cashout/cashout-e2e.mjs:189) confirms the intended usage is to sweep the full balance for one user, implicitly assuming single-tenant timing.
safetyReasoning:
createDepositFromBalance (src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:260-277) is owner-only (line 261: `if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner()`), so nothing here is reachable by an unprivileged actor — every scenario requires a trusted-operator mistake. Two of the finding's sub-claims hold as real properties of the code, but its "permanently strand" framing is refuted:

(1) requestHash = keccak256(abi.encode(params.depositor, block.timestamp)) (line 267) is indeed a weak, collidable hash. However the collision guard (line 271) only fires on the FAILURE path, and it only matters when a PRIOR FAILED record already exists for the identical (depositor, timestamp). When that revert fires, the second batch of fresh funds is NOT written to failedAmount and totalFailedAmount is NOT bumped (lines 272-274 never execute), so those funds are neither reserved nor lost — the owner can retry next block or sweep them via emergencyRecover (line 317, which only blocks withdrawals below totalFailedAmount, line 323). So "permanently strand recovery funds" is overstated; funds are recoverable.

(2) The cross-contamination claim is accurate as an inherent design property, not a failure-path-only bug: createDepositFromBalance takes no amount parameter and sweeps the ENTIRE free balance `available = balanceOf - totalFailedAmount` (line 264) into one depositor on BOTH the success path (line 268 deposits `available` to params.depositor's escrow) and the failure path (line 273 records failedAmount=available for params.depositor). Compare executeData (line 135, uses per-request amounts[0]) and completeCashOut (line 238, uses freshly-minted `minted`), both of which scope to a specific request. createDepositFromBalance is the outlier with no scoping. So if two users' undeposited funds coexist in the relay and the owner calls this for user B, all funds (including A's) are assigned to B — either deposited into B's escrow order or recorded under B's recoverFailed claim. There is notably NO unit test for createDepositFromBalance, unlike the other two entry paths.

title: Live (non-snapshot) eligibility lets a batch mint voting/creator hats mid-lifecycle; combined with no snapshot this can shift outcomes across sequential proposals
description: Voter eligibility is evaluated live at vote() time via HatManager.hasAnyHat / isWearerOfHat with no block/timestamp snapshot. There is likewise no snapshot of totalWeight semantics beyond the running tally. Because announceWinner can execute arbitrary whitelisted batches (e.g. minting or burning hats through the Executor), passing one proposal can change who is eligible to vote on concurrently-open proposals. Eligibility can also be granted/revoked by an admin at any point during the voting window.
impact: Outcome manipulation is possible where an org runs overlapping proposals: proposal A's execution mints voting hats to a faction that then swings still-open proposal B. This is a known trade-off of hat-based live eligibility but is not documented as a constraint, and the docs advertise 'one person one vote' equality.
scenario: 1. Proposals A and B are open simultaneously. 2. A passes and its batch mints the voting hat to N new addresses controlled by one faction. 3. Those addresses immediately vote on still-open B, tilting it. Each address is a distinct 100-point voter, so equal-weight accounting does not prevent the swing.
recommendation: Document the live-eligibility model explicitly, and consider recording eligibility/turnout as of proposal creation or first vote if orgs run concurrent proposals. At minimum warn operators not to schedule hat-mutating executions to overlap with other open votes.
exploitReasoning: The mechanics described are real. Voter eligibility is evaluated live at vote() time with no snapshot: DirectDemocracyVoting.sol line 374 `HatManager.hasAnyHat(l.hats, l.votingHatIds, _msgSender())` and, for restricted polls, line 383 `l.hats.isWearerOfHat(_msgSender(), p.pollHatIds[i])`. Neither reads a per-proposal snapshot of hat-wearership or a block/timestamp checkpoint — the vote counts `p.totalWeight += 100` (line 400) purely off whoever holds the hat at call time. announceWinner (line 414-444) executes arbitrary whitelisted batches through the Executor (`l.executor.execute(id, batch)`, line 438). Executor.sol shows the Executor can indeed cause hats to be minted: `mintHatsForUser` (line 141) mints via `l.hats.mintHat`, and a passed batch can call any whitelisted target (including the Hats contract directly, since batch targets other than the Executor itself are permitted — only `target == address(this)` is blocked at Executor.sol line 162). Therefore proposal A's execution can add voting-hat wearers who then vote on a still-open proposal B, since B re-derives eligibility live. Config-level admin (executor) can also add/remove voting hats mid-window via setConfig HAT_ALLOWED (line 213-220). Docs reinforce the intent mismatch: ORG_DEPLOYER.md line 83 and POP_OVERVIEW.md line 286 advertise DDV as "one-person-one-vote" equality, while HYBRID_VOTING.md (lines 473, 478-483) explicitly documents the analogous live-read caveat for its ERC20_BAL class — DDV has no such documented constraint.
safetyReasoning: The finding accurately describes the code. In vote() (DirectDemocracyVoting.sol), eligibility is evaluated live with no snapshot: line 374 calls HatManager.hasAnyHat(l.hats, l.votingHatIds, _msgSender()) and lines 382-390 call l.hats.isWearerOfHat(_msgSender(), p.pollHatIds[i]) against current hat wearership. There is no per-proposal block/timestamp snapshot anywhere in the contract, and totalWeight (line 400) is a running tally, not a fixed electorate — each distinct voter contributes a fixed +100 (lines 399-401). announceWinner (lines 428-442) executes the winning option's arbitrary whitelisted batch via l.executor.execute(id, batch) with only a target-allowlist check (line 433); the Executor can mint hats (Executor.sol:141-148 mintHatsForUser -> hats.mintHat) and setConfig HAT_ALLOWED is executor-gated (lines 213-220), so a passing proposal can change the eligible electorate for concurrently-open proposals. The docs advertise "one person one vote" equality (docs/ORG_DEPLOYER.md:83, docs/POP_OVERVIEW.md:286) without documenting this live-eligibility caveat, whereas HybridVoting's docs explicitly warn about the analogous live-read manipulation (docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md:478-483). No guard refutes the finding: hasVoted (line 393) is per-address and does not stop newly-minted distinct addresses from voting. The claim stands.

title: announceWinner and Executor do not block the voting contract itself as an execution target, so a whitelisted self-call can invoke executor-gated admin functions
description: The docs (DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md 'Security Checks' / 'Target not self') claim announceWinner reverts TargetSelf if a batch targets address(this). The code does not implement this check — it only verifies allowedTarget (lines 433). The Executor's TargetSelf guard (Executor.sol line 162) protects only against the Executor calling itself, not against calling back into DirectDemocracyVoting. Since batches run via the Executor and onlyExecutor checks msg.sender == executor, a winning batch that targets the (whitelisted) voting contract can successfully call setConfig, pause, unpause, or even vote as the executor.
impact: Any state that onlyExecutor guards (executor address, threshold, quorum, target allowlist, hat allowlist, pause) can be changed by a passing proposal without an explicit governance intent to grant that — it looks like a normal option batch. This is gated behind a passing vote and the target being whitelisted, so it is a governance-authorized path rather than an unprivileged exploit, but it contradicts the documented self-call protection and can surprise operators (e.g. a batch that flips the executor to an attacker if the proposal passes).
scenario: 1. A creator whitelists the DirectDemocracyVoting proxy as an allowed target (itself a governance action, or done at init via initialTargets). 2. A proposal option batch calls dd.setConfig(EXECUTOR, attacker). 3. The option wins and announceWinner->executor.execute calls back into dd.setConfig with msg.sender==executor, passing onlyExecutor and swapping the executor. Executor's TargetSelf check does not fire because target is the voting contract, not the Executor.
recommendation: Add an explicit self-target guard in _validateTargets and in the announceWinner pre-execution loop: revert TargetSelf if batch[i].target == address(this). This matches the documented behavior and prevents a proposal from covertly reconfiguring the governor.
exploitReasoning: The docs (docs/DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md lines 614, 620-634, 650) explicitly claim announceWinner reverts TargetSelf when a batch targets the voting contract, showing the code snippet `if (batch[i].target == address(this)) revert VotingErrors.TargetSelf();`. The actual code does NOT implement this. In `_validateTargets` (src/DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:260-269) and the pre-execution loop in `announceWinner` (lines 432-437), the only check is `!l.allowedTarget[batch[i].target]` — there is no `address(this)` comparison. `VotingErrors.TargetSelf` (src/libs/VotingErrors.sol:21) is defined but never referenced anywhere in DirectDemocracyVoting.sol (grep confirms 0 uses). The Executor's guard at src/Executor.sol:162 only blocks `batch[i].target == address(this)` where `this` is the Executor — it does not block calls back into the voting contract. The onlyExecutor modifier (line 184-187) checks `_msgSender() == address(_layout().executor)`, so a call originating from `executor.execute` into `dd.setConfig`/`pause`/`unpause` passes. No test asserts self-target rejection for DDV.
safetyReasoning: The finding is accurate. In DirectDemocracyVoting.sol `announceWinner` (lines 430-442) the only pre-execution validation is the whitelist check `if (!l.allowedTarget[batch[i].target]) revert TargetNotAllowed();` (line 433). There is NO `address(this)` / `TargetSelf` check anywhere in the contract (grep confirms `TargetSelf` and `address(this)` appear zero times in the file, even though `VotingErrors.TargetSelf` exists, line 21). The documentation explicitly claims otherwise: docs/DIRECT_DEMOCRACY_VOTING.md line 614 ("Target not self: Cannot call the voting contract itself"), line 626 shows a phantom `if (batch[i].target == address(this)) revert VotingErrors.TargetSelf();` line that is not in the real code, and line 650 lists "self-call prevention" as a protection. Executor.sol line 162 (`if (batch[i].target == address(this)) revert TargetSelf();`) only blocks the Executor from calling itself, not from calling back into the voting proxy. The onlyExecutor modifier (line 185) gates setConfig/pause/unpause on `_msgSender() == executor`; when Executor.execute (line 164) low-level-calls back into the whitelisted voting proxy, msg.sender IS the executor, so those admin functions succeed. ddInitialTargets is caller-supplied (GovernanceFactory line 298), and TARGET_ALLOWED can be set via setConfig (line 209), so the voting proxy can become its own allowed target. A winning option batch can therefore call setConfig(EXECUTOR, attacker), pause, or unpause. Note nonReentrant (line 416) does prevent re-entering announceWinner itself, but setConfig/pause/unpause carry no reentrancy guard, so they remain reachable from within the execute() batch.

title: vote() uses require() with a string message, violating the project's custom-errors-only hard rule and breaking uniform revert handling
description: Line 101 uses require(VotingMath.fitsUint128(newVal), "Class raw overflow"). The project hard rules explicitly forbid require() with string messages ('use custom errors: if (cond) revert CustomError()'). VotingErrors already defines Overflow() (VotingErrors.sol:26) for exactly this. Beyond the style violation, string-revert reasons are not machine-decodable the way the rest of the subsystem's custom errors are, so off-chain tooling and callers that switch on error selectors will not recognize this failure.
impact: Inconsistent error surface; a hit here reverts the entire vote with an opaque string instead of the Overflow() selector. Primarily a correctness/hygiene issue, but it also means the one place a voter can DoS an option (see the classRaw overflow scenario) surfaces a non-standard error.
scenario: A very large linear ERC20_BAL power plus repeated votes pushes p.options[ix].classRaw[c] toward uint128.max; the require fires with a string instead of the standard Overflow() custom error, and CI/slither/style gates and selector-based clients mis-handle it.
recommendation: Replace with: if (!VotingMath.fitsUint128(newVal)) revert VotingErrors.Overflow();
exploitReasoning: src/libs/HybridVotingCore.sol:101 literally reads `require(VotingMath.fitsUint128(newVal), "Class raw overflow");` — a `require()` with a string message. This is the sole such usage in the HybridVoting subsystem (grep confirms only one require across HybridVoting*.sol and HybridVoting.sol). The project hard rule ("Do NOT use require() with string messages — use custom errors: if (cond) revert CustomError()") is violated. VotingErrors.sol:26 already defines `error Overflow();`, which is the exact custom error that should be used here. Every other revert in vote() uses the VotingErrors custom-error pattern (lines 33, 34, 53, 56, 87), making this the lone inconsistent revert. The claim about off-chain/selector-based tooling is technically true: a string-revert encodes as Error(string) rather than the 4-byte Overflow() selector, so clients switching on custom-error selectors won't recognize it. The overflow itself (newVal > uint128.max ≈ 3.4e38) is real but only reachable at astronomically large accumulated classRaw values, which the finding correctly does not claim as an easy exploit — the substantive claim is the style/error-surface violation, which is directly verified in code.
safetyReasoning: HybridVotingCore.sol:101 reads `require(VotingMath.fitsUint128(newVal), "Class raw overflow");` — a require with a string message. This is the only such occurrence in the HybridVoting library files (grep confirms exactly one match across HybridVoting*.sol and HybridVoting.sol). The project's CLAUDE.md hard rule explicitly forbids this: "Do NOT use require() with string messages — use custom errors: if (cond) revert CustomError()." A suitable custom error already exists: VotingErrors.Overflow() at VotingErrors.sol:26, and the rest of vote() consistently uses VotingErrors (e.g. line 87 `revert VotingErrors.Unauthorized()`). fitsUint128 is defined at VotingMath.sol:401 and the check itself is correct/functional; the defect is purely the non-standard, non-selector-decodable revert surface. No mitigating guard or intended-design reason justifies the string message — the surrounding code proves the custom-error pattern was the intended convention here.

title: MIN_DURATION diverges between the facade (1) and the library that enforces it (10), making the documented/advertised minimum wrong
description: HybridVoting.MIN_DURATION is a public constant = 1 (commented '1 min for testing'), but the actual enforcement lives in HybridVotingProposals._validateDuration which uses HybridVotingProposals.MIN_DURATION = 10 (HybridVotingProposals.sol:16). The facade constant is purely cosmetic — createProposal delegates to the library — so external readers of hv.MIN_DURATION() (and the docs table which lists MIN_DURATION = 1 min) are told 1 minute is allowed, while any minutesDuration in [1..9] reverts DurationOutOfRange(). MAX_DURATION matches (both 43_200), so only the floor is inconsistent.
impact: Integrators/UIs that read the public MIN_DURATION constant or follow docs will build proposals with durations 1-9 that always revert. Confusing but not a fund/authority risk.
scenario: A front-end reads HybridVoting.MIN_DURATION() == 1, offers a 5-minute poll, and every such createProposal call reverts DurationOutOfRange because the library floor is 10.
recommendation: Make the facade constant reference or equal the library's enforced value (single source of truth), and fix the docs table (docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md lists 'MIN_DURATION | 1 min' and createProposal comment says '10 min - 30 days').
exploitReasoning: The two constants genuinely diverge and only the library one is enforced. src/HybridVoting.sol:22 declares `uint32 public constant MIN_DURATION = 1; /* 1 min for testing */`. This constant is never referenced in any enforcement path — the facade's `createProposal` (HybridVoting.sol:271-280) does zero duration validation itself and delegates the whole call to `HybridVotingProposals.createProposal` (line 279). Inside the library, `_initProposal` calls `_validateDuration(minutesDuration)` (HybridVotingProposals.sol:66), which reverts `VotingErrors.DurationOutOfRange()` when `minutesDuration < MIN_DURATION` using the library's own `MIN_DURATION = 10` (HybridVotingProposals.sol:16, 126-130). So any `minutesDuration` in [1..9] reverts, even though `hv.MIN_DURATION()` returns 1. MAX_DURATION agrees in both files (43_200), so only the floor is inconsistent. The docs table also advertises the wrong value: docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md:497 lists `MIN_DURATION | 1 min | Testing floor`, matching the cosmetic facade constant, not the enforced 10.
safetyReasoning: HybridVoting.sol:22 defines `uint32 public constant MIN_DURATION = 1` (comment "1 min for testing"), a publicly readable constant. The facade createProposal (HybridVoting.sol:279) delegates entirely to HybridVotingProposals.createProposal and never references the facade's own MIN_DURATION. Actual enforcement is HybridVotingProposals._validateDuration (line 127): `if (minutesDuration < MIN_DURATION || minutesDuration > MAX_DURATION) revert VotingErrors.DurationOutOfRange();` where the library's MIN_DURATION = 10 (line 16). MAX_DURATION agrees (43_200 in both). No other guard reconciles the two constants — the facade value is cosmetic. docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md:497 (`| MIN_DURATION | 1 min | Testing floor |`) mirrors the wrong facade value, so both the on-chain public getter and the docs advertise a 1-minute floor that the library rejects for any minutesDuration in [1..9].

title: HybridVotingLens contains dead/placeholder methods that return misleading constants (always-true active check, always-zero end timestamp)
description: getProposalEndTimestamp always returns 0 with a comment that the real getter 'would need to be exposed' (it returns a hardcoded 0 after only validating the proposal exists). isProposalActive returns `pollRestricted(id) || !pollRestricted(id)`, which is unconditionally true for any existing proposal and reverts for non-existing ones — it conveys no activity information at all. These are shipped view helpers a front-end or integrator may call by name and trust.
impact: Any caller relying on getProposalEndTimestamp gets 0 (appears expired/at-epoch) and isProposalActive gets true for every proposal (including finalized/expired ones). This can drive incorrect UI/keeper decisions (e.g. attempting to vote on a closed proposal, or believing a proposal is still open). No on-chain fund risk, but it is a correctness trap in a shipped contract.
scenario: A keeper calls Lens.isProposalActive(id) to decide whether to keep polling for votes; it returns true even after endTimestamp has passed, so the keeper never transitions to announceWinner. Or a UI shows endTimestamp=0 for all proposals.
recommendation: Either expose a real endTimestamp getter on HybridVoting and implement these correctly (compare block.timestamp to endTimestamp), or remove the placeholder functions so integrators cannot depend on misleading return values.
exploitReasoning: Read src/lens/HybridVotingLens.sol in full. Line 17: getProposalEndTimestamp validates the proposal exists (via getProposalClasses at line 13, which carries HybridVoting's exists(id) modifier) then returns a hardcoded `0`, with a self-admitting comment on lines 15-16 ("End timestamp would need to be exposed via a new getter"). Confirmed against src/HybridVoting.sol: the Proposal struct DOES store a real endTimestamp (line 45, used in announceWinner at line 267), but no external getter exposes it, so the Lens genuinely cannot return the true value and instead returns 0. Line 35: isProposalActive returns `voting.pollRestricted(id) || !voting.pollRestricted(id)`, a logical tautology — pollRestricted (line 315, exists(id) modifier) returns a bool, so `x || !x` is unconditionally true for any existing proposal and reverts for nonexistent ones. Lines 33-34 comments explicitly label it a "placeholder." Grep found ZERO callers, tests, or scripts referencing HybridVotingLens, getProposalEndTimestamp, or isProposalActive anywhere in src/test/script, confirming these are unwired placeholders. The methods also use `revert("Invalid proposal")` string reverts (lines 14), violating the project's custom-errors-only rule.
safetyReasoning: The cited code matches the finding exactly. In src/lens/HybridVotingLens.sol: (1) getProposalEndTimestamp (lines 12-18) calls voting.getProposalClasses(id) — which carries the exists(id) modifier and reverts for nonexistent proposals — then unconditionally `return 0;` with a comment "End timestamp would need to be exposed via a new getter... For now, this demonstrates the pattern". The real value exists: HybridVoting.sol:44-45 declares `struct Proposal { uint64 endTimestamp; ... }` and HybridVotingProposals.sol:87 sets it, HybridVotingCore.sol:34 and HybridVoting.sol:267 use it for VotingExpired/VotingOpen, so a correct end timestamp is available in storage but the Lens never reads it. (2) isProposalActive (lines 32-36) returns `voting.pollRestricted(id) || !voting.pollRestricted(id)` — a logical tautology that is always true for any proposal that exists (pollRestricted at HybridVoting.sol:315 has exists(id), reverting for nonexistent ones), with its own comment "This is a placeholder showing the lens pattern". No mitigation exists; these are genuine placeholder returns. grep confirms HybridVotingLens is not imported, deployed, or referenced by any other .sol file, so there is no on-chain consumer that could be misled.

title: createProposal's batch target validation is effectively a no-op (only checks call count, not targets), contradicting the documented 'target allowlist' protection
description: _validateTargets (lines 132-135) only checks batch.length <= MAX_CALLS; it validates nothing about the targets themselves. The Layout.allowedTarget mapping and the TARGET_ALLOWED config path are deprecated/no-ops, and initialize explicitly notes 'HybridVoting passes batches directly to Executor without target restrictions'. Yet docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md (Security Considerations, 'Target Allowlisting: Only pre-approved contracts can be called' and 'The Executor enforces: Target must be on the allowlist') describe a target allowlist as an in-force mitigation for this module.
impact: No target restriction exists at the voting layer. The only backstop is whatever the Executor enforces. If the Executor does not itself allowlist targets, a winning proposal batch can call arbitrary targets — the documented mitigation is illusory. This is a documentation/design-mismatch that could give operators false assurance; actual safety depends entirely on Executor's own checks (out of this subsystem's scope).
scenario: An operator reads the HybridVoting docs, believes malicious targets are blocked at the voting layer, and configures a permissive Executor. A crafted proposal wins and its batch calls an arbitrary target because HybridVoting never checked it.
recommendation: Either restore a target allowlist check in _validateTargets (using the still-present allowedTarget storage) or correct the docs to state clearly that HybridVoting performs NO target validation and all target safety is delegated to the Executor. Remove the misleading '_validateTargets' name if it only bounds call count.
exploitReasoning: The code matches the finding exactly. In src/libs/HybridVotingProposals.sol, `_validateTargets` (lines 132-135) only checks `batch.length > MAX_CALLS` and validates nothing about the `target` addresses themselves. The intent is explicit and deliberate: HybridVoting.sol line 64 marks `allowedTarget` as "deprecated: kept for storage layout compatibility", line 213 marks `TARGET_ALLOWED` as "deprecated: kept for enum ordering compatibility", and line 151 states "HybridVoting passes batches directly to Executor without target restrictions." So the code is behaving as designed — no bug. However, docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md is stale/contradictory: line 461 lists "Target Allowlisting: Only pre-approved contracts can be called" under Security Considerations, and lines 220-221 claim "The Executor enforces: Target must be on the allowlist." I read Executor.execute (src/Executor.sol lines 155-166): it only enforces msg.sender==allowedCaller, non-empty batch, len<=MAX_CALLS_PER_BATCH, and target != address(this) (TargetSelf). There is NO target allowlist in the Executor either. Thus the documented mitigation is illusory at BOTH the voting layer and the Executor layer.
safetyReasoning: The finding is factually accurate on every point. HybridVotingProposals.sol `_validateTargets` (lines 132-135) only checks `if (batchLen > MAX_CALLS) revert TooManyCalls()` — it never inspects `batch[i].target`, so the name is a misnomer and it enforces no target allowlist. The `allowedTarget` mapping (HybridVoting.sol:64) and `TARGET_ALLOWED` enum value (line 213) are both explicitly marked "deprecated: kept for ... compatibility," and initialize documents (line 151) "HybridVoting passes batches directly to Executor without target restrictions." Critically, the Executor does NOT enforce an allowlist either: Executor.execute (lines 155-173) checks only msg.sender==allowedCaller, non-empty batch, len<=MAX_CALLS_PER_BATCH, and target!=address(this) (TargetSelf) — the Executor Layout struct (lines 43-49) contains no target-allowlist mapping at all. Yet docs/HYBRID_VOTING.md asserts a target allowlist is an in-force mitigation in at least four places: line 462 ("Target Allowlisting: Only pre-approved contracts can be called"), lines 220-221 ("The Executor enforces: Target must be on the allowlist"), lines 437-440 ("Executor validates targets against an allowlist"), and the attack-mitigation table (line 467-474). The documented mitigation therefore does not exist anywhere in the actual code path.

title: All owner-only functions (pause, sweep, beacon ownership, eligibility config) become permanently unreachable after ownership renounce
description: Executor exposes seven onlyOwner functions: acceptBeaconOwnership, pause, unpause, sweep, configureVouching, batchConfigureVouching, and setDefaultEligibility. During deployment OrgDeployer calls renounceOwnership() (OrgDeployer.sol:561), setting owner() to address(0). OpenZeppelin's onlyOwner requires msg.sender == owner(); no external actor can ever equal address(0), so every one of these functions is dead for the entire post-deploy life of the org. The design intent (per the NatSpec 'guardian helpers' and 'ETH recovery' comments) is that these are callable functions, but only setDefaultEligibility/configureVouching are genuinely deploy-only; pause/unpause/sweep are clearly intended as ongoing operational levers and are silently bricked.
impact: There is no emergency pause once an org is live: if a governance bug or malicious winning proposal is discovered, guardians cannot freeze execute(). The sweep() ETH-recovery path is also permanently dead (ETH is still recoverable via a governance batch that sends value, but the documented owner recovery lever does not exist). This is a loss of the entire guardian/pause safety mechanism the contract advertises.
scenario: 1. OrgDeployer.deployOrg() runs to completion; at line 561 renounceOwnership() sets owner()=address(0). 2. Weeks later a griefer gets a malicious proposal to quorum, or a HybridVoting bug is found. 3. A guardian tries exec.pause() to stop execute() — the call reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount because owner() is address(0). 4. No actor can pause; the only recourse is winning a counter-proposal through the same compromised governance path.
recommendation: Either (a) split deploy-only config functions from operational ones and gate pause/unpause/sweep on a persistent guardian hat (HatManager.hasAnyHat) instead of owner(), or (b) explicitly document that these functions are deploy-window-only and remove pause/unpause/sweep to avoid a false sense of a pause safety net. If an emergency pause is desired, it must be authorized by something that survives renounce.
exploitReasoning:
The mechanism is real and deterministic. Executor.sol declares seven onlyOwner functions: acceptBeaconOwnership (176), pause (181), unpause (185), sweep (190), configureVouching (207-213), batchConfigureVouching (232-238), setDefaultEligibility (260-263). OrgDeployer.sol:561 calls OwnableUpgradeable(result.executor).renounceOwnership() at the end of deployOrg, which sets owner() to address(0). OZ's onlyOwner requires msg.sender == owner(); no external caller can be address(0), so every onlyOwner function reverts OwnableUnauthorizedAccount for the rest of the org's life. There is no transferOwnership override or re-acquisition path in Executor (only __Ownable_init at line 79), and execute() cannot restore ownership because it reverts TargetSelf (line 162) when target == address(this). So the claimed dead-code condition holds exactly.

However, the finding conflates two categories. The vouching/eligibility functions (configureVouching/batchConfigureVouching/setDefaultEligibility) carry explicit NatSpec 'Only callable by owner before renouncing ownership' (lines 200, 225, 254) and are invoked during deploy (OrgDeployer.sol:556) BEFORE the renounce at 561 — they are intentionally deploy-only, not a bug. acceptBeaconOwnership is likewise consumed once at deploy (OrgDeployer.sol:408, before renounce) as a one-time beacon handshake. The only genuine defect is pause/unpause/sweep, which are labeled 'Guardian helpers' / 'ETH recovery' with no deploy-only qualifier yet are equally bricked — advertised ongoing levers that never work post-deploy.

The claimed security impact is overstated.
