Line 92 `return hatArray;` in getHatArray returns a storage array, which the compiler realizes as a full storage->memory copy of every element. findHatIndex (line 77) re-evaluates `hatArray.length` on every loop iteration (default profile has the optimizer OFF per project config, so this SLOAD/length-read is not hoisted). hasAnyHat -> _checkHatsBatch (lines 123-139) allocates two fresh len-sized memory arrays (wearers, hatIds) and issues a balanceOfBatch of that width on every call. There is no upper bound on array length anywhere in setHatInArray (lines 24-42) — each HAT_ALLOWED config just push()es. These functions sit on genuinely hot paths: DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:232 (onlyCreator -> createProposal) and :374 (vote) call hasAnyHat; ParticipationToken/EducationHub/TaskManager call it in mint/permission checks; getHatArray backs public views. So the linear scaling described is real. However, the array-growing mutation is gated: setConfig is `onlyExecutor` (DirectDemocracyVoting.sol:197) and the per-add setHatInArray calls only run under that executor/governance path — an unprivileged actor cannot inflate the arrays. In real deployments these arrays hold a handful of role hats. The finding itself correctly frames this as a privileged-mistake/self-grief surface, not an unprivileged DoS, and does not overclaim.
safetyReasoning: The code matches the finding exactly. HatManager.getHatArray (line 92) does `return hatArray;` on a storage array, which the compiler realizes as a full storage->memory copy of every element. findHatIndex (line 77) re-evaluates `hatArray.length` each loop iteration. _checkHatsBatch (lines 127-136) allocates two fresh length-`len` memory arrays and issues a length-`len` balanceOfBatch on every hasAnyHat call. setHatInArray (lines 24-42) enforces NO upper bound on array length. These hot paths are reached from DirectDemocracyVoting.createProposal (line 232), vote (line 374), HybridVoting.createProposal (line 257), TaskManager (line 1474), etc. However, all mutations are privilege-gated: DirectDemocracyVoting.setConfig is `onlyExecutor` (line 197, modifier onlyExecutor line 184), and HAT_ALLOWED routes through setHatInArray (lines 213-219). The same executor/permission gating holds for the other consumers (HybridVoting.setConfig, TaskManager permission bootstrap, ParticipationToken/EducationHub/QuickJoin admin setters). So the array can only grow via governance/executor action — this is a self-inflicted griefing/privileged-mistake surface, exactly as the finding claims, not an unprivileged DoS. There is no security or correctness bug: the balanceOfBatch is a legitimate optimization, and no state is corrupted. The claimed "paymaster budget rejection" outcome is downstream and speculative (it presumes governance deliberately adds hundreds of hats, i.e. self-harm).

title: Non-standard execute() dataOffset leaves selector as the outer 0xb61d27f6, allowing a rule check against the wrong selector
description: In _extractTargetSelector for RULE_ID_GENERIC + execute(address,uint256,bytes) (0xb61d27f6), the inner selector is only extracted when dataOffset == 0x60 and dataStart < callData.length. Otherwise selector remains the outer execute selector 0xb61d27f6 while target is the decoded (attacker-controlled) address. The rule allowlist is then checked against (target, 0xb61d27f6) rather than the real inner selector the account will actually invoke. The account itself, not the paymaster, decodes/executes the true inner call. The code comment acknowledges the non-standard-offset risk but still proceeds with a mismatched selector.
impact: Low in practice: the org must have whitelisted rules[target][0xb61d27f6] for the op to pass, which is unusual. But if any org ever whitelists the execute selector itself as a rule (or a target that happens to expose a 0xb61d27f6 function), an attacker could route an unintended inner call past the allowlist. It weakens the selector-allowlist guarantee against adversarially-encoded calldata.
scenario: 1. Org whitelists (someToken, 0xb61d27f6) by mistake or because someToken exposes that selector. 2. Attacker crafts execute(someToken, 0, innerData) with a non-standard bytes offset so the inner selector is not parsed; paymaster checks (someToken, 0xb61d27f6) -> allowed -> sponsors. 3. The account executes whatever innerData actually encodes against someToken, bypassing the intended per-selector restriction.
recommendation: When dataOffset != 0x60 or dataStart is out of range, treat the op as non-conforming and revert (RuleDenied/InvalidPaymasterData) instead of falling back to the outer selector, or require the inner selector to be explicitly extractable before allowing sponsorship.
exploitReasoning: The cited code at src/PaymasterHub.sol:1834-1866 confirms the finding. At line 1836 `selector = bytes4(callData[0:4])` sets selector to the outer 0xb61d27f6. At line 1843 `target := calldataload(callData.offset + 0x04)` decodes the attacker-controlled address param. The inner selector is only re-read (lines 1852-1857) when `dataOffset == 0x60`; the assembly block has no `else` that resets selector, so for any non-standard offset the selector remains 0xb61d27f6 while target is the decoded address. `_validateRules` (line 1779) then checks `rules[target][0xb61d27f6]`. Meanwhile PasskeyAccount.execute (src/PasskeyAccount.sol:433-454) uses standard Solidity ABI decoding, which accepts any valid (non-canonical) bytes offset and executes the real inner `data` via `target.call(data)` at line 444 — so the account performs an inner call whose true selector was never checked. The batch path (0x47e1da2a/0x18dfb3c7) is intercepted earlier (lines 1769-1772) and is unaffected. The offset math is sound: standard inner selector sits at 0x84 = 0x04+0x60+0x20, matching line 1853. Tests (test/PasskeyPaymasterIntegration.t.sol:91, test/PaymasterLibsUnit.t.sol:345) confirm the intended per-selector allowlist semantics that this gap defeats.
safetyReasoning: The code behavior described is real. In `_extractTargetSelector` (src/PaymasterHub.sol:1834-1860), for RULE_ID_GENERIC + `execute(address,uint256,bytes)` (0xb61d27f6), `selector` is initialized to the outer `0xb61d27f6` at line 1836 and is only overwritten with the inner selector when `dataOffset == 0x60` AND `dataStart < callData.length` (lines 1852-1856). If the ABI `bytes` offset pointer at position 0x44 is non-standard, the inner selector is NOT parsed and `selector` stays `0xb61d27f6` (line 1859 just truncates it to bytes4). `target` is still the attacker-decoded address at 0x04 (line 1843). The account (PasskeyAccount.execute, src/PasskeyAccount.sol:433-454, and EOADelegation) uses Solidity's standard ABI decoder which honors the offset pointer, so it will execute the true inner call encoded at the non-standard location — a genuine divergence between what the paymaster checks and what the account runs.\n\nHOWEVER, the finding overstates the impact by framing this as a fail-OPEN bypass; it is actually fail-CLOSED. At src/PaymasterHub.sol:1778-1781 the rule lookup is `rules[target][0xb61d27f6]` and reverts `RuleDenied` unless `rule.allowed == true`. In generic mode the intended, documented rule keys are the INNER `(target, innerSelector)` pairs (see `_validateBatchRules` at 1794-1823 and the auto-whitelisting of inner selectors). `0xb61d27f6` is never auto-whitelisted anywhere: rules come only from operator-supplied arrays via `_setRulesBatch`/`setRule` (lines 318-322, 1012-1020, gated by `onlyOrgOperator`). So a non-standard-offset op normally hits `rule.allowed == false` and is DENIED. The `ruleId` is attacker-chosen (unsigned, decoded from paymasterAndData at line 1584), but choosing GENERIC does not create the `(target, 0xb61d27f6)` rule entry — that still requires a privileged operator to explicitly whitelist the outer execute selector against some target, which is a misconfiguration, not a normal state.

title: parseExecuteCall reads a full 32-byte inner-selector word while only bounds-checking a single byte, allowing an out-of-bounds calldata read past the callData slice
description: When dataOffset == 0x60, dataStart is computed as 0x04 + 0x60 + 0x20 = 0x84 and the inner selector is read with `calldataload(add(callData.offset, dataStart))`, which loads a full 32-byte word. The only guard is `if lt(dataStart, callData.length)`, i.e. it merely requires 0x84 < callData.length (one byte present at that position). It does NOT require dataStart + 32 <= callData.length. For a `bytes calldata` slice, calldataload beyond callData.length does not zero-pad; it reads whatever calldata bytes follow the slice (the callData length word, then paymasterAndData / other UserOp fields inside EntryPoint's handleOps calldata). An attacker crafting a UserOp whose callData declares an inner-bytes length word but is truncated (logical length between 0x85 and 0x84+0x1F) causes the parser to read the inner selector from adjacent, attacker-adjacent calldata rather than from the actual execute() payload. The identical pattern exists inline at PaymasterHub.sol:1852-1856 (_extractTargetSelector).
impact: The parsed innerSelector can differ from the bytes the account's execute() will actually invoke, because it is read from beyond the logical callData region. This is a spoofing/consistency hazard against the onboarding, org-deploy, and generic rule whitelists. Exploitability for privilege escalation is limited: PasskeyAccount.execute() decodes and calls the SAME callData, so an inconsistent length generally makes the real execution decode differently or revert, and only the EntryPoint may invoke validation. It is primarily a robustness/defense-in-depth defect rather than a confirmed bypass.
scenario: 1) A registered account owner (adversary) builds a UserOp with callData = selector(execute) + target(=whitelisted registry) + value(0) + bytesOffset(0x60) + a length word, but sets the UserOp's callData field so its logical length is 0x85..0xA3 (declared inner-data shorter than a full word). 2) EntryPoint calls validatePaymasterUserOp; onboarding validation calls parseExecuteCall. 3) `0x84 < 0x85` passes, so calldataload reads 32 bytes starting at offset 0x84, pulling the low bytes from the callData length word / next calldata region rather than the intended inner selector. 4) innerSelector is derived from out-of-slice bytes; whitelist matching operates on a value not present in the payload the account will execute.
recommendation: Require the full inner selector word to be in-bounds before reading: change the guard to `if iszero(gt(add(dataStart, 0x20), callData.length))` (equivalently require dataStart + 32 <= callData.length), or, since only 4 bytes are needed, require dataStart + 4 <= callData.length and mask. Apply the same fix to the inline copy in PaymasterHub._extractTargetSelector (lines 1852-1856). Add a unit test with a truncated inner-data length to lock the behavior.
exploitReasoning: The low-level premise is accurate: at PaymasterCalldataLib.sol:44-46 (and the identical inline copy at PaymasterHub.sol:1853-1855), dataStart = 0x04+0x60+0x20 = 0x84, and the only guard is `if lt(dataStart, callData.length)`, i.e. it requires only 0x84 < callData.length while `calldataload(add(callData.offset,0x84))` reads a full 32-byte word. Since userOp.callData (PaymasterHub.sol:1692, 1757, 1830) is a `bytes calldata` slice into EntryPoint.handleOps calldata, bytes past the slice are NOT zero-padded — for callData.length in [0x85,0x87] the top-4-byte innerSelector partially reads adjacent handleOps calldata. So an out-of-slice read genuinely exists. However, NO security impact is reachable: (1) Org-deploy path discards the selector — `_validateOrgDeployCallData` calls `parseExecuteCall(callData, orgDeployer)` and ignores innerSelector `(bool valid,)` at line 1757. (2) For onboarding (line 1692-1697) and generic rules (line 1855), `target` (offset 0x04) and `value` (offset 0x24) are fully in-bounds and unspoofable, so target==registry still holds. For a spoofed selector to matter the account's real PasskeyAccount.execute() (PasskeyAccount.sol:433-444) must land a *different* call on that same target — but it strictly ABI-decodes the SAME truncated callData: with length <= 0x87 the inner-bytes length word at 0x64 must declare n<=3 for the decode to succeed, so `registry.call(data)` sends <=3 bytes (fallback, not registerAccount); to make an n>=4 real call requires length >= 0x88, at which point the selector is fully in-bounds and un-spoofed. Either branch, the account never invokes a whitelisted privileged function that the paymaster wasn't shown. (3) Worst case is a sponsored UserOp whose execute() reverts/hits fallback — already inside the threat model, bounded by per-account lifetime caps + daily caps + gas caps (lines 1657-1673) and org deposit accounting; the comment at 1650-1656 explicitly accounts for failed onboarding ops charging the fund. The finding itself concedes it is "primarily a robustness/defense-in-depth defect rather than a confirmed bypass."
safetyReasoning: The OOB-read defect is real. In PaymasterCalldataLib.sol:44-46 the only bound is `if lt(dataStart, callData.length)` (dataStart=0x84 when dataOffset==0x60), which requires merely `0x84 < callData.length` (>=0x85). Line 46 then does `innerSelector := calldataload(add(callData.offset, dataStart))`, reading a full 32-byte word; `bytes4()` at line 50 keeps bytes 0x84..0x87. There is NO check that `dataStart+4 <= callData.length`. `calldataload` on a `bytes calldata` slice does not respect the slice boundary — inside EntryPoint.handleOps, userOp.callData is followed by other UserOp fields, so bytes 0x85..0x87 can be read from adjacent attacker-controlled calldata. The identical pattern is duplicated at PaymasterHub.sol:1852-1856 (_extractTargetSelector). No test (test/PaymasterLibsUnit.t.sol:351-435) covers a truncated inner-bytes slice; all fixtures are well-formed. So the finding's technical premise is confirmed. However the claimed whitelist-bypass/privilege-escalation impact is not reachable: `target` (line 39) and `value` (line 40) are read from fixed in-slice offsets 0x04/0x24 (always in-bounds given the `callData.length < 0x64` guard at line 34) and are hard-pinned at line 53 (`target != expectedTarget || value != 0` → invalid). The OOB read only affects the inner selector.

title: signCount is written during validateUserOp and enforced strictly-increasing, breaking bundling and enabling replay-order griefing
description: _validateSignature calls WebAuthnLib.verifyWithSignCount and then unconditionally writes cred.signCount = newSignCount (line 230) during the ERC-4337 validation phase. WebAuthnLib (lines 213-214) rejects any assertion whose newSignCount <= lastSignCount once lastSignCount>0. For counter-supporting authenticators the signCount increments per assertion, so two UserOps signed close together must land on-chain in strictly increasing signCount order. If a later-count UserOp is mined first (bundler reordering, mempool races, a dropped/replaced op), every earlier-count UserOp becomes permanently invalid — the user must re-sign. Worse, a griefer who observes a signed UserOp in the mempool can copy it verbatim and submit it via a different bundler, or reorder the user's own two pending ops, to bump the stored signCount and invalidate the user's other in-flight operations. The write also mutates account storage during validation, which is legal for the sender's own slot under ERC-7562 but couples anti-replay to inclusion ordering rather than to the EntryPoint nonce.
impact: Denial of service / UX breakage: legitimate UserOps become spuriously invalid when signCount ordering is violated, and an attacker can intentionally invalidate a user's pending operations by racing a copied op. No fund loss, but reliable griefing and broken batching for counter-enabled authenticators.
scenario: 1) User's authenticator supports counters (signCount increments). 2) User signs UserOp A (count=5) and UserOp B (count=6) and broadcasts both. 3) A bundler includes B first: stored signCount becomes 6. 4) UserOp A (count=5) now fails the newSignCount<=lastSignCount check and is rejected forever. Alternatively a griefer replays the user's own count=6 op to bump storage and strand count=5.
recommendation: Rely on the EntryPoint nonce (2D nonce) for replay protection instead of on-chain signCount ordering, and treat signCount only as an optional clone-detection heuristic that does not hard-fail ordinary ordering (e.g., accept equal/any count, or only reject on strong evidence of cloning). If signCount must be enforced, document that counter-enabled authenticators cannot have multiple concurrent in-flight UserOps.
exploitReasoning: The cited code is exactly as described. In src/PasskeyAccount.sol, _validateSignature (line 193) runs inside the ERC-4337 validation phase (validateUserOp -> _validateSignature, lines 170-177) and unconditionally writes cred.signCount = newSignCount at line 230 after WebAuthnLib.verifyWithSignCount returns valid. In src/libs/WebAuthnLib.sol line 213, `if (lastSignCount > 0 && (newSignCount == 0 || newSignCount <= lastSignCount)) return (false, newSignCount);` — so once lastSignCount>0, any assertion with newSignCount <= lastSignCount is rejected, and _validateSignature returns SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED (lines 225-227) with no fallback. newSignCount is parsed from auth.authenticatorData (WebAuthnLib lines 196-205), i.e. from attacker-supplied signature calldata, but it must still pass the P256 verify() at line 217 against the stored pubkey, so an attacker cannot forge an arbitrary/higher signCount — they can only replay a legitimately signed op. The account has no local nonce field (grep for nonce in PasskeyAccount.sol returns nothing); anti-replay for ordering relies on the EntryPoint v0.7 nonce, and signCount is an additional monotonicity layer. Thus for a counter-incrementing authenticator, two in-flight ops with counts 5 and 6 can indeed be reordered by bundlers, and if 6 lands first the count-5 op is stranded permanently (must re-sign) — the described reordering DoS is a genuine consequence of the code.
safetyReasoning: The code behaves exactly as the finding states. In src/PasskeyAccount.sol, `_validateSignature` (called from `validateUserOp` at line 177, during the ERC-4337 validation phase) invokes `WebAuthnLib.verifyWithSignCount(... cred.signCount)` (lines 216-223) and, on success, unconditionally writes `cred.signCount = newSignCount` (line 230). In src/libs/WebAuthnLib.sol line 213, `if (lastSignCount > 0 && (newSignCount == 0 || newSignCount <= lastSignCount)) return (false, newSignCount);` strictly rejects any equal-or-lower count once `lastSignCount > 0`. There is NO guard in either file that decouples anti-replay from inclusion ordering — the stored counter is bumped at validation time and future ops are gated on it, so for a counter-enabled authenticator two ops signed close together (count 5 then count 6) must be included in strictly increasing order or the lower-count op is permanently invalidated. So the ordering/batching-breakage core of the finding is real (CONFIRMED mechanism). HOWEVER two things sharply limit the real-world impact: (1) The griefer "copy the op verbatim / replay to bump storage" sub-claim is refuted — the WebAuthn signature commits to `userOpHash` (verified via `_verifyChallenge`), and the account does not manage its own nonce; EntryPoint enforces nonce uniqueness per sender, so a copied op consumes the same nonce and cannot be replayed to independently bump signCount. An attacker racing a copied op merely wins the inclusion race for the user's own op. (2) The lib's own comment (lines 208-210) notes counters=0 authenticators pass freely; the dominant target authenticators (Apple/Google platform passkeys) report signCount=0 always, so `lastSignCount > 0` never triggers and the entire issue is inert for them. The residual is a UX/batching hazard limited to hardware-key-style counter-enabled authenticators with concurrent in-flight ops, with no fund loss and no privileged-actor takeover.

title: MAX_CREDENTIALS constant is unenforced when factory config returns >10, contradicting the documented global limit
description: addCredential enforces the limit returned by _getMaxCredentials(), which reads config.maxCredentialsPerAccount and only falls back to the hardcoded MAX_CREDENTIALS (10) when the factory value is 0 or the call reverts (lines 553-565). PoaManager can call factory.setMaxCredentials(255) (PasskeyAccountFactory line 187 accepts any uint8 with no upper bound), so accounts can exceed the 'global limit' of 10 that the NatSpec (line 51-52) and interface docs advertise. Since removeCredential and completeRecovery iterate credentialIds unbounded (PasskeyAccount lines 368-379, 525-532), a large max increases the worst-case gas of recovery/removal, and the documented invariant is not actually enforced.
impact: Documentation/behavior mismatch and mild gas-griefing surface: the '10 max' invariant is not a hard cap; a high configured value inflates loop costs in recovery and credential removal.
scenario: 1) PoaManager calls factory.setMaxCredentials(200). 2) An account adds up to 200 credentials. 3) completeRecovery/removeCredential now loop over 200 entries, and the advertised MAX_CREDENTIALS=10 invariant is violated.
recommendation: Clamp the effective max to min(configValue, MAX_CREDENTIALS) in _getMaxCredentials (or add an upper bound in setMaxCredentials), and align NatSpec with the real behavior.
exploitReasoning:
The finding treats MAX_CREDENTIALS=10 (PasskeyAccount.sol line 52) as a documented hard invariant, but the code and tests show it is deliberately a *fallback default*, not a ceiling. _getMaxCredentials() (lines 553-566) returns config.maxCredentialsPerAccount and only falls back to 10 when the config is 0 or the call reverts — this is by design. Corroborating intent: PasskeyAccountFactory names its constant DEFAULT_MAX_CREDENTIALS (line 47-48, "Default max credentials"), the PasskeyAccount docstring line 34 says "up to maxCredentials per org", and test/Passkey.t.sol testFactorySetMaxCredentials (line 212-218) sets the value to 15 (above 10) and asserts it is honored, while testMaxCredentialsGlobal (line 638-653) sets it to 2 and asserts enforcement. So the configurable limit overriding 10 is the intended, tested behavior — not a violated invariant.

The gas-griefing claim is also refuted. setMaxCredentials (factory line 187) is gated by onlyPoaManager (modifier line 113-116; poaManager is the trusted protocol governor set at init). Only trusted governance can raise the cap, and the parameter is uint8, so the array is hard-bounded at 255. The completeRecovery/removeCredential loops (lines 368-379, 521-533) over at most 255 entries (mapping delete + array pop per iter) remain far under block gas limits — no DoS, no permanent lock, and no unprivileged actor can inflate the array (addCredential is onlySelf, line 238).

The only kernel of truth is that the NatSpec comment on line 51 uses the imprecise phrase "global limit" for what is actually a fallback default. That is a pure documentation-wording nit (info), not a correctness or security defect.
safetyReasoning: The code matches the finding. PasskeyAccount.sol line 52 declares `MAX_CREDENTIALS = 10` with NatSpec "Maximum number of credentials per account (global limit)". addCredential (lines 248-250) enforces `_getMaxCredentials()`, not the constant. `_getMaxCredentials()` (lines 553-565) returns `config.maxCredentialsPerAccount` whenever it is > 0 (line 562), falling back to the hardcoded 10 only when the factory value is 0 or the call reverts. PasskeyAccountFactory.setMaxCredentials(uint8) (line 187-191) stores any uint8 (0-255) with no upper-bound validation. Therefore the advertised hard cap of 10 is not enforced: an effective cap up to 255 is honored. The recovery/removal loops are genuinely unbounded over credentialIds (completeRecovery lines 368-379, _removeCredentialFromArray lines 525-532), so a higher cap does raise worst-case loop cost. All claimed facts are verified in the actual code.

title: Recovery installs a key with no on-curve / P256 validity check, permitting a permanently unusable (bricked) account
description: initiateRecovery and completeRecovery only reject zero pubKeyX/pubKeyY (line 323); they never call P256Verifier.isValidPublicKey to confirm the recovery key is a real on-curve P-256 point. completeRecovery then deletes ALL existing credentials and installs only the (possibly invalid) recovery key. If the guardian supplies coordinates that are non-zero but not a valid curve point, every future validateUserOp fails P256 verification and the account is permanently unusable — no credential remains to add a new one, and completeRecovery cannot be re-run (executeAfter was zeroed and pending array cleared). The same missing curve check applies to initialize/addCredential (lines 141, 239) but those are self-authorized; recovery is the dangerous one because it wipes the only working key first.
impact: A guardian mistake (or malice) can irrecoverably brick an account by replacing the sole credential with an invalid P-256 point, with no self-recovery path afterward.
scenario: 1) Guardian initiates recovery with non-zero but off-curve (or garbage) pubKeyX/Y. 2) After the delay, completeRecovery wipes the real credential and installs the bad key. 3) All subsequent UserOps fail signature verification; the account holds funds but can never transact.
recommendation: Validate the recovery public key with P256Verifier.isValidPublicKey before accepting it in initiateRecovery (and ideally in addCredential/initialize), reverting on invalid points so a working credential is never destroyed in favor of an unusable one.
exploitReasoning: The factual core is correct. src/PasskeyAccount.sol:322-347 (initiateRecovery) and 350-413 (completeRecovery) validate only non-zero coordinates (line 323 checks `pubKeyX == bytes32(0) || pubKeyY == bytes32(0)`); neither calls P256Verifier.isValidPublicKey, which exists and does full on-curve validation (src/libs/P256Verifier.sol:305-321). initialize (line 141) and addCredential (line 239) share the same zero-only check. completeRecovery deletes every existing credential (lines 366-379) and installs only the recovery key (lines 384-391). If a guardian supplies non-zero but off-curve coordinates, WebAuthnLib.verify -> P256Verifier.verify (src/libs/P256Verifier.sol:123-155) will always return false for that key, so every subsequent validateUserOp returns SIG_VALIDATION_FAILED (src/PasskeyAccount.sol:225-226) and the account cannot self-transact — addCredential/removeCredential are onlySelf and only reachable through the EntryPoint with a valid signature. The tests corroborate that only zero is rejected (test/Passkey.t.sol:1003,1011) and even install garbage keys like keccak256("x") without ever exercising a real signature afterward, so the brick path is genuinely untested. HOWEVER the "permanent / no self-recovery path" claim is overstated: initiateRecovery is gated by onlyGuardian (line 322 / modifier lines 100-103), which depends on l.guardian, NOT on any credential. Each call derives a fresh recoveryId = keccak256(credentialId, block.timestamp, msg.sender) (line 327), and only requires the new credentialId not already exist (line 335). So a guardian who made a mistake can simply call initiateRecovery again with a valid key and a fresh credentialId, wait the delay, and completeRecovery — the account is recoverable, not irreversibly bricked, as long as the guardian is intact. The account only becomes truly stuck if guardian == address(0) or the guardian key is also lost, which is a separate precondition.
safetyReasoning: The factual core is correct: initiateRecovery (PasskeyAccount.sol:323), initialize (:141), and addCredential (:239) only reject zero coordinates; none call P256Verifier.isValidPublicKey (which exists and does a full on-curve check at P256Verifier.sol:305-321 but is referenced only in tests, per grep). completeRecovery (:366-391) does wipe all credentials and install only the recovery key. An off-curve pubKey would make WebAuthnLib.verify -> P256Verifier.verify (WebAuthnLib.sol:149) return false for every future validateUserOp, so the smart wallet can no longer authorize UserOps and cannot self-add a credential (addCredential is onlySelf). HOWEVER the finding's central impact claim — "permanently unusable, no self-recovery path afterward, completeRecovery cannot be re-run" — is refuted by the code. completeRecovery only zeroes that one request's executeAfter (:394) and clears the pending array; it never disables the guardian (guardian is only mutated at :146 init and :304 setGuardian). The guardian can therefore call initiateRecovery again — it derives a fresh recoveryId from keccak256(credentialId, block.timestamp, msg.sender) (:327) — and complete a new recovery with a valid on-curve key, restoring access. So the mistake is recoverable, not permanent. Additionally the guardian is the privileged POA-controlled poaGuardian (PasskeyAccountFactory.sol:253/291), not an unprivileged actor, and a malicious guardian could already install a valid key they control to fully seize the account — a strictly worse and pre-existing trust assumption.

title: WebAuthn verification never checks rpIdHash or origin — assertions from any relying party are accepted
description: WebAuthnLib.verify() validates the authenticatorData length, the UP/UV flags, the base64url-decoded challenge, the type=="webauthn.get" string, and the P256 signature. It never inspects authenticatorData[0:32] (the rpIdHash) against any expected relying-party-ID hash, and it never parses or checks the `origin` field inside clientDataJSON. The AuthenticatorData struct even has an rpIdHash field and parseAuthenticatorData() extracts it, but nothing in the verify path consumes it. This means the only thing binding an assertion to POP is the 32-byte challenge (the userOpHash / EIP-712 digest).
impact: A passkey that a user registered for POP is fully usable by any origin/RP the user can be induced to authenticate against, and vice versa. Because signature replay is otherwise prevented by the userOpHash/nonce, the practical residual risk is a phishing/cross-context signing scenario: if an attacker can get the victim's authenticator to sign an attacker-chosen challenge under a DIFFERENT rpId (e.g. a lookalike site the attacker controls that requests a WebAuthn assertion whose challenge equals a target POP userOpHash), the resulting assertion verifies on-chain even though the browser believed it was authenticating to attacker.com, not the POP RP. Standard WebAuthn relying parties MUST pin rpIdHash to prevent exactly this; omitting it removes a core WebAuthn security guarantee.
scenario: 1. Victim has a passkey registered with credentialId C and pubkey (x,y) on their PasskeyAccount. 2. Attacker computes a target userOpHash H for a UserOp that drains the victim's account (attacker can compute H since it is deterministic from the UserOp fields). 3. Attacker lures the victim to attacker-controlled site evil.com, which invokes navigator.credentials.get({ challenge: base64url(H), rpId: 'evil.com' }). The browser signs with the victim's passkey; authenticatorData.rpIdHash = sha256('evil.com'), origin='https://evil.com'. 4. Attacker submits the assertion as the UserOp signature. WebAuthnLib.verify ignores rpIdHash and origin, checks only that the decoded challenge == H and type=='webauthn.get', and the P256 sig is valid — all true. validateUserOp returns 0 and the malicious UserOp executes.
recommendation: Bind the assertion to POP's relying party: (a) store an expectedRpIdHash per account/credential (or a protocol-wide constant) and require authenticatorData[0:32] == expectedRpIdHash; and (b) optionally verify the `origin` value in clientDataJSON against an allow-list. At minimum enforce rpIdHash. This is the standard WebAuthn RP obligation and the struct/parse plumbing is already present.
exploitReasoning: The technical defect is real. WebAuthnLib.verify() (src/libs/WebAuthnLib.sol:110-150) validates: authenticatorData length (line 116), UP/UV flags (lines 121-131), the base64url challenge with a "challenge":" prefix guard (line 134 → _verifyChallenge), the "type":"webauthn.get" string with a "type":" prefix guard (line 139 → _verifyType), and the P256 signature over sha256(authenticatorData || sha256(clientDataJSON)) (lines 145-149). It never reads authenticatorData[0:32] (rpIdHash) against any expected value, and never parses the `origin` field of clientDataJSON. parseAuthenticatorData() extracts parsed.rpIdHash at line 234, but no code path consumes it — grep across src/ and test/ shows rpIdHash referenced ONLY inside WebAuthnLib.sol and one test, never at a call site. The callers confirm this: PasskeyAccount._validateSignature (src/PasskeyAccount.sol:193-233) passes only pubKeyX/pubKeyY/signCount to verifyWithSignCount and stores no expected rpIdHash in PasskeyCredential (lines 254-256); UniversalAccountRegistry.sol:175,291 and QuickJoin.sol likewise call verify() with no rpId pinning. So the only binding of an assertion to POP is the 32-byte challenge (userOpHash). This is a genuine deviation from WebAuthn RP requirements, which mandate verifying rpIdHash == sha256(rpId).
safetyReasoning: The code exactly matches the finding. In WebAuthnLib.verify() (lines 110-150), the verification steps are: (1) auth data length >= 37 (L116), (2) UP/UV flag checks reading only authenticatorData[32] (L121-131), (3) challenge match via _verifyChallenge (L134), (4) type=="webauthn.get" via _verifyType (L139), (5) message hash (L145-146), (6) P256 signature (L149). authenticatorData[0:32] (the rpIdHash) is never read in the verify path. The AuthenticatorData struct has an rpIdHash field (L94) and parseAuthenticatorData extracts it (L234), but nothing consumes it. There is no `origin` parse of clientDataJSON anywhere in the file — only "challenge", "type", and the challenge value are inspected. Callers confirm no compensating check: PasskeyAccount._validateSignature (L193-233) stores only publicKeyX/Y/signCount/active per credential (L150-152, L254-256) — no expected rpIdHash — and passes userOpHash straight to verifyWithSignCount (L216) with requireUserVerification=false (L221). UniversalAccountRegistry.sol:175 and :291 likewise call verify() with no rpId argument. So on-chain, the only binding of an assertion to POP is the 32-byte challenge (userOpHash). The finding is factually accurate.

title: P256 public key is never validated on-curve/in-range in the live verification path
description: P256Verifier.verify() forwards (x,y) straight to the precompile/fallback verifier without ever calling isValidPublicKey(). isValidPublicKey (which does the full on-curve and range check) exists but is only referenced from tests. The security of rejecting off-curve / point-at-infinity / out-of-range public keys is therefore delegated entirely to whichever verifier is reachable on-chain. EIP-7951 and the daimo-eth verifier both perform these checks, so this is currently safe, but it is a single point of trust with no defense-in-depth.
impact: If a chain's RIP-7212 precompile implementation is buggy/lenient about invalid public keys (historically some early RIP-7212 implementations differed from the EIP-7951 hardening around point-at-infinity), or if the fallback address ever holds a different contract, an invalid/malicious public key could slip through. Public keys are attacker-supplied at credential-registration time (addCredential / initialize only reject zero coordinates), so an on-curve check at verify time (or, better, at registration) is the correct guard.
scenario: 1. On a chain whose 0x100 precompile does not reject point-at-infinity or off-curve points, an attacker registers a crafted credential with an off-curve (x,y). 2. Verification behavior for such keys becomes verifier-implementation-defined rather than protocol-enforced. Because the library omits its own isValidPublicKey check, POP inherits any weakness of the underlying verifier instead of failing closed.
recommendation: Call isValidPublicKey(x,y) at credential registration (PasskeyAccount.addCredential/initialize and UniversalAccountRegistry) and/or as a cheap pre-check in verify(). It is pure arithmetic (a few mulmod/addmod) and provides defense-in-depth independent of the reachable verifier.
exploitReasoning: The factual core of the finding is accurate against the real code. In src/libs/P256Verifier.sol, verify() (lines 123-155) packs (messageHash, r, s, x, y) and forwards them directly to the PRECOMPILE staticcall (line 137) and, on empty return, to the FALLBACK_VERIFIER staticcall (line 147). It never calls isValidPublicKey(). isValidPublicKey() (lines 305-321) does the full non-zero, <p, and on-curve (y^2 == x^3-3x+b mod p) check, but a grep shows it is referenced ONLY from src/libs/P256Verifier.sol itself and two test files (test/P256SignatureTest.t.sol, test/Passkey.t.sol) — never from any live contract. The live callers WebAuthnLib.verify (src/libs/WebAuthnLib.sol:149) → UniversalAccountRegistry (lines 175, 291) reach verify() without any curve validation. The registration/write paths in src/PasskeyAccount.sol (initialize:141, addCredential:239, initiateRecovery:323) only reject bytes32(0) coordinates, confirming there is NO on-curve gate anywhere in the pipeline. So on-curve/point-at-infinity/range rejection is fully delegated to whichever verifier is reachable on-chain. HOWEVER, no concrete exploit exists: EIP-7951 (the documented target, line 12) mandates the point-at-infinity check, and the daimo-eth fallback verifier performs on-curve validation, so both reachable verifiers fail closed today. The described exploit requires a hypothetical chain whose 0x100 precompile is lenient about off-curve/infinity points AND the attacker producing a signature that verifies under that off-curve key — the stated outcome is 'verifier-implementation-defined,' not a demonstrable fund loss or takeover.
safetyReasoning:
The finding is factually correct. In src/libs/P256Verifier.sol, isValidPublicKey (lines 305-321, a real on-curve + range check) is defined but grep confirms it is called from NOWHERE in src/ — only from tests. The live path verify() (lines 123-155) forwards (x,y) straight to the 0x100 precompile (line 137) and daimo fallback (line 147) with no on-curve check. Registration paths in PasskeyAccount.sol (initialize L141, addCredential L239, initiateRecovery L323) and UniversalAccountRegistry only reject zero coordinates (pubKeyX == bytes32(0) || pubKeyY == bytes32(0)), never off-curve or out-of-range (>= P256_P) points. So the description's core claim — no protocol-level public-key validation, sole reliance on the underlying verifier — is accurate.

However, the exploitability is weak. (1) Credentials are added only by trusted principals relative to the account: addCredential is onlySelf, initialize sets the owner's own key at creation, initiateRecovery is onlyGuardian. An attacker who registers an off-curve key is registering it for an account they already control (or via a guardian), so a bad key only bricks their own account — no privilege escalation against a third party. (2) A non-compliant precompile that accepts off-curve points does not hand an attacker a signature-forgery primitive against a VICTIM's already-registered valid key; the malformed point is chosen at registration by whoever controls the credential. (3) On every currently supported chain, both EIP-7951 (0x100) and the daimo-eth fallback (0xc2b7...) enforce on-curve/range, so the guard is already applied one layer down. The claimed scenario reduces to "verification behavior becomes verifier-defined," which is a defense-in-depth gap, not a concrete unprivileged exploit.

title: Permissionless deployFullOrg allows front-running / squatting of a specific orgId
description: `deployFullOrg` is `external payable` with no access control, and `orgId` is fully caller-chosen (`params.orgId`). It calls `createOrgBootstrap(orgId,...)` which reverts `OrgExists` if the orgId is already taken, and `deployFullOrg` itself reverts `OrgExistsMismatch` (line 399). Because org creation is first-come-first-served on an attacker-chosen `bytes32`, an attacker who can predict/observe a target orgId (e.g. derived off-chain as keccak of a known org name, or seen in the mempool) can deploy first and permanently consume that orgId. The squatted org has the attacker's `deployerAddress` as ADMIN and the attacker cannot be evicted (Executor ownership is renounced, orgId is immutable in the registry).
impact: Denial of a specific namespace: a legitimate team can be permanently blocked from ever registering their intended orgId, forcing them to a different id and breaking any off-chain systems keyed to the expected id (subgraph lookups, frontends, deterministic tooling). It is griefing rather than fund theft — the attacker gains a useless org and pays the full org-deploy gas (~22M) per squat, so mass squatting is expensive, but targeted squatting of a high-value/known id is cheap enough to matter.
scenario: 1. Team plans to deploy org with `orgId = keccak256("AcmeCoop")`, a value publicly derivable. 2. Attacker calls `deployFullOrg` with that `orgId`, minimal roles, and their own `deployerAddress`, before the team's tx lands (or by mempool front-run). 3. Registry now has that orgId with `exists=true`. 4. Team's `deployFullOrg` reverts `OrgExistsMismatch`; the id is unusable forever.
recommendation: Bind orgId to the caller/deployer or a nonce so it cannot be squatted, e.g. derive `orgId = keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, params.deployerAddress, userSalt))` inside the deployer rather than accepting an arbitrary caller-supplied id, or gate `deployFullOrg` behind an allowlist/registrar if permissioned creation is acceptable. If arbitrary ids must be supported, document the squatting risk prominently for integrators.
exploitReasoning: The mechanism is exactly as described. `deployFullOrg` (OrgDeployer.sol:365) is `external payable` with only a manual reentrancy guard (lines 368-369) and no caller access control. `orgId` is entirely caller-supplied via `params.orgId` (struct field line 290), and every deploy script derives it as `params.orgId = keccak256(bytes(config.orgId))` (DeployOrg.s.sol:483, RunOrgActions.s.sol:904, MainDeploy.s.sol:331 `keccak256("poa")`), i.e. the keccak of a human-readable org name — publicly predictable. Org creation is first-come-first-served: `_deployFullOrgInternal` checks `_orgExists(params.orgId)` (line 396) and either calls `createOrgBootstrap` or reverts `OrgExistsMismatch` (line 399); `OrgRegistry.createOrgBootstrap` itself reverts `OrgExists` when `l.orgOf[orgId].exists` (OrgRegistry.sol:149). The `onlyOwner` on `createOrgBootstrap` only means OrgDeployer is the registry owner — it does not gate who calls `deployFullOrg`. I grepped OrgDeployer and OrgRegistry for any reserve/allowlist/authorized-deployer/permit mechanism and found none. So an attacker can front-run/squat a predictable orgId, becoming its immutable ADMIN with Executor ownership renounced (line 561). The finding is technically real.
safetyReasoning: The code mechanics in the finding are accurate. `deployFullOrg` (OrgDeployer.sol:365) is `external payable` with no access-control modifier — any address may call it. `params.orgId` (DeploymentParams.orgId, line 290) is a fully caller-supplied `bytes32`; there is no on-chain derivation forcing it to equal keccak(orgName) (grep confirms no such linkage). At lines 396-400, `_deployFullOrgInternal` reverts `OrgExistsMismatch` if the org already exists, otherwise calls `l.orgRegistry.createOrgBootstrap(params.orgId, ...)`. `createOrgBootstrap` (OrgRegistry.sol:144-159) is `onlyOwner` (OrgDeployer is the registry owner) and reverts `OrgExists` (line 149) on a duplicate id, and permanently records `exists: true`. So org creation is first-come-first-served on an attacker-chosen `bytes32`, and a squatted id can never be reused (no eviction path; Executor ownership is renounced at line 561). The finding's claim stands as written.

title: Cross-chain beacon upgrade permanently stalls the Hyperlane message if version/impl already registered (VersionExists / SameImplementation revert in handle)
description: PoaManagerSatellite.handle() calls poaManager.upgradeBeacon(typeName, newImpl, version) directly with no try/catch. upgradeBeacon (PoaManager.sol:99-103) reverts SameImplementation if beacon already points at newImpl, and registry.registerImplementation (ImplementationRegistry.sol:80) reverts VersionExists if (typeName, version) is already registered. Since the beacon and registry share no atomic rollback with the Hyperlane message, a duplicate or already-applied upgrade message reverts inside handle(). Hyperlane treats a reverting handle as undelivered and the message cannot make forward progress — the version string is now 'burned' and the same message body will revert forever.
impact: A satellite-chain upgrade can get permanently stuck. If an operator retries a cross-chain upgrade after a partial/failed prior attempt reused the version string (a documented real hazard in this repo — CREATE2/registry collisions), the message is undeliverable and the intended upgrade never applies on that chain until a new message with a fresh version is dispatched (extra fee, manual intervention).
scenario: 1. Operator dispatches upgradeBeaconCrossChain("TaskManager", implX, "v4") from the Hub. 2. Relay is slow; operator also runs upgradeBeaconDirect("TaskManager", implX, "v4") on the satellite as an emergency local fix, which succeeds and registers v4. 3. The original Hyperlane message finally arrives and handle() calls upgradeBeacon("TaskManager", implX, "v4") → beacon.implementation()==implX so SameImplementation reverts (or VersionExists if impl differs). 4. handle() reverts; Hyperlane keeps the message pending and every retry reverts identically — the cross-chain path for that (type,version) is dead.
recommendation: Wrap the upgradeBeacon call in handle() in try/catch and emit a failure event (or no-op) on SameImplementation/VersionExists so the message is consumed rather than stuck, OR make upgradeBeacon idempotent (skip instead of revert when the beacon already targets newImpl and the version already maps to it). Prefer consuming the message and emitting UpgradeSkipped.
exploitReasoning: The code-level facts are accurate. PoaManagerSatellite.handle() (src/crosschain/PoaManagerSatellite.sol:69) calls poaManager.upgradeBeacon(typeName, newImpl, version) with no try/catch. PoaManager.upgradeBeacon (src/PoaManager.sol:99) reverts SameImplementation when beacon.implementation()==newImpl, and registry.registerImplementation (src/ImplementationRegistry.sol:80) reverts VersionExists when (typeId,vId) already stored. Because upgradeBeacon calls registry.registerImplementation BEFORE beacon.upgradeTo (PoaManager.sol:102-103), a version-string collision reverts the whole handle() deterministically. Test testHandleUpgradeWithSameImplReverts (test/PoaManagerSatellite.t.sol:284-292) confirms handle() reverts on same-impl. A Hyperlane handle() that reverts stays undelivered and re-reverts identically on every retry, so 'the message reverts forever' is mechanically true. HOWEVER the impact is far smaller than 'medium correctness bug': in the SameImplementation case the beacon ALREADY points at newImpl, so the stuck message is a pure no-op — the intended end-state is already achieved and nothing is lost. In the VersionExists-same-impl case (the exact scenario given, where upgradeBeaconDirect at line 115 pre-registered v4→implX) the beacon is likewise already at implX. The only genuinely-conflicting case (same version string, different impl) is a privileged operator mistake — precisely the version-string collision the repo's own version-probing ritual exists to prevent. Critically, a full unilateral recovery path exists: the satellite owner can call upgradeBeaconDirect(typeName, newImpl, freshVersion) (line 115) to reach any implementation locally at any time, independent of the cross-chain message. There is no permanent lock, no lost governance capability, and no unprivileged actor. Residual cost is a burned Hyperlane fee plus needing a fresh version string on re-dispatch.
safetyReasoning: Code claims verify exactly. PoaManagerSatellite.handle() at line 69 calls `poaManager.upgradeBeacon(typeName, newImpl, version)` with no try/catch. PoaManager.upgradeBeacon reverts `SameImplementation` (PoaManager.sol:99) when `beacon.implementation() == newImpl`, and calls `registry.registerImplementation` (line 102) which reverts `VersionExists` (ImplementationRegistry.sol:80) when `l._impls[tId][vId] != address(0)`. The test suite explicitly locks in this behavior: `testHandleUpgradeWithSameImplReverts` (PoaManagerSatellite.t.sol:284-292) asserts `handle()` reverts with `PoaManager.SameImplementation.selector`. Because these reverts are deterministic and state-dependent, once the target (type,version)/impl state exists on the satellite, every Hyperlane `process()` retry of the same message body reverts identically — the message can never be delivered. There is no idempotency guard, no try/catch, and no operator function to clear or skip a stuck message, so the finding's core mechanism stands. I found no mitigation in the code that refutes it.

title: updateImplRegistry does not verify PoaManager owns the new registry, allowing all future upgrades/type-adds to be bricked
description: updateImplRegistry only rejects address(0); it swaps the registry pointer to any non-zero address. Both addContractType (line 86) and upgradeBeacon (line 102) call registry.registerImplementation, which is onlyOwner on the registry (must be PoaManager). If the pointer is moved to a registry that PoaManager does not own (e.g. a fresh ImplementationRegistry whose owner is still the deployer, or a wrong/foreign address), every subsequent upgradeBeacon reverts on the registry's onlyOwner check, and addContractType reverts too (its guard only skips when registry==address(0), not when the call would revert).
impact: A single owner mistake (pointing at a not-yet-transferred or wrong registry) silently disables the entire upgrade + type-registration path until updateImplRegistry is called again with a correctly-owned registry. Combined with the cross-chain path this can wedge a satellite until manually corrected.
scenario: 1. Owner deploys a new ImplementationRegistry proxy but forgets to transferOwnership to PoaManager. 2. Owner calls updateImplRegistry(newReg). 3. Owner calls upgradeBeacon("TaskManager", impl, "v4") → registry.registerImplementation reverts OwnableUnauthorizedAccount because PoaManager is not the registry owner. 4. All upgrades/type-adds are blocked; the beacon upgrade never happens.
recommendation: In updateImplRegistry, sanity-check the new registry: require ImplementationRegistry(registryAddr).owner() == address(this) (try/catch to also reject non-registry addresses), or at minimum document that ownership must be transferred first. This turns a silent brick into an explicit revert at configuration time.
exploitReasoning: The mechanics described are accurate. `updateImplRegistry` (src/PoaManager.sol:41-46) validates only `registryAddr == address(0)` and swaps the pointer to any non-zero address. `upgradeBeacon` (line 102) unconditionally calls `registry.registerImplementation(...)`, and `addContractType` (lines 85-86) calls it whenever `registry != address(0)`. `registerImplementation` in ImplementationRegistry.sol:70-73 is `onlyOwner` (OwnableUpgradeable, owner set at initialize). So if the owner points PoaManager at a registry it does not own, every subsequent `upgradeBeacon`/`addContractType` reverts `OwnableUnauthorizedAccount`. HOWEVER, the impact is far smaller than "brick": (1) the ONLY actor who can cause this is the trusted `onlyOwner` — no unprivileged reachability; (2) it is fully and trivially reversible: `updateImplRegistry` (line 41) is itself `onlyOwner` and has NO dependency on the registry being valid/owned, so the owner just calls it again with a correctly-owned registry, or transfers the misconfigured registry's ownership to PoaManager; (3) no funds lost, no governance takeover, and existing beacons/proxies keep functioning normally (beacon.implementation() is untouched). It is a self-inflicted, self-healing config error, not a permanent lock.
safetyReasoning: The two mechanical claims are code-accurate. PoaManager.updateImplRegistry (src/PoaManager.sol:41-46) only rejects address(0) — it reassigns `registry` to any non-zero address with no verification that PoaManager owns the target. ImplementationRegistry.registerImplementation is `onlyOwner` (src/ImplementationRegistry.sol:70-73, OwnableUpgradeable), so if PoaManager is not the registry's owner, upgradeBeacon's call at PoaManager.sol:102 and addContractType's call at line 86 both revert (addContractType's guard at line 85 only skips the call when registry==address(0), not when the call would revert). So a bad pointer does block future upgradeBeacon/addContractType. However, the finding's severity/impact framing is overstated. This is a purely owner-inflicted misconfiguration: updateImplRegistry, upgradeBeacon, and addContractType are all `onlyOwner`, so no unprivileged actor can trigger or exploit it. It is fully and trivially reversible — updateImplRegistry never calls into the registry (it only swaps the storage pointer), so the owner recovers with a single onlyOwner call re-pointing to a correctly-owned registry. No funds are at risk, existing beacons and deployed proxies are unaffected (only future registrations fail), and there is no permanent lock. The claimed "bricks/wedges until corrected" is technically true but the correction is one owner transaction.

title: registerHatsTree leaves stale role-hat entries when re-registered with a shorter array
description: registerHatsTree writes role hats into the sparse mapping l.roleHatOf[orgId][i] for i in [0, roleHatIds.length) but never clears indices >= roleHatIds.length that were written by a previous call. The mapping has no length tracking and no truncation. If the executor (post-bootstrap governance path) or the owner (bootstrap path) calls registerHatsTree a second time with a shorter roleHatIds array, the trailing indices from the first call remain in storage. RoleResolver.resolveRoleHats / resolveRoleBitmap (src/libs/RoleResolver.sol:28,57) resolve role indices to hat IDs by reading getRoleHat(orgId, roleIndex) with no awareness of how many roles actually exist, so a stale index silently resolves to an old, possibly revoked hat ID.
impact: A re-registered hats tree can leave dangling role->hat mappings that downstream role resolution (used when granting permissions during redeploys/bootstrap of new modules) reads as authoritative, granting authority to a hat that governance intended to remove. Also poisons the subgraph's role-hat view.
scenario: 1. Org deployed with roleHatIds = [h0,h1,h2,h3] (4 roles). 2. Governance later reorganizes to 2 roles and the executor calls registerHatsTree(orgId, topHat, [h0',h1']). 3. roleHatOf[orgId][0]=h0', [1]=h1' are updated, but [2]=h2 and [3]=h3 persist. 4. A later call that resolves role index 2 or 3 (e.g. resolveRoleBitmap over a bitmap that still references bit 2/3, or a subgraph reading getRoleHat(2)) returns the stale h2/h3, granting or displaying authority for a hat governance meant to drop.
recommendation: Track the number of registered role hats per org (e.g. store roleHatCount[orgId]) and either (a) reject re-registration, (b) clear indices from the new length up to the old count, or (c) have getRoleHat/resolvers bound reads to the stored count. At minimum, document that registerHatsTree is single-shot and add a guard preventing a second call.
exploitReasoning: The code observation is accurate but the claimed on-chain impact is not reachable. OrgRegistry.sol:461-463 writes only indices [0, roleHatIds.length) and never clears trailing indices, and there is no length tracking; the executor path (line 456) has no bootstrap gate, so the executor CAN re-call registerHatsTree with a shorter array, leaving stale entries in l.roleHatOf. That much is real. However, the ONLY production consumers of getRoleHat via RoleResolver.resolveRoleBitmap/resolveRoleHats are the three deploy factories (AccessFactory.sol:93,122,126; GovernanceFactory.sol:245,275,279; ModulesFactory.sol:89,115,119). All three run exclusively inside OrgDeployer._deployFullOrgInternal, in the SAME transaction as the single registerHatsTree call (OrgDeployer.sol:414), and only for a freshly-created org — OrgDeployer reverts OrgExistsMismatch (OrgDeployer.sol:396-400) if the org already exists, so it can never re-deploy modules against a twice-written hats tree. The finding's "redeploys/bootstrap of new modules" path that re-resolves roles post-deploy does not exist in the codebase. The only way to produce stale entries is a direct governance (executor) call to registerHatsTree, but NO on-chain contract reads getRoleHat afterward — resolution is deploy-time only. The stale entry sits inert; module permissions (eligibility, hat-minter auth, voting hats) are set from resolved hats at deploy time, not re-derived from roleHatOf later. The only readers of a stale getRoleHat(orgId, 2/3) are off-chain: the subgraph and the RunOrgActions*.s.sol scripts (which read fixed indices 0-3).
safetyReasoning: The code-level claim is factually correct: registerHatsTree (OrgRegistry.sol:461-463) writes l.roleHatOf[orgId][i] for i in [0, roleHatIds.length) and never clears indices >= roleHatIds.length, and the mapping has no length tracking. RoleResolver.resolveRoleHats/resolveRoleBitmap (RoleResolver.sol:28,57) read getRoleHat for arbitrary indices with no awareness of the real role count. So a shorter re-registration would leave stale trailing entries readable. HOWEVER, the claimed *impact* (granting authority to a hat governance meant to remove) does not hold against the actual code paths: (1) The only on-chain caller of registerHatsTree is OrgDeployer.sol:414, executed exactly once during the atomic deployFullOrg of a NEW org — the org is created via createOrgBootstrap in the same tx (line 397) and deployFullOrg reverts OrgExistsMismatch (line 399) for an existing org, so OrgDeployer never re-registers. (2) The resolvers are consumed ONLY by GovernanceFactory/ModulesFactory/AccessFactory, which run ONLY inside that same atomic deploy tx, immediately after registerHatsTree, against a freshly-written mapping with zero stale entries. (3) The finding's scenario requires the executor to re-call registerHatsTree post-bootstrap (access control at lines 450-458 does permit this) AND a downstream on-chain consumer to re-resolve roles into a permission grant — but no such re-resolving/redeploy path exists; module redeploys go through OrgDeployer which won't touch an existing org. Thus no unprivileged actor, and no privileged path either, can turn a stale index into an on-chain authority grant. The only real residual effect is off-chain: getRoleHat is read by scripts (RunOrgActions.s.sol:301-304, fixed indices 0-3) and the subgraph, which could display a stale hat if an executor ever re-registers with a shorter array.

title: Executor (and bootstrap owner) can register arbitrary unvalidated proxy/beacon module mappings that off-chain consumers trust
description: registerOrgContract accepts any proxy, beacon, and moduleOwner addresses with only non-zero validation; it never checks that proxy is actually a BeaconProxy pointing at beacon, that beacon is a legitimate SwitchableBeacon, or that the code at proxy is a known module type. The executor path (msg.sender == o.executor) has no bootstrap restriction, so after deployment the org's governance can register any new typeId -> arbitrary-address mapping. None of these mappings are consumed on-chain within src/ (grep shows no on-chain readers of proxyOf/getOrgContract/getContractBeacon/isAutoUpgrade); they are consumed off-chain by the subgraph, frontend, and paymaster tooling, which treat the registry as the canonical (orgId -> module address) source of truth.
impact: A malicious or compromised governance proposal (or a buggy factory during bootstrap) can seed the canonical registry with a rogue address under a well-known typeId (e.g. a fake ParticipationToken or TaskManager) that off-chain systems and users then trust and interact with. Existing types cannot be clobbered (TypeTaken guard), so this is additive poisoning of the namespace rather than overwrite.
scenario: 1. Org is live; executor is the DAO voting contract. 2. Attacker passes a governance proposal that calls registerOrgContract(orgId, keccak256('SomeNewModule'), rogueAddr, rogueBeacon, false, attacker, false). 3. The registry now returns rogueAddr for that typeId. 4. Subgraph indexes ContractRegistered and surfaces rogueAddr as the org's module; users/paymaster tooling interact with the attacker-controlled contract.
recommendation: This is partly inherent to a governance-writable registry, but robustness would improve by validating that beacon has code, that proxy's beacon slot (EIP-1967) matches beacon, and/or restricting post-bootstrap type registration to a curated set of known typeIds. At minimum document that off-chain consumers must not treat arbitrary typeIds as trusted module types without on-chain verification.
exploitReasoning: The mechanical claims are accurate against src/OrgRegistry.sol. registerOrgContract (264-308): the executor branch at lines 278/284-286 (`callerIsExecutor = o.executor != 0 && msg.sender == o.executor`) has NO bootstrap gate — only the owner branch (280-283) is restricted to bootstrap. Validation at 288-291 is limited to non-zero checks on typeId/proxy/beacon/moduleOwner plus a `TypeTaken` guard (291). There is no BeaconProxy/SwitchableBeacon/code-identity verification, so an executor can register any new typeId -> arbitrary (proxy,beacon,owner) tuple. I confirmed the on-chain-consumption claim by grep: no contract under src/ reads proxyOf/getOrgContract/getContractBeacon/isAutoUpgrade — only OrgDeployer.sol writes them (lines 758, 789), and all readers live in script/ and test/ (off-chain/tooling). The registry is a pure directory; batchRegisterOrgContracts (318-381) shares the identical caller logic. So the described additive namespace-poisoning is technically reachable.
safetyReasoning: The finding's factual claims check out against the real code. registerOrgContract (lines 264-308) and batchRegisterOrgContracts (318-381) validate only non-zero (lines 288-290, 349-354): they never verify that `proxy` is a BeaconProxy pointing at `beacon`, that `beacon` is a SwitchableBeacon, or that code at `proxy` is a known module type. The executor path (lines 278, 284) has no bootstrap gate — after bootstrap ends, `msg.sender == o.executor` can register any new typeId->address mapping. I confirmed via grep that NO on-chain code in src/ reads proxyOf/getOrgContract/getContractBeacon/isAutoUpgrade (the only callers of registerOrgContract are OrgDeployer.sol:758/789, which forward from the trusted factories). So these mappings are purely off-chain-consumed indexing data. However, two strong bounds cap the impact: (1) the TypeTaken guard (line 291, 357) makes existing well-known slots (ParticipationToken, TaskManager, etc.) unclobberable for a live org whose real modules are already registered and bootstrap-locked — so an attacker cannot impersonate a real module, only add new/unknown typeIds; (2) the only unprivileged-relative-to-normal path is the executor, which requires a fully-passed governance proposal — an actor that already controls the Executor has strictly greater powers (it IS the DAO execution layer) and gains nothing meaningful from poisoning an off-chain registry hint. There is zero on-chain fund/control risk.

title: handle() has no replay/dedup and dispatch fee is unquoted, but a single reverting satellite bricks the whole broadcast
description: _broadcast loops over all active satellites and calls mailbox.dispatch{value: fee}. The fee is computed as msg.value/count rather than from a Hyperlane quoteDispatch, so if the owner underpays, dispatch reverts on the underlying IGP and the entire transaction reverts, meaning no satellite receives the message and the local upgrade/adminCall is rolled back too (upgradeBeaconCrossChain runs poaManager.upgradeBeacon first in the same tx). More importantly, if any single active satellite's dispatch reverts (e.g., mailbox rejects a domain, or one satellite entry is misconfigured), the whole loop reverts and NO cross-chain upgrade can proceed until the bad satellite is removed. Because activeSatelliteCount can be large and fee = msg.value/count is integer-divided, an owner who registered N satellites but only funded for N-1 quotes will have all upgrades blocked. This is availability/robustness, not fund loss, and it is owner-triggered, hence medium.
impact: A single misconfigured or unreachable satellite domain blocks all cross-chain beacon upgrades and admin calls protocol-wide until an owner tx removes it. Combined with the fact that the local upgrade is executed before dispatch, a dispatch revert also blocks the intended home-chain upgrade.
scenario: 1. Owner registers satellites for domains 100 (Gnosis) and 8453 (Base). 2. The Base Hyperlane IGP requires a higher fee than 100. 3. Owner calls upgradeBeaconCrossChain with msg.value split evenly; the Gnosis dispatch succeeds but the Base dispatch reverts on underpayment. 4. The whole tx reverts; the home-chain beacon is not upgraded and no message is sent. Owner must guess correct per-domain fees or remove Base to make any progress.
recommendation: Quote each satellite's fee via IMailbox.quoteDispatch and dispatch the exact quoted amount per satellite (with per-satellite fee accounting), and/or make one satellite's dispatch failure non-fatal (try/catch, emit a failure event) so a single bad domain cannot block all upgrades. Consider decoupling the local upgrade from the broadcast so home-chain upgrades are not blocked by remote fee issues.
exploitReasoning:
The code mechanics the finding describes are all real. In `_broadcast` (PoaManagerHub.sol:193-208), `fee = msg.value / count` (line 196) is a flat even split, NOT a per-domain Hyperlane `quoteDispatch` — IHyperlane.sol only exposes `dispatch`, no quote function. The loop (lines 198-206) calls `mailbox.dispatch{value: fee}` for every active satellite, so if any single dispatch reverts (underpayment on that domain's IGP, mailbox rejecting a domain, misconfigured entry), the whole loop and thus the whole transaction reverts. Because `upgradeBeaconCrossChain` runs `poaManager.upgradeBeacon(...)` at line 71 BEFORE `_broadcast` at line 73 (same for `addContractTypeCrossChain` line 94→96 and `adminCallCrossChain` line 115→117), a dispatch revert also rolls back the intended home-chain state change. So the scenario (satellites for domains with differing IGP fees + even split → cheaper domain succeeds in isolation but the expensive one reverts the whole tx) is a real code path.

HOWEVER the severity is overstated. Every entry point is `onlyOwner` (lines 67, 91, 112) and the Hub owner is trusted governance (Executor / Hudson EOA per project docs), never an unprivileged actor — so there is no attacker-triggered exploit. The 'block' is fully self-inflicted and self-recoverable by the same owner in one tx: `removeSatellite` (line 150) disables the bad domain, or the owner simply retries with more ETH (excess is refunded via `_refundExcess`, lines 212-218, and `withdrawETH` line 183 rescues stuck ETH — no fund loss). Critically, escape hatches exist for the home-chain action: `upgradeBeaconLocal` (line 77), `addContractType` (line 84), and `adminCall` (line 104) perform the local mutation with NO broadcast, so the home-chain upgrade is never permanently blocked — only cross-chain propagation is, and only until the owner removes/refunds. The finding's title also references 'handle() has no replay/dedup', but `handle()` lives on PoaManagerSatellite, not this cited file, so that portion is out of scope for the cited lines.
safetyReasoning: The code matches the finding exactly. In _broadcast (PoaManagerHub.sol:193-208): line 196 computes `uint256 fee = msg.value / count;` — a naive even split with no Hyperlane quoteDispatch, so underfunding causes the underlying IGP to revert. Lines 198-206 loop over ALL satellites calling `mailbox.dispatch{value: fee}(...)` with NO try/catch, so any single dispatch revert (underpayment, rejected/misconfigured domain) reverts the entire transaction — every other satellite dispatch is rolled back. Because the local mutation runs first — upgradeBeaconCrossChain calls poaManager.upgradeBeacon at line 71 before _broadcast at line 73 (same pattern for addContractTypeCrossChain L94/96 and adminCallCrossChain L115/117) — a dispatch revert also rolls back the intended home-chain upgrade. There is no per-satellite isolation, no fee quoting, and no dedup/replay guard on the receiving handle side either. So a single bad/underfunded satellite blocks ALL cross-chain upgrades until removed.

title: executeData uses expectedAmount (claimed amounts[0]) as the deposit amount rather than the actual available balance
description: The comment at 142 says 'Use the actual available amount (in case bridge delivered slightly more/less)', but the code sets amount = expectedAmount (the caller-supplied amounts[0]) after only checking available >= expectedAmount. If the bridge delivered MORE than amounts[0], the surplus is not deposited and is left in the relay balance (not tracked by totalFailedAmount), where the permissionless executeData issue (finding 1) or the owner emergencyRecover can later sweep it. If it delivered slightly less but the check passed because held recovery funds inflate the balance, this reinforces finding 1. The code does not do what its own comment claims.
impact: Bridge over-delivery leaves untracked surplus USDC in the relay that is not credited to the depositor and can be captured via the permissionless executeData path or by owner recovery.
scenario: 1. Bungee delivers 51 USDC but callData/amounts claims 50e6 due to accounting rounding. 2. executeData deposits exactly 50 for the user, leaving 1 USDC untracked in the relay. 3. That 1 USDC is now claimable by anyone via a follow-up executeData (finding 1) or by the owner via emergencyRecover.
recommendation: Either deposit the actual available amount as the comment states, or explicitly document that amounts[0] is authoritative and reconcile surplus handling; combined with fixing finding 1 this becomes low risk.
exploitReasoning: At src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:135-143, `expectedAmount = amounts[0]` (caller-supplied), line 140 only checks `available >= expectedAmount` (permitting `available > expectedAmount`), and line 143 sets `amount = expectedAmount` — NOT `available`. The comment at line 142 ("Use the actual available amount (in case bridge delivered slightly more/less)") directly contradicts the code, which always deposits the claimed amounts[0]. So on a bridge over-delivery, the surplus `available - expectedAmount` stays in the relay balance and is never added to `totalFailedAmount` (line 155 only tracks the on-failure path). That surplus is untracked and capturable: (a) owner `emergencyRecover` (line 317-327) passes its guard `balance - amount >= totalFailedAmount` for the surplus since it sits above totalFailedAmount; and (b) `executeData` (line 121-126) has no access control beyond `nonReentrant`, so any caller can supply `amounts[0] = surplus` with their own `params.depositor` and, since `available >= expectedAmount` holds, mint a ZKP2P deposit owned by the attacker from that surplus. The test suite (test/CashOutRelay.t.sol) never exercises `available > expectedAmount`: every _callExecuteData delivers exactly amounts[0] (e.g. lines 294, 593, 600, 612), so the mismatch is untested. That said, in the normal Bungee flow amounts[0] equals the delivered amount, so a true over-delivery is atypical; and using expectedAmount instead of `available` is actually the intended protection against crediting stale/pre-existing relay balances (comment at lines 137-138), so the behavior is defensible even though the line-142 comment is wrong. No normal user loses funds, and the leaked surplus is recoverable by the owner.
safetyReasoning:
The narrow factual claim is CONFIRMED: at src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:142 the comment says "Use the actual available amount (in case bridge delivered slightly more/less)" yet line 143 assigns `uint256 amount = expectedAmount;` (i.e. the caller-supplied amounts[0] from line 135), not `available` (computed line 139). So the code genuinely does not match its own comment. Compare the other two entry points that DO deposit the actual delivered amount: completeCashOut deposits `minted = balanceAfter - balanceBefore` (lines 238/243) and createDepositFromBalance deposits `available` (lines 264/268). Only executeData deviates.

However, the finding's *security impact* is overstated to the point of being largely refuted. (1) Using `expectedAmount` instead of `available` is the MORE defensive choice, not a bug that enables theft: if executeData used `available` as the comment suggests, ANY caller could sweep the entire untracked relay balance into a single deposit. By pinning to amounts[0] the contract limits the per-call amount, which is safer. (2) The "surplus captured via permissionless executeData" path is entirely a restatement of the separate finding 1 (executeData at line 126 has only `nonReentrant`, no access control); it is not an independent defect of the amount-selection line. testSecurity_AttackerCannotStealFailedDeposits (test lines 474-502) shows the `available = balance - totalFailedAmount` guard (lines 139-140) already blocks capture of *held recovery* funds. (3) The "owner emergencyRecover sweeps surplus" path is intended, explicitly-tested behavior: testSecurity_EmergencyRecoverCannotDrainUserFunds (lines 504-517) asserts "Owner recovers surplus" as correct — owner is a trusted party (controls upgrades via _authorizeUpgrade line 311, completeCashOut, createDepositFromBalance). (4) In the normal Bungee flow amounts[0] == delivered amount and there is no leftover balance, so available == expectedAmount and no legitimate depositor is under-credited.

title: CashOutRelay UUPS implementation is never disabled — attacker can initialize the impl and brick/hijack it via upgrade
description: CashOutRelay is a UUPS-upgradeable contract (`is Initializable, UUPSUpgradeable, ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable`) deployed behind an ERC1967Proxy (see script/cashout/DeployCashOutRelay.s.sol lines 43-47: `impl = new CashOutRelay(); new ERC1967Proxy(address(impl), initData)`). It has NO constructor and therefore never calls `_disableInitializers()`. It is the ONLY upgradeable contract in src/ missing this call — every other of the 17 upgradeable contracts has `constructor(){ _disableInitializers(); }`. This directly violates the project hard rule 'Every upgradeable contract constructor MUST call _disableInitializers()'. Because the implementation contract itself is left uninitialized, `initialize()` (line 299, only guarded by the `initializer` modifier) can be called by anyone directly on the implementation address, and `_authorizeUpgrade` (line 311) only checks `msg.sender == owner`.
impact: An attacker who takes over the bare implementation gains `owner`, then calls `upgradeToAndCall` on the implementation with a malicious logic contract. On chains without EIP-6780 semantics (or via a delegatecall to a destructive routine), this can selfdestruct / permanently corrupt the shared implementation, bricking the live proxy and freezing all USDC held for user cashouts and recovery (totalFailedAmount funds). Classic uninitialized-UUPS-implementation attack. It is deployed and actively upgraded (UpgradeCashOutRelay.s.sol exists) so the exposure is live.
scenario: 1. Team deploys via DeployCashOutRelay.s.sol: `impl = new CashOutRelay()` (uninitialized) + proxy. 2. Attacker sees the impl address on-chain and calls `impl.initialize(attackerEscrow, usdc, cctp, attacker)` directly — succeeds because the impl's `initializer` slot is fresh (never disabled). 3. Attacker is now `owner` of the implementation. 4. Attacker calls `impl.upgradeToAndCall(evilImpl, data)`; `_authorizeUpgrade` passes since msg.sender==owner. 5. evilImpl selfdestructs/guts the implementation → the ERC1967Proxy's delegatecalls now hit empty/hostile code, freezing all funds in the proxy.
recommendation: Add `/// @custom:oz-upgrades-unsafe-allow constructor` + `constructor() { _disableInitializers(); }` to CashOutRelay, matching every other upgradeable contract. Also add CashOutRelay to test/UpgradeSafety.t.sol's `...ImplCannotBeInitialized` suite so this regression is caught by CI.
exploitReasoning: The finding correctly observes that CashOutRelay (src/cashout/CashOutRelay.sol:20) is UUPS-upgradeable with no constructor, so `_disableInitializers()` is never called and `initialize()` (line 299, only `initializer`-guarded) is callable directly on the bare implementation. But the claimed impact chain — attacker becomes impl `owner`, then calls `upgradeToAndCall` to brick/selfdestruct the impl and freeze proxy funds — is blocked at step 4. `upgradeToAndCall` in the linked OZ v5 UUPSUpgradeable (lib/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/contracts/proxy/utils/UUPSUpgradeable.sol:92) carries the `onlyProxy` modifier, whose `_checkProxy()` (lines 102-108) reverts with `UUPSUnauthorizedCallContext()` whenever `address(this) == __self`, i.e. exactly when the function is called directly on the implementation rather than through a delegatecall. So even after an attacker calls `initialize()` on the impl and passes the `msg.sender == owner` check in `_authorizeUpgrade` (line 311), the outer `onlyProxy` guard reverts before `_authorizeUpgrade` runs — no upgrade, no selfdestruct. Additionally, this OZ version's proxy/UUPS code contains no selfdestruct at all (grep confirms none in lib/.../proxy/), so the "corrupt shared implementation" outcome is impossible via any standard upgrade. The implementation's storage is also fully separate from the ERC1967Proxy's storage (script/cashout/DeployCashOutRelay.s.sol:43-47), so initializing the impl never affects the live proxy or its held USDC. Value-moving functions the attacker could call on the impl (completeCashOut, createDepositFromBalance, emergencyRecover, withdrawETH) act on the impl's own empty balance.
safetyReasoning: The factual claims are all accurate. CashOutRelay.sol line 20 declares `contract CashOutRelay is Initializable, UUPSUpgradeable, ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable`. A grep for "constructor" in the file returns nothing — there is no constructor, so `_disableInitializers()` is never called. It is the ONLY upgradeable contract in src/ lacking this: all 17 others plus PaymasterHub (the other UUPS contract, PaymasterHub.sol:177) call `_disableInitializers()`. `initialize()` (line 299) is guarded only by the `initializer` modifier, and `_authorizeUpgrade` (lines 311-313) checks only `if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner();`. So an attacker can call `initialize()` directly on the bare implementation, become its `owner`, and call `upgradeToAndCall` on the implementation. This confirms the uninitialized-UUPS-implementation defect and violates the project hard rule 'Every upgradeable contract constructor MUST call _disableInitializers()'.
